Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 01

California mortgage brokerage and regulatory structure

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Explain the mortgage authority a California real estate broker license carries and what it does not cover.
  • Describe the mortgage loan originator endorsement, what triggers the requirement, and what it adds to a license.
  • Distinguish the DRE from the other regulators a mortgage transaction touches, and identify which answers which question.
  • Determine whether a given activity is licensed, exempt, or unlicensed, and identify what compensation does to the analysis.
  • Describe the broker's supervisory duty over mortgage activity and what a real supervision system contains.
  • Identify how consumer complaints and enforcement reach a mortgage broker and what a licensee does when contacted.

1. DRE real estate broker mortgage authority

1.1 What this course is about

Mortgage brokering is licensed activity, and in California it can be conducted under more than one licensing framework. This course addresses the activity as conducted by a real estate broker licensed by the Department of Real Estate, and by salespersons acting under such a broker.

That framing matters immediately, because the same functional activity — arranging a loan secured by real property — is conducted in California by firms licensed under different statutes, supervised by different regulators, subject to overlapping federal requirements.

A licensee who does not know which framework they operate under cannot answer a compliance question correctly, because the answer frequently depends on it.

1.2 The broker's mortgage authority

A California real estate broker license authorizes, among other activities, soliciting borrowers or lenders for, negotiating, arranging, and performing services in connection with loans secured by real property.

Two features of that authority are worth stating precisely at the start.

It is activity-based. The license authorizes the acts. It does not create a separate "mortgage license" — the same license that permits listing a house permits arranging a loan secured by one, subject to the additional requirements this lesson develops.

It carries the same supervisory structure. A salesperson performing mortgage activity does so for and under the responsible broker, exactly as in a sales transaction, and the brokerage is the party to the engagement.

1.3 What the authority does not include

Not includedWhere it belongs
Making loans as a lender under a lending statuteA lending license, where the activity requires one
Acting as an escrow holder outside an applicable exemptionEscrow licensure or an exemption
AppraisingAppraiser licensure or certification
Giving legal adviceCounsel
Giving tax adviceA tax professional
Servicing loans where servicing requires its own authorityThe applicable framework

The recurring error is the last several. A mortgage broker sits at the center of a transaction where legal, tax, appraisal, and title questions all arrive, and the temptation to answer them is constant. Section 3 develops the routing.

1.4 Broker and salesperson, restated for this context

The relationship from the Principles course applies without modification:

  • A broker may conduct mortgage activity independently and may employ salespersons.
  • A salesperson may conduct it only for and under a responsible broker, and may accept compensation for licensed activity only from that broker.
  • The brokerage is the party to the engagement with the borrower.
  • A salesperson may not contract in her own name for licensed mortgage activity.

1.5 Why the DRE framework exists for mortgage activity

The consumer-protection logic is the same as in a sales transaction and is worth being explicit about, because it explains the rules that follow:

  • Consumers transact infrequently, in a market with imperfect information, on the largest obligation most of them will incur.
  • The broker is accountable for the salesperson, because the consumer deals with an individual and the accountable party must be one with the resources and duty to supervise.
  • Trust fund rules are strict, because the money is not the licensee's.
  • Advertising is regulated, because a consumer cannot evaluate a claim about terms they have not received.
  • Records are retained, because a complaint about a loan can arrive long after it funded.

1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what a DRE broker license authorizes in mortgage activity and name four things it does not cover.

2. MLO endorsement orientation

2.1 What the endorsement is

A licensee who acts as a mortgage loan originator must hold an MLO license endorsement on their DRE license, and must be registered through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System and Registry.

This is an endorsement on the existing license, not a separate license. The underlying broker or salesperson license remains the license; the endorsement records that the licensee is authorized to act as an MLO.

2.2 What triggers the requirement

In outline, a person acts as a mortgage loan originator when they, for compensation or gain or in the expectation of it:

  • Take a residential mortgage loan application, or
  • Offer or negotiate terms of a residential mortgage loan.

Two elements do the work, and both must be present: the activity, and the compensation or expectation of it.

"Residential mortgage loan" is the scope limiter. The endorsement requirement is tied to consumer residential lending, which is why business-purpose and certain commercial transactions are analyzed differently — a distinction Lesson 12 develops in detail and that licensees regularly get wrong in both directions.

2.3 What the endorsement requires

The endorsement framework, which implements the federal SAFE Act, generally involves:

RequirementIn outline
Pre-licensing educationApproved coursework
ExaminationA national test with content on federal and state law
Background and credit reviewFingerprints and a review of financial responsibility and character
NMLS registrationA unique identifier assigned to the individual
Continuing educationAnnual, to maintain the endorsement
Annual renewalSeparate from the underlying license renewal

Two points licensees miss. The unique identifier follows the individual, not the employer, and it must appear on communications and advertising as required. And the endorsement renews on its own cycle — a licensee whose broker license is current but whose endorsement lapsed is not authorized to originate.

2.4 The individual and the company

Both levels exist. The individual holds the endorsement and the unique identifier. The company — here, the brokerage — has its own registration and identifier.

Advertising and communications carry both identifiers as required, which is why a compliant mortgage advertisement carries more identification than a compliant sales advertisement.

2.5 What the endorsement does not do

  • It does not expand what the underlying license authorizes. A salesperson with an endorsement is still a salesperson acting under a broker.
  • It does not substitute for the underlying license. Both must be current.
  • It does not make the licensee a lender.
  • It does not authorize legal or tax advice.

2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what triggers the MLO requirement, name what the endorsement involves, and explain the relationship between the endorsement and the underlying license.

3. DRE and other regulator boundaries

3.1 The regulators a mortgage transaction touches

A single residential mortgage transaction can involve the following, and a licensee should be able to say which answers which question.

BodyWhat it addresses
Department of Real EstateThe real estate broker license, its mortgage activity, MLO endorsements on DRE licenses, trust funds, advertising, supervision, discipline
Department of Financial Protection and InnovationFirms licensed under California's lending and financing statutes, and certain other financial services
NMLSThe registry through which MLO licensing and registration is administered across states
Consumer Financial Protection BureauFederal consumer financial law — disclosure, servicing, and related rules
HUDFederal housing programs and fair housing enforcement
Federal banking regulatorsDepository institutions and their subsidiaries
California Civil Rights DepartmentState housing discrimination enforcement
Bureau of Real Estate AppraisersAppraiser licensing and certification
Local jurisdictionsLand use, permits, and local ordinances

3.2 The California licensing frameworks, in outline

The point most often confused: the same functional activity is conducted in California under more than one licensing framework.

A firm arranging residential mortgage loans may operate under a DRE real estate broker license, or under a license issued by the DFPI pursuant to California's residential mortgage lending or finance lending statutes.

The frameworks differ in what they authorize, what they require, how compensation and fees are treated, and which regulator examines the firm.

For a licensee, the practical rule is narrow and important: know which license your firm holds, and do not import a rule you learned from a different framework. A requirement that applies to a DFPI-licensed lender may not apply to a DRE broker, and vice versa — and a licensee who answers a compliance question from the wrong framework has answered confidently and wrongly.

3.3 Federal law applies across frameworks

The federal consumer mortgage statutes taken up in Lesson 07 — Truth in Lending, RESPA, ECOA, HMDA, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the SAFE Act framework — apply according to their own terms rather than by reference to the state license held.

This is why the federal material is a separate lesson. A licensee cannot reason from "we're a DRE broker" to a conclusion about a federal disclosure obligation.

3.4 The routing discipline

The single most useful skill in this section is knowing where a question goes.

QuestionGoes to
"Is this activity licensed?"The licensing framework, and where genuinely unclear, counsel
"What must this disclosure say and when?"The federal rule and the firm's compliance function
"Can we charge this fee?"The applicable framework and compliance — not industry custom
"Is this property worth enough?"The appraiser, through the proper channel
"Does the borrower have good title?"Title, through escrow
"Can the borrower cancel?"Counsel
"What will this do to the borrower's taxes?"A tax professional
"Should the borrower take this program?"A suitability discussion the licensee may hold — and never a legal or tax recommendation

3.5 The standard a licensee actually applies

Would answering require a legal conclusion, a tax conclusion, a valuation, or an underwriting decision I am not authorized to make? If yes, route it.

Experience does not extend the scope of a license. A licensee with twenty years of origination experience is no more entitled to tell a borrower whether they may rescind than one with two weeks.

3.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the regulators a mortgage transaction touches, explain why "we're a DRE broker" does not answer a federal question, and route a set of questions correctly.

4. Licensed and exempt activity

4.1 The analysis

Whether a person needs a license turns on what they do and whether compensation is involved or expected — not on the title they use.

Activity that is licensed in the mortgage context includes soliciting borrowers or lenders, negotiating or offering terms, taking a residential mortgage loan application, arranging loans secured by real property, and performing services in connection with such loans, where done for another for compensation or its expectation.

4.2 The title is not the test

A person who performs licensed activity does not escape the requirement by being called a loan coordinator, transaction assistant, marketing associate, or consultant.

This matters because mortgage operations are staffed with people whose roles sit close to the line:

RoleGenerally administrativeCrosses into licensed activity
ProcessorCollecting documents, ordering third-party reports, tracking conditionsDiscussing terms with the borrower, negotiating, advising on program choice
AssistantScheduling, data entry, sending formsTaking the application, quoting rates, soliciting
Marketing staffProducing materials under approvalSoliciting borrowers, discussing terms in response
Referral sourceMentioning the firmBeing paid for producing borrowers

The last row is the recurring compliance failure, and it appears in Lesson 09 again from the federal side: paying an unlicensed person for producing loans is both an unlicensed activity problem and, where a settlement service referral is involved, a separate federal prohibition that disclosure does not cure.

4.3 Exemptions

Exemptions exist and are narrow. They can turn on the nature of the entity, the nature of the transaction, the number of transactions, or the purpose of the loan.

Three disciplines about exemptions:

  1. An exemption is a legal conclusion. Whether one applies to a particular arrangement is a question for counsel and the firm's compliance function, not for an originator in a conversation with a prospect.
  2. A federal exemption is not a state exemption, and vice versa. The analyses are separate.
  3. "We're exempt" is a reason to escalate, not a reason to proceed.

4.4 The business-purpose distinction

The distinction generating the most misapplied exemptions in mortgage practice, and Lesson 12 develops it fully.

Consumer residential mortgage requirements — including the MLO endorsement requirement and much of the federal disclosure regime — attach to consumer-purpose loans secured by a dwelling. Loans made primarily for a business purpose are treated differently.

Two errors, running in opposite directions:

  • Treating a consumer loan as business-purpose because the borrower signed a statement saying so, or because the property is a rental. The determination is based on the actual purpose and the facts, not on a certification the borrower was handed.
  • Treating every investment property loan as exempt from everything, which sweeps in requirements that still apply.

A borrower's signature on a business-purpose certification does not make a loan business-purpose. The certification records the borrower's statement; it does not establish the fact, and a file assembled around a certification that the surrounding facts contradict is a file with a problem in it.

4.5 Compensation and the expectation of it

Compensation is what converts assistance into licensed activity, and it is defined broadly — money, but also things of value, referral arrangements, and reciprocal benefits.

An arrangement structured to avoid the word "compensation" while delivering value for producing loans is a compensation arrangement. That analysis belongs to compliance and counsel, and an originator's role is to recognize the pattern and escalate rather than to assess whether the structure works.

4.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to determine whether an activity is licensed, explain why a title does not resolve it, and state what a business-purpose certification does and does not establish.

5. Broker supervision

5.1 The duty

The responsible broker must exercise reasonable supervision over the licensed activities conducted under the license. In mortgage activity, this reaches origination, disclosure delivery, advertising, fee handling, trust funds, and records.

Supervision is an affirmative duty discharged by a system, not by a manual.

5.2 What a real system contains

ElementWhat it does
Written policiesState what the firm requires, in terms a licensee can follow
File reviewClose enough in time to catch a problem before the loan closes
Disclosure trackingConfirms what was delivered, to whom, when, and by what method
Advertising reviewBefore publication, including identifiers and rate claims
Fee and compensation controlsSo charges match what was disclosed and what is permitted
Trust fund controlsIncluding reconciliation, where the firm handles trust funds
TrainingParticularly for new licensees and on rule changes
A usable escalation pathSo a problem raised is a problem addressed
Vendor oversightFor third parties acting on the firm's behalf
Complaint handlingA defined route, and a record

A policy nobody follows is not supervision, and it is not a defense for anyone — not for the broker who wrote it and not for the licensee who departed from it.

5.3 Why mortgage supervision is harder than sales supervision

Three structural features:

The timelines are compressed and the deadlines are legal. Disclosure timing rules attach consequences to dates, and a missed delivery is not a service failure but a compliance failure.

Much of the work is invisible to the client. A borrower cannot evaluate whether an application was accurately completed or whether a fee was properly disclosed.

The volume is transactional. A defect in a process repeats on every file until someone notices — which is the property management lesson from the Principles course in a different setting.

5.4 Supervision from the receiving end

Licensees encounter supervision failures from below, and the responses matter:

SituationResponse
A manager tells you to omit or alter something on an applicationRefuse. Escalate to the responsible broker. The instruction does not protect you
Office practice deviates from the written policyRaise it; a policy nobody follows protects no one
You are asked to originate a product you do not understandSay so in writing and ask for training or reassignment
A file is submitted with information you know to be inaccurateEscalate. Do not sign or transmit it

Following an improper instruction and documenting that it came from someone else does not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.

5.5 Independent contractor status changes nothing

Many originators are compensated as independent contractors. That characterization addresses the tax and compensation relationship. It does not reduce the broker's supervisory duty or the licensee's obligation to act under the broker.

5.6 The records are the brokerage's

Loan files, disclosures, communications, and trust fund records belong to the brokerage, and the responsible broker answers for them whoever created them.

A licensee leaving a firm may not unilaterally take files. What may be taken is governed by firm policy and by client direction — a question that should be settled in writing in the policy long before anyone departs.

5.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to describe a real supervision system, explain why mortgage supervision is structurally harder, and state the correct response to an improper instruction.

6. Consumer complaint and enforcement context

6.1 How a matter reaches a regulator

Complaints arrive from borrowers, from other participants in a transaction, from other licensees, and from a regulator's own examination or data review.

A licensee should understand that the routes are plural. A file with a defect is not safe because the borrower is satisfied — an examination, a data submission, or an unrelated complaint can surface it.

6.2 What produces enforcement in mortgage practice

CategoryTypical conduct
Misrepresentation to a borrowerTerms, rates, costs, or what a disclosure means
Misrepresentation to a lenderIncome, occupancy, assets, or the source of funds
Unlicensed activityOriginating without an endorsement, or paying an unlicensed person
Trust fund violationsCommingling, conversion, shortages, inadequate records
Advance fee violationsCollecting a fee in advance without meeting the applicable requirements
Advertising violationsMissing identifiers, unsupported rate or terms claims, misleading comparisons
Disclosure failuresLate, missing, or inaccurate required disclosures
Compensation violationsProhibited arrangements, undisclosed compensation, referral payments
Fair lending violationsDiscrimination in any aspect of a credit transaction
Failure to superviseA broker who did not review, enforce, or notice
FalsificationBackdating, altering, or creating records

Most of these do not require anyone to have set out to defraud. Late disclosures, inaccurate applications assembled carelessly, and inadequate records are the ordinary cases.

6.3 The one that ends careers

Everything on that list is survivable — errors, complaints, findings, even discipline — provided the licensee's conduct in response was honest.

Falsifying the record is not. Creating a document after the fact and dating it to match, altering an executed document, deleting records that reflect badly, or removing surrounding documents so an inconsistency does not show converts a compliance problem into a question about integrity.

A documented gap is survivable. A manufactured document ends a career.

Corrections are made visibly, with the original preserved and the change attributable. A record that can be silently altered is not a record.

6.4 When a regulator makes contact

Notify the broker immediately. Preserve records. Do not respond independently or informally.

Cooperation is expected. Improvised cooperation without review is where licensees make statements they cannot support — and in a mortgage file, a statement about what was disclosed and when can be checked against the file within minutes.

6.5 Responding to a borrower complaint

The first response frequently determines whether the matter resolves or escalates:

  1. Acknowledge promptly. Silence reads as evasion.
  2. Notify the broker immediately.
  3. Preserve everything — the file, the disclosures as delivered, communications, drafts, texts, and the advertising as it ran.
  4. Respond factually, without admitting or denying liability before the file has been reviewed.
  5. Do not offer a fee reduction or credit on your own initiative.
  6. Report to the carrier where the matter could become a claim.

Deleting a record that reflects poorly is far worse than the record. It is generally discoverable anyway, and it changes the subject from professional judgment to integrity.

6.6 What to report to the broker, promptly

Any error affecting a borrower's decision or a loan's terms; any borrower dissatisfaction that could become a complaint; any allegation of misrepresentation or discrimination; any contact from counsel or a regulator; any suspected fraud; any wire fraud incident or near-miss; any request to alter, backdate, or omit anything; and any instruction you declined to follow.

The bias should be toward reporting. A report that turns out unnecessary costs a conversation. An unreported matter that becomes a claim costs the coverage and the credibility.

6.7 The record is the defense

In a mortgage file, nearly every question a regulator or a borrower asks is answerable from documents: what was disclosed, to whom, when, by what method; what the borrower was told; what the file contained when the decision was made; what was verified and how.

The test is reconstructability: could a person who was not there determine what happened, when, and on what basis?

That test governs the rest of this course.

6.8 A worked regulatory boundary problem

A DRE-licensed real estate broker operating a mortgage brokerage is presented with six proposed activities in one week. For each, the questions are the ones this lesson has been building: what authority does it require, whose framework governs, and who supervises it?

1. Arranging a residential purchase loan for a consumer with third-party lenders. Within the broker's mortgage authority, and Section 2's endorsement requirement attaches to the individual performing the activity. Ordinary, and the file is built accordingly.

2. Making a loan with the brokerage's own funds. A different capacity — principal rather than agent — with different disclosure consequences and a different analysis under Section 3's regulator boundaries. The characterization is not the brokerage's to choose after the fact; it follows from what actually happened.

3. Soliciting private individuals to fund loans the brokerage arranges. This engages frameworks beyond the ones governing the borrower side, and the question of what may be offered, to whom, and with what disclosure is not answered by holding a real estate broker license. Route to counsel before anything is offered.

4. An unlicensed assistant taking applications by telephone "just to gather the information." Section 4's boundary. Taking a residential mortgage loan application is the activity the endorsement framework exists for, and calling it information gathering does not change what occurred. The correct answer is that it does not happen.

5. A referral arrangement with a real estate brokerage that sends borrowers, paid per closed loan. Two separate questions, and Section 3's boundaries do not answer both. Whether the payment is permissible at all comes first; whether it is disclosed comes second, and disclosure does not cure a prohibited payment. Route it.

6. Servicing the loans the brokerage arranged. A different activity with its own framework, and whether the brokerage's existing authority reaches it is a question with an answer — obtained before the first payment is collected rather than after.

What the week demonstrates. Four of the six require an authority determination before anything happens, and none of the four is obvious from the activity's description. A brokerage that answers these by analogy to what it already does will be wrong on at least one.

The operating rule this lesson produces: before a new activity begins, name the authority that permits it and the person who supervises it. Where either answer is "I assume so," the activity does not start. Section 5's supervision requirement and Section 4's licensing boundary are the same question asked from two directions, and the cost of asking is a phone call; the cost of not asking is Section 6.2's list.

6.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the enforcement categories, state the correct response to regulator contact and to a borrower complaint, and explain the line between a documented gap and a falsified record.

Key terms

TermDefinition
Mortgage activity under a DRE licenseSoliciting borrowers or lenders for, negotiating, arranging, and performing services in connection with loans secured by real property.
Activity-based licensingThe license authorizes acts. The title a person uses does not resolve whether a license is required.
Responsible brokerThe broker under whom a salesperson acts, from whom the salesperson may accept compensation for licensed activity, and who answers for the supervision.
The brokerage is the partyEngagements, records, and files belong to the brokerage, not the individual.
MLO endorsementAn endorsement on a DRE license authorizing a licensee to act as a mortgage loan originator. Not a separate license, and it renews on its own cycle.
Acting as an MLOTaking a residential mortgage loan application, or offering or negotiating terms — for compensation or its expectation. Both elements required.
NMLSThe registry through which MLO licensing and registration is administered, assigning a unique identifier to the individual.
Individual and company identifiersBoth appear on communications and advertising as required — which is why a compliant mortgage advertisement carries more identification than a sales advertisement.
DFPIThe California regulator for firms licensed under the state's lending and financing statutes — a different framework from the DRE broker framework.
Framework confusionImporting a rule from a different licensing framework. The recurring source of confidently wrong compliance answers.
Federal law applies on its own termsA conclusion about a federal disclosure obligation cannot be reasoned from which state license the firm holds.
The routing standardWould answering require a legal conclusion, a tax conclusion, a valuation, or an underwriting decision I am not authorized to make?
CompensationMoney or anything of value, including referral arrangements and reciprocal benefits. What converts assistance into licensed activity.
ExemptionA legal conclusion, narrow, and separate under state and federal law. "We're exempt" is a reason to escalate.
Business-purpose loanA loan made primarily for a business purpose, analyzed differently from a consumer-purpose loan secured by a dwelling.
Business-purpose certificationRecords the borrower's statement. Does not establish the fact — the actual purpose and surrounding facts govern.
Reasonable supervisionAn affirmative duty discharged by a system: policies, file review, disclosure tracking, advertising review, fee and trust controls, training, escalation, vendor oversight, and complaint handling.
Independent contractor statusA tax and compensation characterization. Reduces neither the broker's duty nor the licensee's obligation to act under the broker.
Documenting an improper instructionDoes not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.
Advance feeA fee collected before services are rendered, subject to specific requirements. Developed in Lesson 08.
FalsificationCreating, backdating, altering, or deleting records. The one category that is not survivable.
ReconstructabilityCould a person who was not there determine what happened, when, and on what basis. The governing test of this course.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A salesperson at a DRE-licensed brokerage takes residential mortgage applications and quotes terms. Her real estate salesperson license is current. Her MLO endorsement lapsed eleven weeks ago and she did not notice because her license renewal is not due until next year. She also signs the engagement letters with borrowers in her own name.

Identify both problems.

Solution. She is originating without authorization. The MLO endorsement is an endorsement on the existing license, not a separate license — but it renews on its own cycle, separate from the underlying license renewal. A licensee whose broker or salesperson license is current but whose endorsement has lapsed is not authorized to act as an MLO, and taking applications and offering or negotiating terms for compensation is exactly what the endorsement covers.

The engagement letters are a second, independent problem. The brokerage is the party to the engagement with the borrower. A salesperson may not contract in her own name for licensed activity, and she acts for and under the responsible broker — including for compensation, which she may accept only from that broker.

Both should be escalated to the broker immediately, and the files opened during the lapse examined by compliance rather than by her.

Problem 2

A borrower asks a mortgage originator four questions in one conversation: whether the appraisal came in high enough, whether he can rescind if he changes his mind, what the loan will do to his taxes, and whether the fee the firm charges is "standard."

Route each and state the standard.

Solution. The appraisal is a valuation question for the appraiser, reached only through the proper channel — and the originator may supply information, never a target.

Rescission is a legal conclusion. It goes to counsel, and the originator may explain that a right exists in defined circumstances without telling this borrower whether it applies to him.

The tax question goes to a tax professional, and it should be flagged early, because most tax considerations in a financing decision close when the transaction does.

"Is the fee standard?" is the one that sounds harmless and is not. Fees are governed by the applicable framework, by what was disclosed, and by the firm's compliance function — not by industry custom, and describing a charge as standard is both unsupported and the kind of statement that later gets quoted.

The standard: would answering require a legal conclusion, a tax conclusion, a valuation, or an underwriting decision I am not authorized to make? If yes, route it. Experience does not extend the scope of a license.

Problem 3

A brokerage's compliance manager tells a new originator that a particular fee cap "doesn't apply to us" because she read it in a bulletin about California mortgage lenders. The brokerage is licensed as a DRE real estate broker. The originator also assumes a federal disclosure obligation does not apply for the same reason.

Assess both conclusions.

Solution. The first is the classic framework error. The same functional activity — arranging residential mortgage loans — is conducted in California under more than one licensing framework: a DRE real estate broker license, or a license issued by the DFPI under the state's residential mortgage lending or finance lending statutes. The frameworks differ in what they authorize, what they require, how fees and compensation are treated, and which regulator examines the firm.

Importing a rule from a different framework produces confidently wrong answers in both directions — a requirement that binds a DFPI-licensed lender may not bind a DRE broker, and one that binds the broker may not appear in lender guidance at all. Know which license your firm holds.

The second reasoning is worse, because it is a category error. Federal consumer mortgage law applies according to its own terms, not by reference to the state license held. A conclusion about a federal disclosure obligation cannot be reasoned from "we're a DRE broker" at all.

Both questions go to the firm's compliance function and, where genuinely unclear, to counsel.

Problem 4

A brokerage employs a "loan coordinator" who collects documents and orders reports, and a "marketing associate" who calls prospects from a purchased list, quotes current rates, and is paid $400 for each prospect who ends up funding. Neither holds a license. The broker says the titles make clear they are support staff.

Analyze.

Solution. The title is not the test. The activity is.

The coordinator's described work is generally administrative — collecting documents, ordering third-party reports, tracking conditions. That does not require a license, and it stays that way only as long as the work stays there.

The marketing associate is performing licensed activity. Soliciting borrowers and quoting terms is exactly what the license covers, and the compensation element is present and explicit — $400 per funded loan is compensation whatever it is called. Compensation is defined broadly: money, things of value, referral arrangements, and reciprocal benefits.

This is two problems at once. It is unlicensed activity, and paying an unlicensed person for producing loans is separately a compensation problem — and where a settlement service referral is involved, a federal prohibition that disclosure does not cure.

An arrangement structured to avoid the word "compensation" while delivering value for producing loans is a compensation arrangement, and assessing whether a structure works belongs to compliance and counsel, not to the people inside it.

Problem 5

An originator is preparing a file on a four-unit property. The borrower will live in one unit. The originator's manager instructs him to process it as business-purpose, "since it's an income property," and to have the borrower sign the business-purpose certification.

Assess.

Solution. The instruction inverts the analysis, and the certification does not fix it.

Consumer residential mortgage requirements — including the MLO endorsement requirement and much of the federal disclosure regime — attach to consumer-purpose loans secured by a dwelling. A borrower occupying one unit of a fourplex is a fact pointing hard toward consumer purpose, and "it's an income property" is not the test.

The determination rests on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts, not on a certification the borrower was handed. A borrower's signature on a business-purpose certification records his statement; it does not establish the fact — and a file assembled around a certification the surrounding facts contradict is a file with a problem in it, visible to any examiner who reads the occupancy line.

Both errors run in this area, and this is the more common one: treating a consumer loan as business-purpose. The mirror error is treating every investment property loan as exempt from everything, which sweeps in requirements that still apply.

What the originator does: decline the instruction, escalate to the responsible broker, and route the purpose determination to compliance. Following it while noting that the manager directed it documents that he knew.

Problem 6

A branch manager tells an originator to "clean up" a borrower's application before submission — moving a recent job change to an earlier date so the employment history reads better, and omitting a small consumer debt that "won't matter to the ratios anyway."

What does the originator do, and what does not protect him?

Solution. Refuse, do not transmit the file, and escalate to the responsible broker immediately.

This is misrepresentation to a lender — one of the enforcement categories — and the fact that the omitted debt is small does not change what the file now asserts. An application is a set of representations the lender relies on in pricing risk, and altering an employment date is not tidying; it is changing a fact.

What does not protect him: doing it and documenting that the manager directed it. Following an improper instruction and documenting that it came from someone else does not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.

Nor does the reasoning that the ratios would work anyway. If that were true, the alteration was unnecessary — and it was still made.

The escalation goes above the person who gave the instruction, and the matter belongs on the report-promptly list along with any request to alter, backdate, or omit anything.

Problem 7

A firm's compliance manual is thorough and current. In practice, disclosures are tracked on a spreadsheet nobody updates, advertising goes out without review because the approval turnaround is four days, and file review happens quarterly — after most loans in the quarter have closed. No borrower has complained.

Assess the supervision.

Solution. A policy nobody follows is not supervision, and it is not a defense for anyone — not for the broker who wrote it and not for the licensees who departed from it.

Each failure defeats the control's purpose. File review must be close enough in time to catch a problem before the loan closes; quarterly review after closing documents history rather than preventing harm. Advertising review must precede publication, and a four-day turnaround is the cause of the non-compliance, not an excuse for it — most routing around an approval process is caused by the process being slow. Disclosure tracking must show what was delivered, to whom, when, and by what method, because disclosure timing rules attach consequences to dates.

Mortgage supervision is structurally harder than sales supervision for three reasons visible here: the timelines are compressed and the deadlines are legal rather than service commitments; much of the work is invisible to the borrower, who cannot evaluate whether a disclosure was timely; and the volume is transactional, so a defect in a process repeats on every file until someone notices.

The absence of complaints is not evidence of compliance. Complaints are only one of several routes — an examination, a data submission, or an unrelated complaint can surface the same defect.

Problem 8

A borrower emails alleging he was misled about his rate lock. The originator replies within the hour with a detailed defense, apologizes for "the confusion I caused," offers to credit $750 at closing, and deletes a text thread with the borrower that reads badly. He plans to tell his broker only if it escalates. Two days later the DRE calls him directly and he answers the questions on the spot.

Identify every error and state the correct sequence.

Solution. Six errors, and two of them are categorically worse than the rest.

The immediate defense commits a position before anyone has reviewed the file — and in a mortgage file, what was disclosed and when can be checked within minutes. The apology accepting fault may be treated as an admission and can compromise coverage. The $750 credit commits the brokerage, may read as an admission, and rarely ends the matter. Waiting to tell the broker compounds the original problem with a supervision failure.

Deleting the thread is falsification territory — the one category that is not survivable. It is generally discoverable anyway, and it changes the subject from professional judgment to integrity. A documented gap is survivable; a manufactured or destroyed record ends a career.

Answering the regulator on the spot is the second serious error. On regulator contact: notify the broker immediately, preserve records, and do not respond independently or informally. Cooperation is expected; improvised cooperation without review is where licensees make statements they cannot support.

The correct sequence: acknowledge promptly, because silence reads as evasion; notify the broker immediately; preserve everything — the file, the disclosures as delivered, communications, drafts, texts, and the advertising as it ran; respond factually without admitting or denying liability before the file is reviewed; offer nothing on your own initiative; and report to the carrier where the matter could become a claim.

Chapter summary

A California real estate broker license authorizes mortgage activity — soliciting, negotiating, arranging, and performing services in connection with loans secured by real property — under the same supervisory structure as sales activity, with the brokerage as the party.

It does not authorize lending, escrow, appraisal, legal advice, or tax advice.

An MLO endorsement is required to act as a mortgage loan originator — taking a residential mortgage loan application, or offering or negotiating terms, for compensation or its expectation. It is an endorsement rather than a separate license, it carries a unique identifier that follows the individual, and it renews on its own cycle.

The same activity is conducted in California under more than one licensing framework. Know which one your firm holds, and never import a rule from another. Federal law applies on its own terms, not by reference to the state license.

Route by the standard: would answering require a legal conclusion, a tax conclusion, a valuation, or an underwriting decision you are not authorized to make?

Licensing turns on the activity and on compensation, not on a title. Paying an unlicensed person for producing loans is both an unlicensed activity problem and a compensation problem.

Exemptions are narrow legal conclusions, separate under state and federal law. "We're exempt" is a reason to escalate.

A business-purpose certification records a statement; it does not establish a fact. The actual purpose governs, and the error runs in both directions.

Supervision is a system, not a manual, and mortgage supervision is structurally harder because the deadlines are legal, the work is invisible to the borrower, and process defects repeat on every file. Independent contractor status changes none of it.

Following an improper instruction and documenting its source does not transfer responsibility. It documents that you knew.

Enforcement reaches mortgage practice through many routes, and most categories require no intent to defraud. On regulator contact: notify the broker, preserve, and do not respond informally. On a borrower complaint: acknowledge, notify, preserve, respond factually, commit nothing, notify the carrier.

Falsifying or destroying a record is the one thing that is not survivable, and the governing test of this course is reconstructability.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify which licensing framework governs and what authority it does and does not confer, determine whether each activity described is licensed, exempt, or unlicensed and state your reasoning, identify every question in the scenario you would route and to whom, identify any supervision failure and what control would have prevented it, state what you would decline to do and the words you would use, identify what you would escalate to the responsible broker and what you would refer to compliance or counsel, and state the evidence you would create and retain. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A California real estate salesperson working under a licensed broker wants to originate residential mortgage loans. She plans to solicit borrowers, take applications in her own name, collect an advance fee for her services, and be paid directly by the lender. Which parts of her plan are problems?

  1. A. Acting in her own name rather than for her broker, taking direct payment from the lender, and collecting an advance fee without the required authorization — and residential mortgage origination additionally requires an MLO endorsement.
  2. B. Only the advance fee, since fees collected before services are rendered are the sole regulated element.
  3. C. Only the direct payment, since compensation routing is the only structural requirement.
  4. D. None of it, provided she discloses her broker relationship to each borrower.

Answer: A. Four separate requirements are engaged at once: licensed activity is conducted for and under the broker, compensation flows through the broker, advance fee arrangements are specially regulated, and residential mortgage loan origination requires the endorsement. Disclosure does not substitute for any of them.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What authority does a California real estate broker license confer regarding mortgage loans?

  1. A. It permits the broker to solicit borrowers or lenders for, and negotiate, loans secured by real property, as licensed activity performed under the broker's responsibility.
  2. B. It permits the broker to make loans only from the broker's own funds.
  3. C. It permits the broker to service loans but not to originate them.
  4. D. It permits mortgage activity only if the broker holds no other real estate listings.

Answer: A. Soliciting and negotiating loans secured by real property is within the broker's licensed activity. It is not confined to the broker's own funds, not limited to servicing, and not conditioned on abstaining from other brokerage work.

2. What is the purpose of the mortgage loan originator endorsement on a California real estate license?

  1. A. It authorizes the licensee to engage in residential mortgage loan origination, reflecting the federal framework requiring originators to be licensed or registered and identified in the national registry.
  2. B. It replaces the underlying real estate license for mortgage activity.
  3. C. It permits the licensee to originate loans without broker supervision.
  4. D. It is required only for licensees who originate commercial mortgage loans.

Answer: A. The endorsement adds residential origination authority to an existing license within the national licensing framework. It does not replace the license, remove supervision, and it addresses residential rather than commercial lending.

3. How does the broker's supervisory obligation apply to mortgage activity?

  1. A. The broker remains responsible for supervising the licensed mortgage activity of those acting under the license, including advertising, disclosures, and handling of funds.
  2. B. Supervision applies to sales activity but not to loan origination, which is governed federally.
  3. C. Supervision is satisfied by the originator's own compliance training.
  4. D. Supervision applies only where the broker personally participates in the transaction.

Answer: A. Supervision follows the license into mortgage work. Federal overlay does not displace it, training is not supervision, and the obligation does not depend on the broker's personal involvement in each file.

4. A borrower complains that a mortgage broker misrepresented the loan terms. Which body has authority over the licensee's real estate license?

  1. A. The Department of Real Estate, which licenses and disciplines California real estate brokers and salespersons.
  2. B. The lender that funded the loan, which may bar the broker from future submissions.
  3. C. The national mortgage registry, which issues and revokes state licenses.
  4. D. The escrow company, which handled the closing.

Answer: A. Licensing authority over a California real estate broker rests with the Department. A lender may end a business relationship and the registry records licensure, but neither disciplines the license.

5. Why does the distinction between licensed and exempt mortgage activity matter?

  1. A. Because engaging in activity that requires a license without holding one is unlawful, and the applicable exemptions are specific rather than general.
  2. B. Because exempt entities are held to stricter standards than licensees.
  3. C. Because exemption determines which lender may fund the loan.
  4. D. Because exempt activity may be performed by a salesperson without a broker.

Answer: A. The line determines whether conduct is lawful at all, and exemptions are narrow and defined. Exemption is not a stricter standard, does not select the lender, and does not remove broker supervision for licensees.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A licensee proposes to collect a fee from a borrower before performing any services in exchange for arranging a loan. What is required?

  1. A. Advance fee arrangements are specially regulated in California, including requirements about the agreement and the handling of the funds, and the licensee must satisfy those requirements before collecting anything.
  2. B. Nothing, provided the fee is refundable if the loan does not close.
  3. C. Nothing, provided the borrower signs a written acknowledgment of the fee.
  4. D. The fee is prohibited in all circumstances.

Answer: A. Advance fees are permitted only within a specific regulatory framework, which is why neither refundability nor an acknowledgment satisfies the requirement. A blanket prohibition overstates the rule.

2. A mortgage broker advertises 'guaranteed approval regardless of credit.' What is the concern?

  1. A. The claim is misleading because approval depends on underwriting the borrower and the collateral, and misleading advertising is itself a violation.
  2. B. There is no concern if some applicants with poor credit have in fact been approved.
  3. C. The concern is only whether the broker's license number appears in the advertisement.
  4. D. The concern arises only if a specific consumer relied on the claim and was denied.

Answer: A. The claim promises an outcome that no originator controls. Isolated approvals do not make a guarantee accurate, license identification is a separate requirement, and the violation does not wait for a particular consumer's reliance.

3. How do the Department of Real Estate and other financial regulators divide authority over mortgage activity in California?

  1. A. Different regulators license different categories of mortgage participant, so the applicable rules depend on which license the entity holds and what activity it conducts.
  2. B. The Department of Real Estate regulates all mortgage lending in California.
  3. C. Federal regulators have exclusive authority over all residential mortgage activity.
  4. D. Authority is determined by the size of the loan rather than by the participant's license.

Answer: A. License type and activity determine the applicable regime, which is why the same conduct can sit under different regulators. Neither exclusive state nor exclusive federal authority describes it, and loan size does not allocate jurisdiction.

4. A salesperson with an MLO endorsement wants to be paid a bonus directly by a wholesale lender. What is the defect?

  1. A. Compensation for licensed activity must be paid through her employing broker, and separate federal rules restrict originator compensation arrangements.
  2. B. There is no defect, since the lender is not her client.
  3. C. The defect is only that the bonus was not disclosed to the borrower.
  4. D. The defect arises only if the bonus varies with the interest rate.

Answer: A. Two frameworks apply: compensation routing under state licensing law, and the federal restrictions on how originators may be compensated. The payer's identity does not resolve either, and disclosure does not cure improper routing.

5. What is the practical purpose of a mortgage broker's licensing framework from the consumer's perspective?

  1. A. It provides accountability — an identifiable licensee, a supervising broker, disclosure requirements, and a regulator with authority to investigate and discipline.
  2. B. It guarantees that the borrower receives the lowest available interest rate.
  3. C. It ensures that every borrower who applies will qualify for a loan.
  4. D. It transfers responsibility for the loan's performance to the regulator.

Answer: A. Licensing delivers accountability and a complaint path. It does not guarantee pricing, approval, or performance of the loan.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 02

Money, interest, notes, and loan mathematics

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Define principal, interest, and term, and compute simple interest in all four directions.
  • Build an amortization schedule and explain how each payment splits and why the split shifts.
  • Identify the operative provisions of a promissory note and distinguish acceleration from alienation.
  • Compute points and fees, explain the annual percentage rate's purpose and limits, and work a break-even.
  • Compute loan-to-value and combined loan-to-value and apply the lower-of-value-or-price rule.
  • Compute payments, balances, and yield, and apply a reasonableness check to every figure reported.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: interest fundamentals and amortization55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: note provisions and the cost of credit50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: loan-to-value and payment mathematics45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Principal, interest, and term

1.1 The three variables

Every loan is described by three quantities, and every calculation in this lesson manipulates them.

VariableWhat it is
PrincipalThe amount borrowed, and thereafter the amount still owed
InterestThe charge for the use of money, expressed as a rate per period
TermThe period over which the obligation runs

Principal changes. The word describes the original amount and the current balance, and a licensee who does not track which one a calculation calls for will compute interest on the wrong number.

1.2 Simple interest

Real estate loans generally use simple interest — computed on the outstanding principal, not on accumulated interest.

I = P × R × T

Rearranged, it answers four questions:

UnknownFormula
InterestI = P × R × T
PrincipalP = I ÷ (R × T)
RateR = I ÷ (P × T)
TimeT = I ÷ (P × R)

1.3 Worked in all four directions

Interest. $400,000 at 6% for one year: 400,000 × 0.06 × 1 = $24,000. One month: 24,000 ÷ 12 = $2,000.

Principal. A borrower paid $18,750 of interest in one year at 7.5%. P = 18,750 ÷ (0.075 × 1) = $250,000.

Rate. A $320,000 loan produced $20,800 of interest in a year. R = 20,800 ÷ 320,000 = 6.5%.

Time. $9,000 of interest accrued on a $240,000 loan at 6%. Annual interest = 240,000 × 0.06 = $14,400. T = 9,000 ÷ 14,400 = 0.625 years = 7.5 months.

1.4 Per diem interest

Interest computed per day, and it appears at every closing.

Per diem = annual interest ÷ days in the year basis

A $400,000 loan at 6% closing on the 22nd of a 30-day month, on a 360-day basis: Annual interest = $24,000. Per diem = 24,000 ÷ 360 = $66.67. Days from the 22nd through month end = 9. 9 × 66.67 = $600.03.

Two conventions change the answer, and both must be read rather than assumed: whether the basis is 360 or 365 days, and which days are counted. A licensee who assumes and is wrong has misstated a closing figure.

1.5 Interest in arrears

Residential mortgage interest is generally paid in arrears — a payment covers interest that has already accrued, rather than interest for the period ahead.

Two practical consequences that surprise borrowers:

The first payment is not due the month after closing. A loan closing in March typically has its first payment in May, because interest for the remainder of March was collected at closing and April's interest accrues before the May payment.

A payoff includes interest through the payoff date, which is why the payoff exceeds the last statement balance.

1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to solve I = P × R × T in all four directions, compute per diem interest, and explain why the first payment is not due the following month.

2. Simple interest and amortization

2.1 What amortization does

Amortization is the retirement of a debt through periodic payments covering both interest and principal.

StructureBehavior
Fully amortizedPayments retire the balance to zero by maturity
Partially amortizedPayments reduce the balance but leave a balloon at maturity
Interest-onlyPayments cover interest only; principal is not retired during the period
Straight (term) noteInterest payments with the full principal due at maturity
Negative amortizationThe payment does not cover accrued interest, and the balance grows

2.2 How each payment splits

Each payment covers the interest accrued since the last payment; the remainder reduces principal.

$400,000 at 6%, monthly payment $2,398.20:

MonthInterestPrincipalEnding balance
1$2,000.00$398.20$399,601.80
2$1,998.01$400.19$399,201.61
3$1,996.01$402.19$398,799.42

Month 1 interest: 400,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $2,000.00. Principal = 2,398.20 − 2,000.00 = $398.20.

Month 2 interest: 399,601.80 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $1,998.01. Principal = $400.19.

2.3 The pattern, and what it explains

Early payments are almost entirely interest. The principal portion grows each month while the interest portion shrinks, slowly at first and then faster.

That single pattern explains several things borrowers ask about:

  • Why five years of payments retired so little principal. On this loan, sixty payments totaling roughly $143,900 reduce the balance by roughly $27,800.
  • Why the payoff exceeds what the borrower expected.
  • Why a small additional principal payment early has a disproportionate effect, since it removes principal that would otherwise accrue interest for the whole remaining term.

2.4 Negative amortization

Where a scheduled payment is less than the accrued interest, the shortfall is added to the balance and the debt grows despite payments being made.

Two features make it dangerous and worth teaching plainly:

The borrower is paying and losing ground, which does not match anyone's intuition about what a payment does.

Recast provisions can produce a payment increase that is large and sudden, when the loan is required to begin fully amortizing the enlarged balance over the remaining term.

A licensee presenting any product with a negative amortization feature must present that mechanism in plain terms, and Lesson 09 addresses the disclosure obligations that attach.

2.5 The effect of term

Term changes the payment and changes the total interest far more than borrowers expect.

$400,000 at 6%:

TermApproximate paymentApproximate total interest
30 years$2,398$463,400
20 years$2,866$287,800
15 years$3,375$207,600

The payment rises by about 41% from 30 to 15 years; the total interest falls by more than half. That comparison is the one a borrower is usually trying to understand, and a licensee can compute and present it — while leaving which to choose to the borrower with their advisors.

2.6 Prepayment

Additional principal reduces the balance and therefore all future interest.

On the loan above, an extra $200 per month from the start retires it roughly six years early and saves well over $100,000 of interest.

Two cautions. Whether a prepayment penalty applies is a note provision, addressed in Section 3, and its permissibility is regulated. And an extra payment must be applied to principal — a borrower who simply sends more may find it applied to the next installment instead.

2.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to build three rows of an amortization schedule, explain the shifting split, and describe negative amortization in terms a borrower would understand.

3. Promissory note terms

3.1 Two documents, two jobs

Restated because everything in this course depends on it:

InstrumentWhat it does
Promissory noteThe promise to repay. It creates the debt and states its terms
Security instrumentPledges the property as security for that debt

The note is the debt. The security instrument is the remedy.

A note without a security instrument is an unsecured obligation. A security instrument without a note secures nothing, because there is no obligation to secure.

3.2 The parties and the essential terms

Maker (borrower) promises to pay; payee (holder) is entitled to receive.

The note states the principal, the rate and how it is determined, the payment amount and schedule, the maturity date, the place and manner of payment, and the consequences of default.

3.3 The provisions that matter operationally

ProvisionWhat it does
AccelerationOn default, makes the entire balance immediately due
Alienation (due-on-sale)Permits the lender to call the loan due on transfer of the property
PrepaymentWhether and on what terms the borrower may pay early, and any penalty
Late chargeA charge for a payment received after a stated period
Default interestA higher rate applying after default, where provided
Attorney feesRecovery of enforcement costs, where provided
SubordinationAgreement to take a lower lien position
ReleaseIn a blanket loan, releasing individual parcels as they are sold
AssumptionWhether and on what conditions the loan may be assumed

3.4 Acceleration and alienation are not the same

The two students merge, and the distinction is clean:

Acceleration responds to default. Alienation responds to transfer.

Without an acceleration clause, a lender could pursue only the missed payments — which is why foreclosure depends on it. Without an alienation clause, a property could be transferred with the loan intact — which is why loans are generally not assumable without lender consent.

"A lender can always call the loan" is wrong. The lender's rights come from the clauses actually in the instrument and the events that trigger them.

3.5 Adjustable-rate provisions

For an adjustable-rate note, four terms determine the rate at every adjustment:

TermWhat it does
IndexThe published measure the rate follows
MarginThe amount added to the index. Set at origination and fixed
Adjustment frequencyHow often the rate resets
CapsPeriodic caps limit change at a single adjustment; a lifetime cap limits total movement

The rate at adjustment is the index plus the margin, subject to the caps. Not the lender's discretion, and not the borrower's credit at that time.

Some notes also carry an initial or first-adjustment cap and a floor below which the rate will not fall.

A licensee who cannot explain a borrower's own index, margin, and caps should not be presenting that product.

3.6 Negotiability and transfer

A note meeting certain requirements is a negotiable instrument, transferable so a subsequent holder may take it free of certain defenses.

Practically, this is why loans are sold and why a borrower's payments may be directed to a servicer they never chose. The obligation follows the note.

Whether a particular note is negotiable and what defenses survive are legal questions.

3.7 What a licensee says about note terms

May: identify each provision and explain what it does mechanically; explain that a rate adjusts by index plus margin within caps; explain that a prepayment provision exists and what it says.

May not: advise whether a provision is enforceable, predict how a court would read it, tell a borrower a provision "never gets enforced," or characterize a term as standard.

3.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the operative note provisions, distinguish acceleration from alienation, and state what determines an adjustable rate at adjustment.

4. Points, fees, and annual percentage rate

4.1 Points

One point equals one percent of the loan amount. Not of the purchase price.

Discount points are paid to reduce the interest rate. Origination points are a charge for making the loan. Both are quoted the same way and do different things, and a borrower asking "how many points?" frequently does not know which is meant.

2 points on a $400,000 loan: 400,000 × 0.02 = $8,000. 1.5 points on a $612,500 loan: 612,500 × 0.015 = $9,187.50.

4.2 The break-even

The computation a borrower actually needs:

Cost of the points ÷ monthly saving = months to recover

Paying 2 points ($8,000) reduces the payment by $140 per month. 8,000 ÷ 140 = 57 months, about 4 years 9 months.

A borrower who expects to hold the loan longer comes out ahead; one who expects to sell or refinance sooner does not.

A licensee may compute and present the break-even. Whether this borrower should pay points depends on his plans, his tax situation, and his alternatives — which is a lender and advisor question.

4.3 The categories of cost

A borrower sees a long list and cannot tell what varies. The useful grouping:

CategoryExamples
InterestThe rate itself
Lender chargesOrigination, underwriting, processing, discount points
Third-party servicesAppraisal, credit report, title, escrow, recording, pest, survey
Prepaid itemsPer diem interest, initial hazard premium, initial impound deposits
Government chargesRecording fees, transfer taxes

Prepaid items are not a cost of the loan in the ordinary sense — they are amounts the borrower would owe anyway, collected at closing. Borrowers who see a large "cash to close" and conclude the loan is expensive are frequently looking mostly at prepaids.

4.4 Annual percentage rate

The APR expresses the cost of credit as a yearly rate, including certain finance charges beyond interest, and it exists to make offers comparable.

What it does: captures costs the note rate alone omits, so two loans with the same note rate and different fees do not appear identical.

What it does not do:

  • It is not the note rate, and the payment is computed from the note rate.
  • It does not include every cost — its contents are defined, and some third-party charges are outside it.
  • It assumes the loan runs its full term, which makes it a poor comparison for a borrower who will refinance or sell in five years.
  • It behaves oddly on adjustable-rate loans, because it must assume future rates.

A licensee explains what the APR is for and points the borrower to it as a comparison tool. A licensee does not compute it, interpret a difference between two APRs as a conclusion, or tell a borrower which loan is cheaper for him.

4.5 Nominal, effective, and note rate

The note rate is stated in the note and drives the payment. The effective rate reflects the actual cost including points and certain fees. The nominal rate is the stated annual rate before considering compounding or costs.

The relationship a borrower needs: a lower note rate purchased with points is not automatically cheaper. The break-even answers it for his holding period.

4.6 The comparison discipline

When presenting alternatives, present them on a common basis:

  1. The same loan amount, or state the difference.
  2. The same term and structure, or state the difference.
  3. The note rate, the payment, the points, and the lender charges, each separately.
  4. The break-even where points differ.
  5. The APR, identified as a comparison tool with its assumptions.
  6. What is a lender charge and what is a third-party or prepaid item.

Comparisons that omit the fee difference, or that compare a lower rate bought with points against a higher rate without disclosing the cost, are misleading even where every individual number is accurate.

4.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to compute points and a break-even, state what the APR does and does not capture, and present two offers on a common basis.

5. Loan-to-value and combined loan-to-value

5.1 Loan-to-value

LTV = loan amount ÷ value, where value is the lower of appraised value and purchase price.

A $920,000 purchase with a $736,000 loan: 736,000 ÷ 920,000 = 80%.

5.2 The rule that explains every low appraisal

Lenders lend against the lower of appraised value and purchase price.

Same purchase, appraisal at $900,000. The lender lends against $900,000. At 80%: 900,000 × 0.80 = $720,000 — $16,000 less than planned.

The borrower's options are then: bring the additional funds, renegotiate the price, negotiate another resolution, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed.

What does not happen automatically: the price does not adjust to the appraised value by operation of any program, the loan is not denied, and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right.

5.3 Refinance transactions

On a refinance there is no purchase price, so value is the appraised value — which is why a refinance is more exposed to an appraisal outcome than a purchase, and why a borrower planning a cash-out refinance should understand that the amount available is not knowable until the appraisal is in.

5.4 Combined loan-to-value

Where more than one loan is secured by the property:

CLTV = total secured debt ÷ value

$920,000 property, $736,000 first and $46,000 second: 782,000 ÷ 920,000 = 85%.

For a home equity line, the full line amount rather than the drawn balance is generally what counts, which surprises borrowers who have drawn little.

5.5 Equity and cash-out

Equity = value − liens.

A $920,000 property with a $600,000 first has $320,000 of equity. A cash-out refinance to 80% CLTV: 920,000 × 0.80 = $736,000 available; less the $600,000 payoff = $136,000 before costs.

Two points a borrower needs. Cash-out proceeds are borrowed money, not income, and the tax treatment is a question for a tax professional. And equity converted to debt is still gone from the equity side — the property has not changed.

5.6 Why LTV matters to the lender

LTV measures the lender's exposure if the loan is not repaid, and it drives:

  • Whether the loan can be made at all under the program.
  • Pricing, since higher LTV generally carries higher risk.
  • Mortgage insurance, commonly required on conventional loans below a down payment threshold — and which protects the lender, though the borrower pays for it.
  • The cushion available if values decline.

5.7 The three numbers, for a borrower

What the borrower can borrow — the lender's number. What cash is available — down payment, closing costs, reserves, and the immediate costs of occupancy. Borrowers routinely plan to the down payment and forget the rest. What the borrower is willing to pay monthly — often lower than the first, and the number that should drive the search.

Where they conflict, the conflict is the conversation — held early and deliberately, rather than discovered at the closing table.

5.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to compute LTV and CLTV, apply the lower-of-value-or-price rule, and compute cash-out availability.

6. Payment and yield calculations

6.1 The payment factor method

A payment on a fully amortized loan can be computed from a factor — the monthly payment per $1,000 of loan at a given rate and term.

Payment = (loan ÷ 1,000) × factor

A factor of 5.9955 per $1,000 at 6% for 30 years: 400,000 ÷ 1,000 = 400 × 5.9955 = $2,398.20.

Factors come from a table or a financial calculator. The examinable skill is applying one correctly, and the recurring error is forgetting to divide the loan by 1,000 first.

6.2 Working backward from a payment

A borrower can afford $2,700 monthly principal and interest. At a factor of 5.9955, what loan does that support?

2,700 ÷ 5.9955 = 450.4 → × 1,000 = $450,400.

6.3 PITI

The housing payment is more than principal and interest:

PITI = Principal + Interest + Taxes + Insurance — plus association dues where applicable, and mortgage insurance where required.

$2,398.20 P&I; taxes $958 monthly; hazard insurance $140; mortgage insurance $122; association dues $310. Total housing payment = $3,928.20.

A borrower quoted a principal and interest figure and then shown a PITI figure will feel misled, which is why the full payment belongs in the first conversation. In California, the property tax line is the one most often understated, because a buyer's taxes are based on a new assessed value rather than the seller's bill.

6.4 Qualifying ratios

RatioFormula
Front-end (housing)Housing expense ÷ gross monthly income
Back-end (total debt)Total monthly obligations ÷ gross monthly income

Gross monthly income $9,000. PITI $2,520; car $480; student loan $300; card minimums $120. Front-end: 2,520 ÷ 9,000 = 28%. Back-end: 3,420 ÷ 9,000 = 38%.

Thresholds vary by program, by compensating factors, and over time. A licensee computes and explains the ratios and never states a threshold as a rule — that is an underwriting question, and stating it produces a confident error that costs a borrower a property.

6.5 Yield

Yield is the return to the holder of a note, and it differs from the note rate whenever the note was acquired for something other than face value.

A $200,000 note at 7% interest-only pays $14,000 a year.

Purchased at par: yield = 14,000 ÷ 200,000 = 7.0%. Purchased at a 10% discount ($180,000): 14,000 ÷ 180,000 = 7.78%. Purchased at a premium ($210,000): 14,000 ÷ 210,000 = 6.67%.

Buying at a discount raises the yield; buying at a premium lowers it.

This matters in Lesson 12's private money material, where notes are bought and sold, and it is the same inverse relationship as the capitalization rate: price and yield move in opposite directions for a given income.

6.6 Discount and points from the lender's side

Discount points paid at origination raise the lender's yield for the same reason: the lender advances less than face while receiving the stated payments.

That is the mechanism behind a rate buydown, and it is worth understanding because it explains why a lower rate has a price rather than being a favor.

6.7 The errors that produce wrong answers

  1. Applying a rate to the wrong base — points to the price rather than the loan; a percentage to the result rather than the source.
  2. Unit and convention errors — annual rate where monthly was needed, 360 versus 365 day basis, forgetting to divide by 1,000 in the factor method.
  3. Confusing note rate with APR, or payment with PITI.
  4. Skipping the reasonableness check.

The reasonableness check catches nearly all of them. A $2,398 payment on a $400,000 loan at 6% is plausible; $23,980 is not. Before reporting a number, ask whether it is the right order of magnitude.

6.8 Every figure carries its basis

A number given to a borrower should carry the assumptions it rests on: the loan amount, the rate, the term, whether it is P&I or PITI, and whether taxes and insurance are estimated.

A quote without its assumptions is not information. It is a number the borrower will hold you to.

6.9 Reading a payment quote critically

Borrowers are quoted payments constantly, and the quoted figure is frequently not the figure they will pay. A broker who can take a quote apart protects the borrower from a surprise and protects himself from having repeated a number he did not verify.

What a quoted "payment" may or may not include:

ComponentFrequently omitted from a quick quote
Principal and interestAlways included — this is usually the whole quote
Property taxesOften omitted, and Section 6.3's PITI is the reason it matters
Hazard insuranceOften omitted, and in some California markets it is now the largest surprise
Mortgage insuranceOmitted whenever the quote assumes a down payment the borrower is not making
Association duesNot part of the loan payment and entirely part of the borrower's obligation
Flood or other required coverageOmitted until a determination is made
Special assessmentsRarely surfaced before closing

Three checks a broker performs on any quote before repeating it:

  1. Does the payment reconcile to the rate, term, and loan amount? Section 6.1's factor method answers this in seconds, and a payment that does not reconcile means one of the four inputs is not what was stated.
  2. What down payment does it assume? A quote built on twenty percent is not a quote for a borrower bringing ten, and the difference is not only the loan amount.
  3. What is the escrow assumption? A quote excluding an escrowed item is a quote for a payment the borrower will not make.

And the disclosure that resolves all of it: Section 6.8's requirement that every figure carries its basis. A payment stated with its rate, term, amount, down payment, and what it includes is a professional statement. The same number without those five is a figure the borrower will hold the broker to.

The failure this prevents. A borrower quoted a payment early, who budgeted against it, and who sees a materially higher figure on his disclosures. Nothing was misrepresented on purpose — the quote assumed a different down payment and excluded taxes and insurance — and the borrower experiences it as having been misled, which for every practical purpose is the outcome that matters.

6.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to compute a payment from a factor and work backward, build a PITI figure, compute both ratios without stating thresholds, and compute yield at a discount and a premium.

Key terms

TermDefinition
