PrincipalThe amount borrowed, and thereafter the amount still owed. Track which one a calculation needs.
Simple interestI = P × R × T, computed on outstanding principal. Solvable in all four directions.
Per diem interestAnnual interest ÷ the day-count basis. Read the basis — 360 or 365 — and which days are counted.
Interest in arrearsA payment covers interest already accrued. Why the first payment is not due the month after closing, and why a payoff exceeds the last statement.
AmortizationRetirement of debt through payments covering interest and principal.
Fully / partially amortizedRetires to zero by maturity; or leaves a balloon.
Interest-onlyPayments cover interest; principal is not retired during the period.
Negative amortizationThe payment does not cover accrued interest and the balance grows, with a recast producing a large sudden increase.
The amortization patternEarly payments are nearly all interest; the principal portion grows over time. Explains slow principal reduction, payoff surprise, and the outsized effect of early prepayment.
Promissory noteThe promise to repay. The note is the debt.
Security instrumentThe pledge of property. The security instrument is the remedy.
AccelerationOn default, the entire balance becomes due. Foreclosure depends on it.
Alienation (due-on-sale)On transfer, the lender may call the loan due. Why loans are generally not assumable without consent.
Index and marginThe published measure the rate follows, and the fixed amount added at origination.
CapsPeriodic caps limit a single adjustment; a lifetime cap limits total movement. Some notes add an initial cap and a floor.
Negotiable instrumentA note transferable so a holder may take free of certain defenses. Why loans are sold and servicing transfers.
PointOne percent of the loan amount — not of the price.
Discount versus origination pointsPaid to reduce the rate; versus a charge for making the loan.
Break-evenCost of points ÷ monthly saving = months to recover.
Prepaid itemsPer diem interest, initial hazard premium, initial impound deposits — amounts owed anyway, collected at closing.
Annual percentage rateThe cost of credit as a yearly rate including certain finance charges. Not the note rate, does not include every cost, assumes the full term, and behaves oddly on adjustable loans.
Loan-to-valueLoan ÷ the lower of appraised value and purchase price. On a refinance, value is the appraised value.
Combined loan-to-valueTotal secured debt ÷ value, generally counting the full amount of a line rather than the drawn balance.
EquityValue − liens. Cash-out converts equity to debt, and the proceeds are borrowed money rather than income.
Mortgage insuranceCommonly required below a down payment threshold. Protects the lender, paid by the borrower.
Payment factorMonthly payment per $1,000 of loan at a rate and term. Divide the loan by 1,000 first.
PITIPrincipal, interest, taxes, insurance — plus dues and mortgage insurance where applicable.
Qualifying ratiosHousing ÷ income; total obligations ÷ income. Computed and explained, with thresholds never stated as a rule.
YieldThe return to the note holder. Discount raises yield; premium lowers it.
Basis of a quoteLoan amount, rate, term, P&I or PITI, and what is estimated. A quote without its assumptions is a number the borrower will hold you to.

Practice problems

Problem 1

Solve each: (a) one month's interest on a $400,000 balance at 6%; (b) the principal, where a borrower paid $18,750 of interest in one year at 7.5%; (c) the rate, where a $320,000 loan produced $20,800 in a year; (d) per diem on a $400,000 loan at 6%, 360-day basis, and the interest collected at a closing on the 22nd of a 30-day month.

Answer, and name the convention that could change (d).

Solution. (a) 400,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $2,000.00.

(b) P = I ÷ (R × T) = 18,750 ÷ 0.075 = $250,000.

(c) R = I ÷ (P × T) = 20,800 ÷ 320,000 = 6.5%.

(d) Annual interest = $24,000. Per diem = 24,000 ÷ 360 = $66.67. Days from the 22nd through month end = 9. 9 × 66.67 = $600.03.

Two conventions change (d) and both must be read rather than assumed: whether the basis is 360 or 365 days — at 365 the per diem is $65.75 — and which days are counted. A licensee who assumes and is wrong has misstated a closing figure to a borrower.

Problem 2

A borrower closing in March asks why his first payment is not due in April, and why his payoff quote five years later exceeds his last statement balance. He also says that after five years of payments he expected to have paid down "at least a fifth" of a $400,000 loan at 6%.

Explain all three.

Solution. Interest is paid in arrears — a payment covers interest that has already accrued, not the period ahead. Interest for the remainder of March was collected at closing, April's interest accrues during April, and the May payment covers it. Hence the first payment in May.

The payoff includes interest through the payoff date, which is why it exceeds the last statement balance — along with any other amounts owed under the note.

The principal expectation is the amortization pattern. Each payment covers accrued interest first and the remainder reduces principal, so early payments are almost entirely interest. Month 1 here is $2,000.00 interest and $398.20 principal. Sixty payments totaling roughly $143,900 reduce the balance by roughly $27,800 — about seven percent, not a fifth.

The same pattern explains the reverse: a small additional principal payment early has a disproportionate effect, because it removes principal that would otherwise accrue interest for the entire remaining term.

Problem 3

A borrower's note has an acceleration clause and an alienation clause. He misses three payments; a different borrower deeds her property to her son. An originator tells both that "the lender can always call the loan." A third borrower asks what his adjustable rate will be next year, and the originator says it depends on the lender and on whether his credit has improved.

Correct every statement.

Solution. Acceleration and alienation respond to different events. Acceleration responds to default — it makes the entire balance immediately due, and without it a lender could pursue only the missed payments, which is why foreclosure depends on it. Alienation responds to transfer — it permits the lender to call the loan due on transfer, which is why loans are generally not assumable without consent. The missed payments trigger the first; the deed to the son triggers the second.

"A lender can always call the loan" is wrong. The lender's rights come from the clauses actually in the instrument and the events that trigger them.

The adjustable rate is index plus margin, subject to the caps. Not the lender's discretion, and not the borrower's credit at that time — the margin was fixed at origination. The borrower should also be shown his periodic cap, his lifetime cap, and any initial cap or floor.

A licensee who cannot explain a borrower's own index, margin, and caps should not be presenting that product.

Problem 4

Two offers on a $400,000 loan. Offer A: 6.25%, no points, $1,200 in lender fees. Offer B: 5.875%, 2 points, $1,200 in lender fees, payment $140 lower. The originator tells the borrower B is "the cheaper loan because the APR is lower."

Compute what matters and assess the statement.

Solution. The points cost 400,000 × 0.02 = $8,000 — one point is one percent of the loan amount, not the price.

Break-even: 8,000 ÷ 140 = 57 months, about 4 years 9 months. A borrower holding longer than that comes out ahead on B; one selling or refinancing sooner does not.

"The cheaper loan" is not the originator's conclusion to draw. The APR exists to make offers comparable by including certain finance charges beyond interest — but it assumes the loan runs its full term, which makes it a poor guide for a borrower who will move in five years. It is also not the note rate, does not include every cost, and behaves oddly on adjustable loans.

What the licensee does: present both on a common basis — same amount, term, and structure; note rate, payment, points, and lender charges each stated separately; the break-even; and the APR identified as a comparison tool with its assumptions. Then let the borrower and his advisors choose.

A comparison that omitted the $8,000 while showing the lower payment would be misleading even though every individual number in it was accurate.

Problem 5

A $920,000 purchase with 20% down. The appraisal comes in at $900,000. Separately, a refinance borrower with a $920,000 home and a $600,000 first asks how much cash he can take out at 80% CLTV, and whether the proceeds are taxable income.

Compute both and correct any assumption.

Solution. Purchase. Lenders lend against the lower of appraised value and purchase price — here $900,000. At 80%: 900,000 × 0.80 = $720,000, against the $736,000 planned. A $16,000 shortfall.

His options: bring the funds, renegotiate the price, negotiate another resolution, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed. The price does not adjust automatically, the loan is not denied, and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right.

Refinance. There is no purchase price, so value is the appraised value — which is why a refinance is more exposed to the appraisal outcome, and why the amount available is not knowable until the appraisal is in. Assuming $920,000: 920,000 × 0.80 = $736,000 available, less the $600,000 payoff = $136,000 before costs.

The proceeds are borrowed money, not income. The tax treatment is a question for a tax professional, and the licensee should say so rather than answering. And the borrower should understand that equity converted to debt is gone from the equity side — the property has not changed.

Problem 6

A borrower is quoted "$2,398 a month" on a $400,000 loan at 6% for 30 years. Later he sees a figure of $3,928 and says he was misled. His California property taxes were quoted from the seller's current bill.

Build the correct figure and identify the two failures.

Solution. P&I from the factor: 400,000 ÷ 1,000 = 400 × 5.9955 = $2,398.20. (The recurring error is forgetting to divide by 1,000 first.)

PITI: P&I $2,398.20 + taxes $958 + hazard insurance $140 + mortgage insurance $122 + association dues $310 = $3,928.20.

The first failure is quoting P&I as the payment. A borrower quoted principal and interest and then shown PITI will feel misled, which is why the full housing payment belongs in the first conversation.

The second is the California property tax line, which is the one most often understated: a buyer's taxes are based on a new assessed value established on the change in ownership, not the seller's bill. Quoting the seller's number can be wrong by a multiple, and the estimate belongs with the county assessor and a tax professional.

Every figure carries its basis — loan amount, rate, term, whether it is P&I or PITI, and what is estimated. A quote without its assumptions is a number the borrower will hold you to.

Problem 7

Gross monthly income $9,000. PITI $2,520; car $480; student loan $300; card minimums $120. The originator computes the ratios and tells the borrower he "qualifies easily, since 38% is well under the 43% limit." Separately, the borrower asks whether a 15-year term is worth it.

Compute, correct, and present the term comparison.

Solution. Front-end: 2,520 ÷ 9,000 = 28%. Back-end: (2,520 + 480 + 300 + 120) ÷ 9,000 = 3,420 ÷ 9,000 = 38%.

Stating a threshold as a rule is the error. Thresholds vary by program, by compensating factors, and over time. A licensee computes and explains the ratios and leaves the qualifying determination to underwriting — and telling a borrower he "qualifies easily" is an underwriting conclusion the licensee is not authorized to make.

The term comparison on $400,000 at 6%, which the licensee may compute and present:

30 years: payment ≈ $2,398, total interest ≈ $463,400. 20 years: ≈ $2,866, ≈ $287,800. 15 years: ≈ $3,375, ≈ $207,600.

The payment rises about 41% from 30 to 15 years; the total interest falls by more than half. That is the comparison the borrower is trying to understand — and which to choose is his decision with his advisors.

Problem 8

An investor is offered a $200,000 note bearing 7% interest-only, at three prices: par, a 10% discount, and a $210,000 premium. He says a 7% note yields 7% regardless of what he pays for it.

Compute each yield and explain the relationship.

Solution. The note pays 200,000 × 0.07 = $14,000 a year at every price — that is fixed by the note.

At par ($200,000): 14,000 ÷ 200,000 = 7.00%. At a 10% discount ($180,000): 14,000 ÷ 180,000 = 7.78%. At a premium ($210,000): 14,000 ÷ 210,000 = 6.67%.

He is wrong: the note rate is fixed, but the yield depends on what he paid. Buying at a discount raises the yield; buying at a premium lowers it — price and yield move in opposite directions for a given income stream, the same inverse relationship as a capitalization rate and value.

The same mechanism explains discount points from the lender's side: the lender advances less than face while receiving the stated payments, which raises its yield. That is why a rate buydown has a price rather than being a favor, and it is worth understanding before presenting one.

Chapter summary

Simple interest is I = P × R × T, solvable in four directions, and per diem interest depends on a day-count basis that must be read rather than assumed.

Mortgage interest is paid in arrears, which explains the first payment date and the payoff figure.

Each amortized payment covers accrued interest first, so early payments are nearly all interest — which explains slow principal reduction, payoff surprise, and why early prepayment has an outsized effect.

Negative amortization means paying while losing ground, with a recast producing a large sudden increase. Present the mechanism plainly or do not present the product.

The note is the debt; the security instrument is the remedy. Acceleration responds to default; alienation responds to transfer.

An adjustable rate is index plus margin within caps — never lender discretion and never the borrower's later credit. Know your borrower's index, margin, and caps.

A point is one percent of the loan. Compute the break-even; leave the decision to the borrower.

The APR is a comparison tool with defined contents and full-term assumptions — not the note rate, not every cost, and not a conclusion about which loan is cheaper for this borrower.

Present offers on a common basis, because a comparison omitting a fee difference misleads even when every number in it is accurate.

Lenders lend against the lower of value or price, and on a refinance value is the appraisal — which is why cash-out availability is unknown until it arrives.

Cash-out proceeds are borrowed money, and the tax treatment goes to a tax professional.

Compute payments from a factor after dividing by 1,000, quote PITI rather than P&I, and remember that California property taxes reset on transfer.

Compute qualifying ratios; never state a threshold as a rule.

Discount raises yield, premium lowers it — which is also why a bought-down rate has a price.

Every figure carries its basis, and every figure gets a reasonableness check before it reaches a borrower.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Perform every computation the scenario requires — interest, per diem, amortization split, points, break-even, loan-to-value or combined loan-to-value, payment, PITI, and qualifying ratios as applicable — showing your bases, units, and conventions; present any loan comparison on a common basis and identify what a comparison omitting it would misstate; identify the note provisions engaged by the facts and the event triggering each; state every assumption underlying each figure you would give the borrower; identify what you would decline to conclude and why; and state what you would route to underwriting, to a tax professional, or to counsel. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A borrower is comparing two offers on a $500,000 loan. Offer A is 6.25 percent with no points and $2,000 in lender fees. Offer B is 5.875 percent with two points and $2,000 in lender fees. He expects to sell the home in about three years. How should the originator frame the comparison?

  1. A. Quantify the $10,000 cost of the points against the monthly payment savings, show roughly how long it takes for the savings to recover that cost, and note that a three-year horizon may not reach the break-even point — while also comparing the disclosed annual percentage rates.
  2. B. Recommend Offer B, because the lower interest rate always produces the lower total cost.
  3. C. Recommend Offer A, because paying points is never advantageous for a residential borrower.
  4. D. Recommend whichever offer shows the lower annual percentage rate, since that figure accounts for all cost differences.

Answer: A. Points are prepaid interest that pay off only if the borrower holds the loan past break-even, which makes the holding period decisive. Neither absolute rule is correct, and the annual percentage rate — while useful — assumes the loan runs its term, so it can mislead a borrower who expects to sell in three years.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What does the annual percentage rate express that the note rate does not?

  1. A. The cost of credit as a yearly rate including certain finance charges beyond interest, which allows comparison across offers with different fee structures.
  2. B. The interest rate the borrower will actually be charged each month.
  3. C. The rate at which the loan balance will amortize over its term.
  4. D. The maximum rate the loan may reach if it is an adjustable-rate loan.

Answer: A. The annual percentage rate folds specified financing costs into a single comparable figure. The note rate is what accrues on the balance, and amortization and rate caps are separate concepts.

2. A $360,000 loan carries a 6 percent annual interest rate. What is the interest portion of the first monthly payment?

  1. A. $1,800.
  2. B. $2,160.
  3. C. $21,600.
  4. D. $600.

Answer: A. $360,000 × 6% = $21,600 per year; divided by 12 months, the first month's interest is $1,800. The $21,600 figure is the annual amount.

3. What distinguishes a fully amortized loan from an interest-only loan?

  1. A. A fully amortized loan's scheduled payments retire the principal by the end of the term; an interest-only loan's payments cover interest only, leaving the principal outstanding.
  2. B. A fully amortized loan has a fixed rate while an interest-only loan has an adjustable rate.
  3. C. A fully amortized loan requires a balloon payment while an interest-only loan does not.
  4. D. A fully amortized loan may be prepaid while an interest-only loan may not.

Answer: A. The difference is whether scheduled payments retire principal. Rate structure, balloon features, and prepayment terms vary independently — and it is the interest-only loan that leaves a balance outstanding.

4. A property is worth $700,000 with a first loan of $490,000 and a second loan of $70,000. What is the combined loan-to-value ratio?

  1. A. 80 percent.
  2. B. 70 percent.
  3. C. 10 percent.
  4. D. 125 percent.

Answer: A. ($490,000 + $70,000) ÷ $700,000 = 80 percent. The 70 percent figure omits the second loan and the 10 percent figure counts only it.

5. What is a balloon payment?

  1. A. A payment substantially larger than the regular periodic payments, due at the end of the term because the scheduled payments did not fully retire the principal.
  2. B. An additional payment the borrower makes voluntarily to reduce principal faster.
  3. C. The final regular payment of a fully amortized loan.
  4. D. A payment required when an adjustable rate reaches its lifetime cap.

Answer: A. A balloon exists because amortization was not scheduled to complete within the term. It is neither a voluntary prepayment, the last payment of a fully amortizing loan, nor a consequence of rate caps.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A borrower pays one point on a $525,000 loan. What is the cost, and how is it characterized?

  1. A. $5,250, generally treated as prepaid interest paid to obtain a lower rate.
  2. B. $525, treated as an administrative fee.
  3. C. $52,500, treated as a down payment toward principal.
  4. D. $5,250, treated as a reduction of the principal balance.

Answer: A. A point is one percent of the loan amount, so $5,250, and discount points function as prepaid interest that buys down the rate rather than reducing principal.

2. How does simple interest differ from compound interest?

  1. A. Simple interest accrues only on the principal, while compound interest accrues on principal plus previously accrued interest.
  2. B. Simple interest is charged monthly while compound interest is charged annually.
  3. C. Simple interest applies to fixed-rate loans and compound interest to adjustable-rate loans.
  4. D. Simple interest is calculated in advance and compound interest in arrears.

Answer: A. What the interest is calculated on is the distinction. Frequency, rate structure, and timing of accrual are separate variables.

3. Which terms would you expect a promissory note to state?

  1. A. The principal amount, the interest rate, the payment terms, the maturity date, and the consequences of default.
  2. B. The property's legal description and the vesting of title.
  3. C. The escrow instructions and the closing date.
  4. D. The appraised value and the loan-to-value ratio.

Answer: A. The note governs the debt: amount, rate, payments, maturity, and default. Legal description belongs to the security instrument, and escrow and valuation details live elsewhere.

4. A borrower's monthly payment is $2,400 and the interest portion in a given month is $1,950. What happens to the balance that month?

  1. A. It decreases by $450, the portion of the payment applied to principal.
  2. B. It decreases by $2,400, the full payment amount.
  3. C. It increases by $450, because the interest exceeds the principal portion.
  4. D. It remains unchanged, because the payment covers only accrued interest.

Answer: A. Interest is paid first and the remainder reduces principal: $2,400 − $1,950 = $450. The balance would only rise if the payment failed to cover accrued interest.

5. Why does a lender care about the loan-to-value ratio?

  1. A. Because it measures the equity cushion protecting the lender if the collateral must be sold, which directly affects the lender's loss exposure.
  2. B. Because it determines the borrower's ability to make the monthly payment.
  3. C. Because it establishes the interest rate the lender must charge.
  4. D. Because it fixes the term over which the loan must be repaid.

Answer: A. Loan-to-value is a collateral risk measure. Capacity to pay is measured by income ratios, and neither the rate nor the term is fixed by it — though risk influences pricing.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 03

Security instruments and lien priority

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the structure of a California deed of trust and identify what the power of sale produces.
  • Compare the deed of trust with the mortgage and explain the consequences of the difference.
  • Identify the three parties to a deed of trust and state what each may and may not do.
  • Apply recording and priority rules, including the exceptions that defeat first-in-time.
  • Explain subordination and reconveyance and identify the risks each carries.
  • Describe the default remedies available and the security risks a lender and a broker must recognize.

1. Deed of trust structure

1.1 What a security instrument does

A security instrument pledges real property as security for an obligation. It does not create the obligation — the note does that — and it has no independent existence: a security instrument without a note secures nothing.

The note is the debt. The security instrument is the remedy.

1.2 The California instrument

California residential and commercial lending overwhelmingly uses the deed of trust, and it involves three parties.

PartyRole
TrustorThe borrower, who conveys title in trust as security
BeneficiaryThe lender, for whose benefit the security is held
TrusteeA neutral third party holding the power of sale

The memory device: the trustor gives the security; the trustee holds the power; the beneficiary benefits.

1.3 What the instrument contains

ElementFunction
PartiesTrustor, trustee, beneficiary
Legal descriptionThe property secured — not a street address
Granting languageThe conveyance in trust
Reference to the obligationIdentifying the note secured
Power of saleThe trustee's authority to sell on default
Borrower covenantsMaintain the property, pay taxes, maintain insurance, not commit waste
Acceleration and default provisionsWhat constitutes default and its consequence
Alienation clauseRights on transfer
Assignment of rentsWhere included, giving the beneficiary rights to rents on default
Future advances / dragnet clauseWhere included, securing additional or later obligations

1.4 The clauses that surprise borrowers

The assignment of rents. On income property, the beneficiary may have the right to collect rents on default. A borrower who assumes rents are his regardless has not read the instrument.

The dragnet (future advances) clause. Where present, it can secure obligations beyond the original loan. Its scope and enforceability are legal questions, and a licensee who tells a borrower it "only covers this loan" has interpreted an instrument.

Covenants to maintain insurance and pay taxes. Failure is a default independent of payment — a borrower current on payments whose hazard policy lapsed is in default under the instrument, and the lender may force-place coverage at the borrower's cost.

1.5 What the borrower retains

The borrower possesses, uses, and may transfer the property, subject to the security interest and to the alienation clause. The deed of trust does not turn the lender into an owner.

That is what Section 2's lien-theory discussion means in practice: the borrower is the owner; the lender holds a claim.

1.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the three parties and their roles, list the operative elements of the instrument, and identify a default that does not involve missing a payment.

2. Mortgage comparison

2.1 The two-party instrument

A mortgage involves two parties: mortgagor (borrower) and mortgagee (lender). There is no trustee and, ordinarily, no power of sale.

Deed of trustMortgage
PartiesThree — trustor, trustee, beneficiaryTwo — mortgagor, mortgagee
Power of saleHeld by the trusteeGenerally absent
ForeclosurePredominantly nonjudicialJudicial
SpeedFasterSlower
Deficiency judgmentGenerally not available after a nonjudicial saleMay be available, subject to limits
Post-sale redemptionGenerally noneA statutory redemption period may apply
Release on satisfactionReconveyance by the trusteeSatisfaction or release by the mortgagee

2.2 Why the third party matters

The trustee holds a power of sale — authority to sell the property on default without going to court.

That single feature produces everything in Section 6: the speed of California foreclosure, the reinstatement window, and the deficiency consequences. A licensee who understands why the trustee exists understands the rest of California's default framework.

2.3 Title theory and lien theory

Jurisdictions describe the security relationship differently. Some treat the instrument as passing legal title to the lender until repayment; others treat it as creating a lien while the borrower retains title.

California's deed of trust is generally treated as a lien for most practical purposes, notwithstanding its form as a conveyance in trust.

For a licensee the practical consequence is the one already stated: the borrower is the owner, and the lender holds a claim. The distinction becomes visible in questions about possession, transfer, and what the lender may do before a foreclosure completes — all of which are legal questions.

2.4 Terminology in practice

Borrowers, and much national material, use "mortgage" for any loan secured by real property. In California the instrument is usually a deed of trust.

A licensee should use the correct term in documents and should not correct a borrower's casual usage into a lecture — but should know which instrument the transaction actually uses, because the default consequences differ.

2.5 Other security devices

A land contract — also called a contract for deed or installment land contract — is a financing arrangement in which the seller retains title until the price is paid. It is treated differently from a deed of trust, carries its own risks for both parties, and its consequences are legal questions.

A security agreement and financing statement cover personal property, which matters where a transaction includes both real and personal property — a common circumstance in commercial and mixed transactions.

2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to compare the two instruments on all seven dimensions and explain what the power of sale produces.

3. Trustor, beneficiary, and trustee

3.1 The trustor

The borrower. Conveys title in trust as security, retains possession and use, and remains the owner for practical purposes.

Obligations under the instrument typically include paying the obligation, paying taxes and assessments, maintaining hazard insurance, maintaining the property, not committing waste, and complying with the alienation clause.

3.2 The beneficiary

The lender. Holds the secured claim, receives payments, and may enforce on default.

What the beneficiary may do: demand payment, declare a default, instruct the trustee to commence a nonjudicial sale, elect judicial foreclosure instead, consent or decline to consent under the alienation clause, and — where the instrument provides — collect rents on default and force-place insurance.

What the beneficiary may not do: take possession without a legal basis, sell without following the applicable procedure, or ignore the borrower-protective requirements that apply in the residential context.

The beneficiary can change. Notes are sold and beneficial interests assigned, which is why a borrower's payments may be directed to a servicer they never chose. The obligation follows the note.

3.3 The trustee

The party students understand least, and the one whose role most needs stating precisely.

The trustee holds bare legal title for the limited purposes of the instrument, and has essentially two functions:

  1. Reconvey when the obligation is satisfied, on the beneficiary's direction.
  2. Sell on default, under the power of sale, following the statutory procedure.

The trustee is not a party's agent in the ordinary sense. It acts on the beneficiary's instruction to commence a sale, and it owes duties in conducting one. It does not decide whether the borrower defaulted, negotiate, or advise anyone.

The trustee can be substituted. A beneficiary may substitute a trustee by recorded instrument, and in practice the trustee acting in a foreclosure is frequently a substituted trustee rather than the one originally named.

3.4 Servicers

Not a party to the instrument, but the party the borrower actually deals with. The servicer collects payments, maintains impound accounts, handles payoffs and loss mitigation, and communicates with the borrower.

Servicing transfers, sometimes repeatedly, and California and federal law impose requirements on servicers in the residential context — including contact and single-point-of-contact obligations in the foreclosure setting, addressed in Lesson 13.

A borrower confused about who owns his loan and who services it is asking a reasonable question, and the answer is that they can be different entities and both can change.

3.5 What a licensee says about the parties

May: identify the parties and explain each role mechanically; explain that the trustee holds a power of sale; explain that servicing may transfer.

May not: advise whether a default has occurred, whether a foreclosure is procedurally proper, whether a substitution was valid, or what a borrower's rights are against a beneficiary or servicer. Every one of those is a legal conclusion, and they arrive in exactly the moments when a borrower most wants a confident answer.

3.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state each party's role and limits, explain what a trustee does and does not do, and distinguish the beneficiary from the servicer.

4. Recording and priority

4.1 What recording accomplishes

California maintains a public record of documents affecting real property, and the system answers one question: who has notice of what?

Recording does not make a document valid, and failing to record does not make it invalid between the parties. Recording protects the recorded party against third parties.

4.2 The three kinds of notice

TypeWhat it is
Actual noticeThe person in fact knows
Constructive noticeThe law charges the person with knowing, because it was recorded
Inquiry noticeFacts that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate

Constructive notice is the engine. A recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so the law treats everyone as knowing it.

Inquiry notice is the one that surprises lenders, because nothing was recorded: someone visibly in possession who is not the record owner, an occupant paying rent to a third party, evidence of recent construction. Each is a fact prompting investigation, and a party may be charged with what the investigation would have revealed.

4.3 The general priority rule

First in time, first in right — as measured by recording, for those entitled to the recording system's protection.

The protection generally runs to a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer: one taking for value, in good faith, and without notice — actual, constructive, or inquiry.

A lender is an encumbrancer for value, which is why a lender's title work and its diligence about what is visible on the property both matter.

4.4 The exceptions that defeat first-in-time

These are what a mortgage licensee actually needs, because each can put a lender behind something recorded later.

ExceptionEffect
Property tax liensGenerally take priority regardless of when they attached
Mechanic's liensPriority may relate back to when work commenced — so a lien recorded after a deed of trust may outrank it
Subordination agreementA lienholder voluntarily takes a lower position
Purchase-money priorityCertain purchase-money security interests receive favored treatment
Special assessment liensMay carry their own priority treatment

4.5 The mechanic's lien problem

The exception a mortgage broker must be able to recognize, because it is the one that surfaces on a file that looked clean.

Priority may relate back to when work commenced — a date earlier than the lien's recording — which means a deed of trust recorded in between can be outranked. And lien rights arise from work rather than from a contract with the owner, so subcontractors and suppliers the owner never dealt with can have them.

The intake question: has any work been done on this property recently, by whom, and is everyone paid?

A borrower who renovated last spring with an unresolved contractor dispute has a title problem that has not appeared yet — and a construction lender has a priority problem.

This is why lenders on construction and recently improved property require indemnities, title endorsements, and evidence of payment. Whether a particular lien is valid or timely is a legal question, and the licensee's role is to surface the facts early and route them to escrow, title, and counsel.

4.6 Position language

First, second, and junior describe recording position, not loan type. A "second" is simply a deed of trust recorded after another.

Priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A junior lienholder wiped out by a senior foreclosure has lost its security whatever the merits of the debt.

4.7 The preliminary report

A preliminary report reports record title and states the terms on which the insurer would issue a policy, including its exceptions.

An exception is an item the policy will not insure against.

Three responses wrong in every case: treating an item as routine because most properties have one; asking title to "remove" an exception; and predicting an easement's or restriction's effect on the borrower's plans.

Distinguish exceptions from requirements. A requirement is something the insurer needs before issuing — a reconveyance, a resolution, evidence of trustee authority — and requirements are the items with deadlines attached.

4.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the priority rule and its exceptions, explain the mechanic's lien relation-back, and distinguish an exception from a requirement.

5. Subordination and reconveyance

5.1 What subordination does

A subordination agreement is a lienholder's agreement to take a lower priority position than it would otherwise hold.

The recurring situations:

Construction lending. A seller who carried financing is asked to subordinate so a construction lender can record in first position.

Refinancing a first with a second in place. Paying off and re-recording a first would ordinarily move the existing second into first position. A subordination agreement from the second keeps the new first ahead of it, and without one the refinance may not close.

Adding a new senior loan.

5.2 Why it matters so much

Priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A lienholder who subordinates has agreed to absorb a loss ahead of the party it moved behind.

Subordination is a significant decision, not a formality, and "it's standard" is the single most expensive sentence a licensee can say about one.

Whether a party should subordinate is a decision for that party with counsel. A licensee explains the mechanism and routes the decision.

5.3 Subordination clauses in the original instrument

Some instruments contain a subordination clause obligating the holder to subordinate to future financing meeting stated conditions. Their scope, the conditions, and their enforceability are legal questions.

A seller carrying financing who signs an instrument with an open-ended subordination clause has agreed to something they may not have understood, which is exactly why seller-carry documentation belongs with counsel rather than being assembled from a form. Lesson 12 develops this.

5.4 Reconveyance

When the obligation is satisfied, the beneficiary directs the trustee to reconvey, and a reconveyance is recorded releasing the deed of trust.

Payment of the debt does not clear the record. The recorded document does.

A borrower who says a loan was paid off in 2016 has stated a fact about the debt and nothing about the title. An unreleased deed of trust in a preliminary report requires a document, and obtaining one from a lender that has merged, been acquired, or ceased to exist can take weeks.

That is why the preliminary report belongs at the front of the queue. An unreleased lien discovered on day twelve of a fourteen-day period is a formality where a resolution should have been.

5.5 Partial reconveyance and release clauses

In a blanket loan securing multiple parcels, a release clause permits individual parcels to be released as they are sold, on the terms the instrument states — typically a release price.

A partial reconveyance effects that release. Whether a particular parcel qualifies, and on what payment, is governed by the instrument.

5.6 Assumption, subject to, and wraparound

Three structures a mortgage licensee must be able to distinguish.

StructureWhat happens
AssumptionThe buyer takes over the loan. Generally requires lender consent under the alienation clause, and the seller remains liable unless released by novation
Subject toThe buyer takes title without assuming; the loan remains the seller's obligation and remains secured by the property. Triggers the alienation clause
Wraparound (all-inclusive)A new loan encompassing an existing one, with the new lender collecting and paying the underlying loan

The assumption point is the one sellers get wrong. A seller who "let the buyer assume" and believes he is released has assumed a novation he did not obtain — and remains liable on a debt secured by property he no longer owns.

Wraparound structures carry particular risk, including exposure if the wrap holder fails to pay the underlying loan, and the alienation clause on the underlying loan. They belong with counsel, and Lesson 12 develops them.

5.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a refinance may require a subordination agreement, state what clears a paid deed of trust, and distinguish assumption from taking subject to.

6. Default remedies and security risk

6.1 What default is

A failure to perform an obligation under the note or the security instrument. Non-payment is the common form, and the instrument creates others: failure to pay taxes, failure to maintain insurance, waste, and unauthorized transfer triggering the alienation clause.

Acceleration is what makes default consequential. Without it a lender could pursue only missed payments; with it, the entire balance becomes due.

6.2 The two foreclosure paths

NonjudicialJudicial
MechanismThe trustee's power of saleA court action
SpeedFasterSlower
CostLowerHigher
Deficiency judgmentGenerally not availableMay be available, subject to limits
Post-sale redemptionGenerally noneA statutory redemption period may apply

The trade-off is the point. A beneficiary proceeding nonjudicially gets speed and gives up the deficiency; one proceeding judicially may preserve a deficiency claim and accepts a slower, costlier process.

In California residential practice, nonjudicial foreclosure predominates.

6.3 The nonjudicial sequence, in outline

The process is statutory and its details are legal. In outline:

  1. Default occurs, and the beneficiary elects to proceed.
  2. A notice of default is recorded, beginning the statutory period.
  3. A reinstatement period runs, during which the borrower may generally cure by paying the arrearage and permitted costs — not the accelerated balance.
  4. A notice of sale is recorded, published, posted, and mailed, after the applicable period.
  5. The trustee's sale occurs, and title passes by trustee's deed.

The reinstatement window is what borrowers misunderstand most. For a period, curing the arrearage restores the loan. After that window closes, the route is generally redemption before sale — paying the full accelerated amount — which is a materially different sum.

California also imposes borrower-protective requirements on servicers in the residential foreclosure context, including contact and single-point-of-contact obligations. The specifics are legal, and a licensee's role is to know they exist and route the borrower to counsel and to a HUD-approved housing counselor.

6.4 Deficiency

A deficiency is the shortfall where sale proceeds do not satisfy the debt. California restricts deficiency judgments substantially:

  • Generally unavailable after a nonjudicial sale, whatever the loan type.
  • Restricted for purchase money loans in defined circumstances — protection connected to the loan having been used to acquire the property.
  • Subject to limits even in judicial foreclosure, including valuation-based constraints.

Whether a deficiency is available in a specific case is a legal question with significant consequences, and it is exactly what a distressed borrower asks. The answer is a referral.

6.5 What happens to junior liens

A senior foreclosure generally extinguishes junior liens as claims against the property — while the underlying debts may survive as personal obligations, subject to the deficiency limits above.

That is why priority matters and why junior lienholders monitor senior loans. A second wiped out by a first's foreclosure has lost its security entirely.

It is also why a lender in second position prices for that risk, and why a broker arranging a second should be able to explain the exposure to an investor.

6.6 Security risk from the lender's and broker's side

The risks a secured lender carries, and that a broker arranging a loan should be able to identify:

RiskWhat it is
Priority riskBeing behind something unexpected — a tax lien, a relating-back mechanic's lien, an unrecorded interest with inquiry notice
Title riskA defect in the chain, a forged instrument, an authority failure
Value riskCollateral worth less than expected, or declining
Occupancy and use riskA property used differently than represented, affecting value and program eligibility
Insurance riskLapsed or inadequate coverage, or unavailability in a mapped hazard area
Condition riskDeferred maintenance, hazards, unpermitted work
Legal riskForeclosure limits, borrower protections, bankruptcy
Fraud riskIdentity, occupancy, income, appraisal, and straw-buyer patterns
Documentation riskAn instrument that does not secure what the parties intended, or a description error

6.7 Bankruptcy, in outline

A borrower's bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay halting collection and foreclosure activity, and a secured creditor's treatment depends on the chapter and the facts.

A licensee's role is recognition and immediate escalation. Continuing collection or foreclosure activity after a filing can carry serious consequences, and the analysis is entirely legal.

6.8 What the broker actually contributes

Nothing in this section authorizes a licensee to advise on remedies. What a broker contributes is surfacing the facts early enough that the right people can act:

  • Ask the recent-work question at intake, before a construction or refinance loan is arranged.
  • Order the preliminary report at the front of the queue and read the exceptions and requirements.
  • Reconcile the legal description across the instruments.
  • Confirm insurance is in force and adequate.
  • Escalate anything about identity, occupancy, authority, or a party who will not appear.
  • Route every question about rights, remedies, and validity to counsel.

A defect surfaced at intake is a condition. The same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

6.9 What the security instrument means to the borrower in front of you

This lesson has treated the deed of trust structurally. Borrowers experience it as a set of consequences, and a broker who can state those plainly is doing the part of the job the documents do not do.

What the borrower is actually agreeing to:

  1. He is conveying an interest as security, and Section 1 explains the mechanism. He keeps possession and use, and he remains the owner for practical purposes — which is the reassurance most borrowers need and rarely receive.
  2. The obligation is the note; the deed of trust is what secures it. Section 3 separates them, and the separation matters: the note is what he owes, and the instrument is what happens if he does not pay it.
  3. Priority is determined by the recording system, Section 4, which is why the order of recording is not a clerical matter and why a subordination — Section 5 — changes his position materially.
  4. A default has a defined sequence, Section 6.3, with defined opportunities that depend on where in the sequence he is. Reinstatement and redemption are different things with different amounts, and the difference is the single most consequential thing a borrower in trouble does not know.
  5. Reconveyance is not automatic in the sense he assumes. Section 5's mechanism should occur; whether it did is a question with a record, and a borrower who paid off a loan years ago and never confirmed may discover the problem at his next transaction.

Three questions to answer before he signs, whether or not he asks:

  • "What happens if I miss a payment?" The sequence, stated accurately, without prediction about what a servicer will do.
  • "What if I want to pay it off early?" Whether a prepayment provision applies, and what the instrument requires on payoff.
  • "What if I want a second loan later?" Priority, and what a lender in second position is agreeing to.

The professional boundary holds throughout. Section 6.8's point governs: the broker explains how the instruments work; the legal effect on this borrower's rights, in his circumstances, is counsel's. A broker who explains reinstatement as a concept is doing his job. A broker who tells a delinquent borrower what he can do about his particular default is not.

And the reason this belongs at the end of a security-instrument lesson. Every concept in Sections 1 through 5 exists in a document the borrower will sign without reading. The broker is the only participant with both the knowledge to explain it and a reason to be in the room — and Lesson 13's finding, that most servicing complaints are origination failures arriving late, begins with the explanation that was never given.

6.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to compare the foreclosure paths, explain the reinstatement window, state what happens to junior liens, and name the security risks a broker should surface.

Key terms

TermDefinition
Note versus security instrumentThe note is the debt; the security instrument is the remedy. Security without a note secures nothing.
Deed of trustCalifornia's dominant security instrument. Three parties: trustor, beneficiary, trustee.
Trustor / beneficiary / trusteeThe borrower conveying security; the lender benefiting; the neutral party holding the power of sale.
Power of saleThe trustee's authority to sell on default without court action. The feature producing nonjudicial foreclosure.
Assignment of rentsWhere included, the beneficiary's right to collect rents on default.
Dragnet (future advances) clauseWhere included, securing obligations beyond the original loan. Scope and enforceability are legal questions.
Non-payment defaultFailure to pay taxes, maintain insurance, or avoid waste — a default even where payments are current.
MortgageA two-party instrument — mortgagor and mortgagee — generally without a power of sale, foreclosed judicially.
Lien theoryCalifornia's deed of trust is generally treated as a lien: the borrower is the owner and the lender holds a claim.
Land contractSeller retains title until the price is paid. Treated differently, with its own risks, and a legal question.
Substituted trusteeA trustee replacing the one originally named, by recorded instrument. Common in foreclosure.
ServicerNot a party to the instrument, but the party the borrower deals with. Servicing transfers, and owner and servicer can differ.
Constructive noticeKnowledge charged because a document was recorded. The system's engine.
Inquiry noticeKnowledge charged from facts that would prompt investigation — an occupant who is not the owner, rent paid to a third party, evidence of recent construction.
Bona fide encumbrancerA lender taking for value, in good faith, and without notice.
First in time, first in rightThe general priority rule, measured by recording.
Property tax lien priorityGenerally takes priority regardless of when it attached.
Mechanic's lien relation-backPriority may run from when work commenced, so a lien recorded later can outrank a deed of trust — and rights arise from work rather than from a contract with the owner.
Exception versus requirementAn item the policy will not insure against; versus something the insurer needs before issuing. Requirements carry deadlines.
Subordination agreementA lienholder's agreement to take a lower position. A significant decision for that party with counsel — never "standard."
Subordination clauseA provision obligating a holder to subordinate to future financing meeting stated conditions.
ReconveyanceThe recorded release when the obligation is satisfied. Payment does not clear the record; the document does.
Release clause / partial reconveyanceIn a blanket loan, releasing individual parcels on the terms the instrument states.
AssumptionThe buyer takes over the loan, generally with lender consent — and the seller remains liable without a novation.
Subject toThe buyer takes title without assuming; the debt stays with the seller and stays secured by the property.
Wraparound (all-inclusive)A new loan encompassing an existing one, with the new lender paying the underlying loan. Carries particular risk and belongs with counsel.
Nonjudicial foreclosureSale under the power of sale. Faster and cheaper; generally no deficiency and no post-sale redemption.
Judicial foreclosureA court action. Slower and costlier; a deficiency may be available and a redemption period may apply.
ReinstatementCuring the arrearage and permitted costs within the statutory window — not the accelerated balance.
Redemption before salePaying the full accelerated amount after the reinstatement window closes.
DeficiencyThe shortfall after sale. Substantially restricted in California, and always a legal question.
Automatic stayThe halt on collection and foreclosure activity generally triggered by a bankruptcy filing. Recognize and escalate immediately.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A borrower is current on every payment. His hazard policy lapsed four months ago and he has not paid the second installment of his property taxes. He tells his broker he "can't be in default — I've never missed a payment."

Assess.

Solution. He may well be in default, and non-payment is only one form of it.

A deed of trust contains borrower covenants independent of the payment obligation: maintain the property, pay taxes and assessments, maintain hazard insurance, and not commit waste. Failure on any of them is a default under the instrument even where payments are current.

Two practical consequences follow. The lender may force-place coverage at the borrower's cost, which is typically far more expensive than a policy he could obtain himself. And the property tax lien attaching is one that generally takes priority regardless of when it attached — so it sits ahead of the lender's deed of trust, which is why lenders care about it more than borrowers expect.

What the licensee does not do is tell him whether a default has occurred or what the lender may do about it. Both are legal conclusions. Surface the facts, tell him to contact his servicer and restore coverage immediately, and route the rest.

Problem 2

A borrower asks why California foreclosures are "so fast" compared with what his cousin experienced in another state, and whether he will owe the difference if his house sells for less than he owes. His loan was used to purchase the home.

Explain the mechanism and address the deficiency question.

Solution. The answer traces to the third party. California uses a deed of trust with a trustee holding a power of sale — authority to sell on default without going to court. A two-party mortgage has no trustee and no power of sale, and is foreclosed judicially, which is slower and costlier.

The trade-off is the point. A beneficiary proceeding nonjudicially gets speed and gives up the deficiency; one proceeding judicially may preserve a deficiency claim and accepts the slower process. Nonjudicial predominates in California residential practice, and the borrower may also have no post-sale redemption period, where a judicial foreclosure might carry one.

On the deficiency: the licensee explains the framework and refers the question. California restricts deficiency judgments substantially — generally unavailable after a nonjudicial sale, and restricted for purchase money loans in defined circumstances, which his loan appears to be. But whether a deficiency is available in his case is a legal question with significant consequences, and the answer is a referral to counsel, not a reassurance.

Problem 3

A borrower says he sent his payment to "the bank that owns my loan," received a letter from a company he has never heard of, and does not know who to call. He also asks whether the trustee named on his deed of trust can help him work something out, and notes a different trustee's name appeared on a recent notice.

Explain each.

Solution. Owner and servicer can be different entities, and both can change. Notes are sold and beneficial interests assigned — the obligation follows the note — and the servicer, which is not a party to the instrument at all, is the entity that collects payments, maintains impounds, handles payoffs and loss mitigation, and communicates with him. Servicing transfers, sometimes repeatedly.

The trustee cannot help him work anything out. The trustee holds bare legal title for the limited purposes of the instrument and has essentially two functions: reconvey when the obligation is satisfied, and sell on default under the power of sale. It does not decide whether he defaulted, negotiate, or advise anyone.

The different name is ordinary. A beneficiary may substitute a trustee by recorded instrument, and the trustee acting in a foreclosure is frequently a substituted trustee rather than the one originally named.

What the licensee must not do is tell him whether a substitution was valid or a foreclosure procedurally proper — legal conclusions arriving exactly when he most wants a confident answer.

Problem 4

A lender is arranging a refinance. The preliminary report is clean. The borrower mentions he completed a $180,000 renovation four months ago and is in an unresolved dispute with the general contractor over the final payment. Two subcontractors he never met have been calling.

Identify the exposure and state what should happen.

Solution. A clean report is a snapshot, not a forecast, and mechanic's lien exposure is precisely what a current report can fail to show.

Two features make this the exception a mortgage licensee must recognize. Priority may relate back to when work commenced — a date months before any lien is recorded — so a lien recorded next month can outrank a deed of trust recorded before it. And lien rights arise from the work rather than from a contract with the owner, which is why subcontractors and suppliers the borrower never dealt with can have them.

This is why lenders on construction and recently improved property require indemnities, title endorsements, and evidence of payment — and why the intake question is has any work been done recently, by whom, and is everyone paid?

What should happen: surface it immediately to escrow, title, and counsel; obtain evidence of payment and any releases; and let title determine what it will insure. Whether a particular lien is valid or timely is a legal question, and the licensee's contribution is the timing — a defect surfaced at intake is a condition; the same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

Problem 5

A refinance is scheduled to close in eight days. The preliminary report, received this morning, shows an existing second deed of trust and an unreleased first from 2016 that the borrower says was paid off "years ago." The originator tells the borrower both are "just paperwork."

Assess and state what each requires.

Solution. Neither is paperwork, and the timing failure came first.

The existing second creates a priority problem. Paying off and re-recording the first would ordinarily move the existing second into first position. Keeping the new first ahead of it requires a subordination agreement from the second — and without one the refinance may not close. That is a decision for the second lienholder, not a formality: priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure, and a lienholder who subordinates has agreed to absorb a loss ahead of the party it moved behind. "It's standard" is the single most expensive sentence a licensee can say about a subordination.

The 2016 first requires a recorded reconveyance. Payment of the debt does not clear the record; the document does — and the borrower's recollection is not that document. Obtaining one from a lender that has merged, been acquired, or ceased to exist can take weeks.

The timing failure: the preliminary report belongs at the front of the queue. Discovered with eight days left, an unreleased lien leaves a scramble where a resolution should have been.

Problem 6

A seller carried a $200,000 second when he sold his rental three years ago. The buyer has now sold the property to a third party who took title "subject to" both loans. The original seller believed he was released when the first buyer "assumed" the underlying first. A wraparound structure has been proposed for the next transfer.

Untangle the positions.

Solution. Three distinct structures, and the seller has misunderstood the one that mattered most to him.

Assumption: the buyer takes over the loan, generally requiring lender consent under the alienation clause — and the seller remains liable unless released by novation. A seller who "let the buyer assume" and believes he is released has assumed a novation he did not obtain, and remains liable on a debt secured by property he no longer owns. That is this seller's position.

Subject to: the current owner took title without assuming. The loans remain the prior parties' obligations and remain secured by the property — so the debt and the ownership have been separated, and the alienation clause was triggered on the transfer.

Wraparound (all-inclusive): a new loan encompassing an existing one, with the new lender collecting and paying the underlying loan. It carries particular risk, including exposure if the wrap holder fails to pay the underlying loan and the alienation clause on that loan.

All of it belongs with counsel. A licensee explains the mechanics and does not assemble a seller-carry or wraparound structure from a form — and should note that an open-ended subordination clause in seller-carry documentation commits the seller to something he may not have understood.

Problem 7

A borrower two payments behind asks his broker: can he still keep the house, what does the notice of default mean, and can he just pay what he missed. The broker tells him the reinstatement period will let him "catch up any time before the sale."

Correct the advice and outline the sequence.

Solution. The advice conflates two different windows, and the difference is a large sum of money.

The nonjudicial sequence in outline: default occurs and the beneficiary elects to proceed; a notice of default is recorded, beginning the statutory period; a reinstatement period runs, during which the borrower may generally cure by paying the arrearage and permitted costs — not the accelerated balance; a notice of sale is recorded, published, posted, and mailed; and the trustee's sale occurs, with title passing by trustee's deed.

"Any time before the sale" is wrong. After the reinstatement window closes, the route is generally redemption before sale — paying the full accelerated amount — which is a materially different sum from the arrearage. That distinction is the one borrowers misunderstand most, and stating it wrongly can cost someone their home.

What the broker actually does: explain that the windows differ, and refer immediately and in writing — to counsel, and to a HUD-approved housing counselor. California also imposes borrower-protective requirements on servicers in the residential foreclosure context, including contact and single-point-of-contact obligations, and the specifics are legal. Predict nothing.

And if a second lienholder asks whether the first's foreclosure affects him: a senior foreclosure generally extinguishes junior liens as claims against the property, while the underlying debts may survive as personal obligations, subject to California's deficiency restrictions. He has lost his security entirely — which is why junior lienholders monitor senior loans, and why a broker arranging a second should explain that exposure to an investor before the money is placed.

Problem 8

A broker is arranging a loan on a property where: the borrower will not appear in person and acts through an intermediary; the occupant paying rent is not the record owner; the legal description on the draft deed of trust differs from the preliminary report; hazard coverage was declined because the property is in a mapped fire area; and the borrower's counsel mentions a bankruptcy filing "next month."

Identify each risk and state the broker's contribution.

Solution. Six risks, and the last requires immediate action.

Fraud and identity risk — a principal who never appears and acts only through an intermediary is a recognized pattern. Escalate to the broker; do not investigate alone or confront anyone.

Inquiry notice — an occupant who is not the record owner is a fact that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate, and a party may be charged with what the investigation would have revealed, recorded or not. It also threatens bona fide encumbrancer status, which requires taking for value, in good faith, and without notice.

Documentation risk — a description mismatch means the instrument may not secure what the parties intend. Reconcile the description across the instruments before anything records.

Insurance risk — coverage unavailability in a mapped hazard area is now a common cause of transactions failing, and it must be resolved early rather than at funding.

Legal risk and the automatic stay — a bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay halting collection and foreclosure activity, and continuing activity after a filing can carry serious consequences. Recognize and escalate immediately; the analysis is entirely legal.

What the broker contributes is timing, not advice: ask the recent-work question at intake, order the preliminary report first and read its exceptions and requirements, reconcile the description, confirm insurance is in force, escalate anything about identity, occupancy, or authority, and route every question about rights and validity to counsel. A defect surfaced at intake is a condition; the same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

Chapter summary

The note is the debt; the security instrument is the remedy, and security without a note secures nothing.

California uses a three-party deed of trust, and the trustee's power of sale produces nonjudicial foreclosure, the reinstatement window, and the deficiency consequences.

Borrower covenants create defaults that do not involve missing a payment — taxes, insurance, waste.

A mortgage is a two-party instrument foreclosed judicially, trading speed for a possible deficiency and a redemption period.

California's deed of trust is treated as a lien: the borrower is the owner and the lender holds a claim.

The trustee reconveys and sells, and does nothing else — it does not decide, negotiate, or advise. It can be substituted. The servicer is not a party to the instrument, and owner and servicer can both change.

Recording answers who has notice. Constructive notice comes from the record; inquiry notice comes from facts on the ground, and it threatens bona fide encumbrancer status.

First in time, first in right — subject to tax lien priority, mechanic's lien relation-back, subordination, and purchase-money priority. The mechanic's lien is the one a mortgage licensee must recognize, and the intake question is whether work was recently done and everyone is paid.

An exception is a risk not insured; a requirement is what must be done before issuing — and requirements carry the deadlines.

Subordination is a significant decision for the subordinating party with counsel, never a formality — and a refinance with an existing second usually needs one.

Payment does not clear the record; a recorded reconveyance does, and obtaining one can take weeks.

Assumption leaves the seller liable without a novation; subject to separates the debt from the ownership; wraparounds carry their own exposure. All belong with counsel.

Nonjudicial foreclosure trades the deficiency for speed. Reinstatement cures the arrearage; redemption requires the accelerated balance — and confusing the two can cost someone their home.

A senior foreclosure generally wipes out junior liens as claims against the property.

A bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay. Recognize and escalate immediately.

The broker's contribution is surfacing facts early, because a defect surfaced at intake is a condition and the same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify the security instrument and each party's role, identify every default asserted or available on the facts and what triggers each, state the priority position of each interest and identify any exception to first-in-time that applies, distinguish the exceptions from the requirements on the report given and state what must be obtained and by when, identify any subordination or reconveyance the transaction requires and whose decision it is, name each security risk present and the intake question that would have surfaced it, state what you would decline to conclude and why, and identify what you would route to escrow, to title, and to counsel and by what deadline. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A homeowner has a first deed of trust recorded in 2019 and a home equity line recorded in 2022. She wants to refinance the first loan into a new loan at a lower rate, keeping the equity line open. The new lender insists on being in first position. What must happen, and why?

  1. A. The equity line holder must agree to subordinate, because paying off and reconveying the 2019 loan would otherwise advance the 2022 line to first position ahead of the new loan.
  2. B. Nothing special is required, because the new loan replaces the old one and inherits its 2019 priority.
  3. C. The homeowner must pay off the equity line, because two liens cannot exist on one property after a refinance.
  4. D. The new lender must record first, which by itself establishes its priority over the existing line.

Answer: A. Priority follows recording order, and the new loan records in 2023 — behind the 2022 line — once the 2019 loan is reconveyed. Priority does not transfer to a replacement loan, multiple liens are perfectly ordinary, and recording a new instrument cannot leapfrog an earlier recorded one without the earlier holder's agreement to subordinate.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What role does the trustee play under a deed of trust?

  1. A. The trustee holds bare legal title for the limited purpose of the security and can convey the property at a trustee's sale on default or reconvey it on payoff.
  2. B. The trustee services the loan and collects the borrower's payments.
  3. C. The trustee owns the property until the loan is repaid and may occupy it on default.
  4. D. The trustee represents the borrower's interests against the lender.

Answer: A. The trustee's role is narrow and functional: hold bare legal title, sell on default, reconvey on payoff. It is neither a servicer, an owner-occupant, nor an advocate for either party.

2. How does a mortgage differ structurally from a deed of trust?

  1. A. A mortgage involves two parties, the mortgagor and mortgagee, while a deed of trust adds a third-party trustee holding title for the security's purpose.
  2. B. A mortgage secures residential loans while a deed of trust secures commercial loans.
  3. C. A mortgage is recorded while a deed of trust is not.
  4. D. A mortgage may be foreclosed nonjudicially while a deed of trust may not.

Answer: A. The number of parties is the structural difference, and it is the trustee's power of sale that makes nonjudicial foreclosure available. Property type and recording do not distinguish them.

3. What is a subordination agreement?

  1. A. An agreement by which a lienholder consents to have its lien take a lower priority than another lien, changing the order recording would otherwise establish.
  2. B. An agreement by which a borrower promises not to take on additional debt.
  3. C. An agreement by which a junior lender agrees to release its lien on payoff.
  4. D. An agreement by which a lender consents to a partial reconveyance of collateral.

Answer: A. Subordination reorders priority by consent. It is not a covenant against further borrowing, a release, or a partial reconveyance.

4. What is the effect of a full reconveyance?

  1. A. It releases the deed of trust from the record, evidencing that the secured obligation has been satisfied.
  2. B. It transfers ownership of the property from the trustee to the beneficiary.
  3. C. It converts the deed of trust into a mortgage.
  4. D. It extends the loan term and reinstates the borrower after default.

Answer: A. Reconveyance clears the security from the record on payoff. It does not transfer ownership to the lender, change the instrument's character, or reinstate a loan.

5. Which lien commonly takes priority regardless of when it was recorded?

  1. A. Property tax liens, which are generally given priority over other liens by statute.
  2. B. The first deed of trust recorded against the property.
  3. C. A judgment lien obtained by a creditor after litigation.
  4. D. A mechanic's lien recorded by a general contractor.

Answer: A. Property tax liens are the classic statutory exception to first-in-time priority. A first deed of trust takes priority by recording order rather than by statute, and judgment and mechanic's liens each follow their own rules without automatic superiority.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A lender is considering a second-position loan. What does the position principally affect?

  1. A. The order of payment from foreclosure proceeds, so a junior lienholder may recover nothing if the sale does not produce enough to satisfy senior liens.
  2. B. Whether the loan may be recorded at all.
  3. C. Whether the borrower may occupy the property during the loan term.
  4. D. Whether the loan may be secured by the same collateral as another loan.

Answer: A. Position determines who is paid first from limited proceeds, which is the entire economic significance of lien priority. Recording, occupancy, and shared collateral are unaffected.

2. What happens to junior liens when a senior deed of trust is foreclosed at a trustee's sale?

  1. A. Junior liens are generally eliminated from the property, though the underlying debts may survive against the borrower personally.
  2. B. Junior liens survive and remain attached to the property in the buyer's hands.
  3. C. Junior liens advance in priority to fill the position of the foreclosed lien.
  4. D. Junior liens must be paid in full by the foreclosing lender before the sale.

Answer: A. Foreclosure by a senior lienholder clears junior liens from the property while leaving the personal obligations in place. They neither survive against the property, advance, nor must be paid before sale.

3. A borrower asks whether a recorded deed of trust means the lender owns his home. What is the accurate explanation?

  1. A. No — the borrower holds ownership; the deed of trust is a security interest that gives the lender rights in the property if the obligation is not performed.
  2. B. Yes — the lender holds title until the loan is repaid in full.
  3. C. Yes — but ownership returns automatically once half the principal is repaid.
  4. D. No — the trustee owns the property and the borrower holds a leasehold.

Answer: A. The borrower owns and the security instrument encumbers. The trustee holds only bare legal title for the security's limited purpose, which is not ownership in any practical sense.

4. Two deeds of trust are recorded the same day against the same property. How is priority determined?

  1. A. By the recording sequence, since recording is timestamped, and by any agreement among the parties addressing priority.
  2. B. By the size of each loan, with the larger loan taking priority.
  3. C. By the date each promissory note was signed.
  4. D. Equally, with both lienholders sharing proceeds proportionally.

Answer: A. Recording is sequenced within the day, and parties can allocate priority by agreement. Loan size, note dates, and automatic pro rata sharing do not determine it.

5. Why does a lender obtain title insurance in a lender's policy separate from the owner's policy?

  1. A. Because the lender's insurable interest is its lien and its priority, which is distinct from the owner's interest in the property.
  2. B. Because owner's policies are optional while lender's policies are mandatory by statute.
  3. C. Because the lender's policy also covers the property's physical condition.
