  4. D. Because the owner's policy expires when the property is refinanced.

Answer: A. The two policies insure different interests — lien and priority versus ownership. Neither insures physical condition, and the owner's policy does not lapse on refinance.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 04

Mortgage markets, sources, and loan products

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish the primary from the secondary market and explain how secondary market standards shape origination.
  • Identify the depository and nondepository sources of mortgage credit and what distinguishes each.
  • Describe conventional, FHA, and VA financing at orientation depth and correct the statements licensees most often get wrong.
  • Compare fixed, adjustable, and balloon structures and explain the exposure each creates for the borrower.
  • Apply the owner-occupied and business-purpose distinction and explain what a certification does and does not establish.
  • Present products on a common basis, document the presentation, and identify what a licensee may not conclude about suitability.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: the two markets and the sources of credit55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: program types and rate structures50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: occupancy, purpose, and product presentation45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Primary and secondary markets

1.1 The two markets

The primary market is where loans are originated — the transaction between the lender and the borrower.

The secondary market is where existing loans are bought and sold between investors.

1.2 What the secondary market is for

Liquidity. A lender who can sell a loan recovers its capital and can lend again, so the supply of mortgage credit does not depend on any single lender's balance sheet or deposit base.

Without it, mortgage credit would be limited by how much capital each lender could hold for thirty years. With it, capital cycles.

1.3 The participants

ParticipantFunction
Government-sponsored enterprisesPurchase qualifying loans from lenders and package them for investors
Government-related issuersGuarantee securities backed by government-insured or guaranteed loans
Private investors and fundsPurchase loans and mortgage-backed securities
ServicersAdminister loans after sale, frequently as a separately traded right

Mortgage-backed securities are the mechanism: pools of loans are securitized and sold to investors, who receive the cash flows. That is how capital markets money reaches a borrower in Bakersfield.

1.4 The consequence that matters most to an originator

Underwriting standards flow backward from the secondary market.

Lenders originate to standards that make loans saleable. That is why documentation requirements can feel disconnected from a particular borrower's obvious ability to pay: the question is not only whether this borrower will repay, but whether the loan will meet the purchaser's requirements.

Three things follow, and they explain most originator frustration:

  • A documentation requirement that seems pointless may exist because an investor requires it, not because the underwriter doubts the borrower.
  • Standards change, sometimes quickly, because investor appetite changes.
  • "But he obviously qualifies" is not an argument that reaches the requirement.

1.5 Conforming and non-conforming

A conforming loan meets the purchasing standards of the enterprises that buy loans — including size limits that vary by area, and credit, documentation, and property requirements.

A non-conforming loan does not, for any reason. The recurring subcategories:

TypeWhy it does not conform
JumboExceeds the applicable size limit
Non-QMDocumentation or product features outside the qualified mortgage parameters
PortfolioHeld by the originating lender rather than sold, so it follows that lender's own standards
Private / hard moneyFunded by private investors on their own criteria

Non-conforming does not mean improper. It means the loan is not saleable into the standard channels, which generally makes it more expensive and sometimes makes it the only workable option.

1.6 Servicing

Servicing is a separate right that can be sold apart from the loan. A borrower's loan may be owned by one entity and serviced by another, and either can change.

A borrower confused about who owns his loan and who services it is asking a reasonable question, and Lesson 13 develops the servicing obligations.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain what the secondary market provides, state why underwriting standards flow backward from it, and distinguish conforming from non-conforming.

2. Depository and nondepository sources

2.1 The sources of mortgage credit

SourceCharacter
Depository institutionsBanks, savings institutions, and credit unions lending from deposits and other funds
Mortgage bankersOriginate and fund loans with their own or warehouse funds, frequently selling them
Mortgage brokersArrange loans between borrowers and lenders; do not lend their own funds
Private and hard money lendersIndividuals or funds, typically shorter term and higher rate, often collateral-focused
Seller financingThe seller carries all or part of the price
Institutional investorsInsurance companies, pension funds, and others, principally in commercial lending

2.2 Banker and broker: the distinction that matters

A mortgage banker funds the loan. A mortgage broker arranges it.

The consequences a licensee should be able to state:

Mortgage bankerMortgage broker
Funds the loanYes, at closingNo
UnderwritesFrequently, to investor guidelinesNo — the lender does
Lender of recordItselfThe funding lender
Access to productsIts own menuMultiple lenders' menus
CompensationFrom the loan's economicsDisclosed compensation, addressed in Lesson 09

A broker's value proposition is access and fit. A broker's compliance exposure is correspondingly about what was represented, what was disclosed, and how compensation worked — which is why Lessons 08 and 09 concentrate there.

A licensee must not describe the firm as a lender if it is a broker. A borrower who believes he is dealing with the lender misunderstands who decides, who is paid, and who holds his file.

2.3 Warehouse lines and correspondent lending

A warehouse line is short-term credit a mortgage banker uses to fund loans before selling them. It explains how a firm that is not a depository can fund at closing.

Correspondent lending is a middle position: the firm originates and funds in its own name to another lender's guidelines, then sells the loan to that lender.

Table funding is an arrangement in which a loan closes in one party's name but is funded by another at closing. Whether a particular arrangement is table funding, and what disclosure it requires, is a compliance question, and its treatment is one of the recurring subjects of examination.

2.4 Why the source affects the borrower

Not merely academic. The source determines:

  • What products are available and on what terms.
  • How quickly decisions are made and by whom.
  • What happens if the file has an exception — a portfolio lender may accommodate what a conforming channel cannot.
  • Where servicing goes.
  • How compensation works, and therefore what must be disclosed.

2.5 Private and hard money

Lending funded by private investors, typically shorter term, higher rate, and focused more on collateral than on the borrower's income.

Legitimate uses: bridge financing, transactions that cannot wait for conventional timelines, property conditions no conforming channel will accept, and business-purpose transactions.

The risks, developed in Lesson 12: cost, short terms and balloons, and the possibility of a borrower placed in a product that does not fit because it was the product available.

A licensee arranging private money must be able to explain why the borrower is in that product rather than a conventional one, and the file should show it.

2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish a banker from a broker and state the consequences, explain what a warehouse line does, and state what a licensee must not represent about the firm.

3. Conventional, FHA, and VA orientation

3.1 Conventional financing

A conventional loan is one not insured or guaranteed by a government agency.

Terms vary by the borrower's credit profile, the down payment, the property type, and occupancy. Where the down payment is below a program threshold, mortgage insurance is commonly required.

Mortgage insurance protects the lender. The borrower pays for it and receives access to financing at a lower down payment in exchange.

Students and borrowers consistently get that backwards, and correcting it is part of presenting the product honestly.

3.2 Government-backed programs: the common structure

An agency insures or guarantees the lender against certain losses, reducing the lender's risk and supporting terms — notably lower down payments — that qualifying borrowers might not otherwise obtain.

Three points licensees regularly misstate:

  1. The government is not the lender. Private lenders make the loans.
  2. The loans bear interest on ordinary terms.
  3. They are not restricted to new construction, and not to first-time buyers as a general matter.

3.3 FHA, in outline

FHA insures loans made by approved lenders. Characteristic features:

  • Lower down payment than most conventional programs.
  • Mortgage insurance — both an upfront amount and an annual amount collected monthly — which is a different structure from conventional mortgage insurance and can behave differently over the life of the loan.
  • Property condition and appraisal requirements the property must satisfy.
  • Loan limits that vary by area.

3.4 VA, in outline

VA guarantees loans made by approved lenders for eligible veterans, service members, and certain surviving spouses.

  • Eligibility is based on service, established by a certificate of eligibility.
  • No down payment is required in many cases.
  • No monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee typically applies, with exemptions.
  • Property condition and appraisal requirements apply, with the valuation issued as a notice of value.

The entitlement can be restored and reused, which matters to a veteran who has used it before, and is a question for the VA and the lender rather than the licensee's to compute.

3.5 The point that affects a seller's decision

Government programs commonly carry property condition requirements, and a property with deferred maintenance may not satisfy them.

That is a closing-probability question, not a preference.

A listing agent advising a seller to weigh offers should be able to explain that in neutral terms — and must not translate it into a preference against buyers using those programs, which raises the fair lending and fair housing issues Lesson 14 develops.

3.6 Other programs

USDA programs support financing in eligible rural areas for qualifying borrowers.

State and local programs, including California housing finance and down payment assistance programs, carry their own eligibility, occupancy, and repayment terms — and assistance that is a silent second or a shared-appreciation obligation is a real obligation the borrower must understand.

A licensee presenting assistance must present what it costs and what it requires, not only what it provides.

3.7 What a licensee may say about programs

May: explain the general characteristics of each program type; explain what mortgage insurance is and whom it protects; explain that eligibility and property requirements exist and where they are determined; recommend the borrower speak with more than one lender.

May not: determine eligibility; state a qualifying threshold as a rule; predict what a lender or agency will approve; recommend a specific program as suitable without the analysis Section 6 describes; or advise on the tax treatment of anything.

3.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the common structure of government-backed programs, correct the three misstatements, and explain whom mortgage insurance protects.

4. Fixed, adjustable, and balloon structures

4.1 The structures

StructureBehaviorThe borrower's exposure
Fixed rateRate and payment fixed for the termNone to rate movement; pays for that certainty
Adjustable rateRate changes per an index plus a margin, within capsPayment changes over time
HybridFixed for an initial period, then adjustableNone during the fixed period; full exposure after
Interest-only periodPayments cover interest only for a periodPrincipal is not retired, and the payment jumps at the end
BalloonPayments do not retire principal by maturityA large sum due at maturity
Negative amortizationPayment does not cover accrued interestThe balance grows, with a recast increase

4.2 The adjustable-rate terms

Four terms determine the rate at every adjustment, and a licensee who cannot state a borrower's own four should not be presenting the product.

TermWhat it does
IndexThe published measure the rate follows
MarginThe amount added to the index — set at origination and fixed
Adjustment frequencyHow often the rate resets
CapsPeriodic caps limit change at one adjustment; a lifetime cap limits total movement

The rate at adjustment is the index plus the margin, subject to the caps. Not the lender's discretion, and not the borrower's credit at that time.

Some notes add an initial cap applying to the first adjustment, and a floor below which the rate will not fall.

4.3 The calculation a borrower needs

Not "what will rates do" — nobody knows — but what happens if they move.

A 5/6 hybrid: 6.0% start, margin 2.75%, index currently 4.50%, caps 2/1/5.

Fully indexed rate today: 4.50 + 2.75 = 7.25%. The start rate is below it.

First adjustment, worst case: limited by the 2% initial cap → 8.0%. Subsequent adjustments: limited by the 1% periodic cap. Ceiling: 6.0 + 5 = 11.0% lifetime.

On a $500,000 balance, the payment at 6.0% is roughly $2,998; at 8.0% roughly $3,619; at the 11.0% ceiling roughly $4,672.

That table is the honest presentation. A borrower who has seen the worst case and accepted it has made a decision. One who was told "rates should come down" has been given a prediction.

4.4 What a licensee may never do with rates

Predict them. Mortgage rates respond to broader capital market conditions and are not set by any single institution.

"Rates will be lower in the spring, you can refinance then" is a prediction stated as certainty, on which a borrower may accept a payment he cannot otherwise afford.

It is also the sentence behind a large share of adjustable-rate complaints.

4.5 Interest-only and balloon exposure

An interest-only period produces a lower initial payment and retires no principal — so at the end, the borrower faces a payment recalculated to amortize the full original balance over the remaining, shorter term. The increase is larger than borrowers expect.

A balloon requires a large payment at maturity. The borrower's realistic paths are to refinance, sell, or pay it — and all three depend on conditions at maturity, including his credit, the property's value, and the availability of credit.

Refinance risk is the exposure to name. A balloon maturing in an unfavorable market is the structure's whole risk, and a borrower who assumes he will "just refinance" has assumed a market.

4.6 Rate locks

A lock fixes the rate for a period, and it is a recurring source of borrower complaints.

What a borrower must understand in writing, before he relies on it: what rate and points are locked, for how long, what happens if the loan does not close in time, whether an extension is available and at what cost, and what circumstances can void it.

A lock is not a guarantee that the loan will close, and a lock that expires because the file moved slowly is a foreseeable event rather than an accident.

4.7 Buydowns

A permanent buydown uses discount points to lower the note rate for the life of the loan — the Lesson 02 break-even calculation applies.

A temporary buydown reduces the payment for an initial period using funds placed in an account, after which the payment rises to the note rate amount.

The disclosure obligation is to present the payment after the buydown ends, with the same prominence as the initial payment. A borrower who budgeted to the first-year payment and did not register the third-year payment has been sold rather than advised.

4.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to compute a fully indexed rate and a worst-case path, name the four adjustable terms, and explain interest-only, balloon, and buydown exposure to a borrower.

5. Owner-occupied and business-purpose distinctions

5.1 Why this distinction carries so much

Consumer residential mortgage requirements — including the MLO endorsement requirement and much of the federal disclosure regime — attach to consumer-purpose loans secured by a dwelling. Loans made primarily for a business purpose are treated differently.

That makes the classification consequential, and it makes it a target for misuse.

5.2 Occupancy

Occupancy — owner-occupied, second home, or investment — affects pricing, program eligibility, and which consumer protections apply.

It is therefore a material fact the lender relies on, and misstating it is loan fraud.

A borrower who asks a licensee to record owner-occupancy on a property he intends to rent is asking for participation in that fraud. Decline plainly, explain why, and record the loan as it actually is.

Whether he could afford the payment either way is beside the point. The misstatement is not about whether he will pay; it is about obtaining terms on a false representation of the risk being priced.

5.3 Occupancy is a fact, not a category on a form

The recurring patterns a licensee should recognize:

PatternWhat it suggests
A "primary residence" the borrower will not move intoOccupancy misrepresentation
A second home in the same city as the primaryInvestment property in another name
A lease on the subject property dated before the applicationThe file contains its own contradiction
A borrower who cannot describe the property's location relative to his workStraw or absentee arrangement
Multiple simultaneous "primary residence" applicationsCoordinated misrepresentation

The third one is different in kind from a missing document. It is not a paperwork gap — the file itself contains the evidence contradicting a material representation to the lender. The response is escalation, not a judgment call about whether it matters.

5.4 Business purpose

A loan is business-purpose when it is made primarily for a business, commercial, agricultural, or investment purpose rather than for personal, family, or household purposes.

The determination rests on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts, and the analysis considers what the proceeds are used for, the borrower's relationship to the property and the activity, and the transaction's overall character.

5.5 What a certification does and does not establish

A borrower's signature on a business-purpose certification records his statement. It does not establish the fact.

A file assembled around a certification that the surrounding facts contradict is a file with a problem in it — visible to any examiner who reads the occupancy line, the intended use, or the lease dated before the application.

5.6 The errors run in both directions

Treating a consumer loan as business-purpose — because the borrower signed a certification, because the property is a rental, or because a manager instructed it. This is the more common error and the more serious one, because it strips protections the borrower was entitled to.

Treating every investment property loan as exempt from everything — which sweeps in requirements that still apply. A business-purpose classification does not suspend fair lending obligations, licensing requirements that attach independently, fraud prohibitions, or the firm's own standards.

5.7 Where the line is genuinely hard

Some transactions are genuinely close: a borrower refinancing a rental he once occupied; a cash-out on a primary residence to fund a business; a loan on a property with both a residence and a commercial use; a fourplex the borrower will occupy.

The response to a genuinely close case is not to pick the classification that is convenient. It is to route it to compliance and, where necessary, counsel — before the file is built around an answer.

A file constructed on the wrong classification is expensive to unwind, because the disclosures, the licensing analysis, and sometimes the product all rest on it.

5.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state why occupancy is material, recognize the misrepresentation patterns, state what a certification establishes, and identify both directions of the business-purpose error.

6. Product suitability and documentation

6.1 What a licensee may and may not conclude

May: describe products and their mechanics; compute and present comparisons; identify the questions a borrower should take to a lender, a tax professional, and counsel; explain what a feature exposes the borrower to; and record what was presented and what the borrower decided.

May not: determine that a product is suitable in the sense an underwriter or an advisor would; predict rates or values; state a qualifying threshold as a rule; advise on tax treatment; or present a comparison that omits a material difference.

6.2 The presentation standard

Products are presented on a common basis, and a comparison that omits a material difference is misleading even when every number in it is accurate.

The elements of an honest comparison:

  1. The same loan amount, or the difference stated.
  2. The same term and structure, or the difference stated.
  3. The note rate, the payment, the points, and the lender charges, each separately.
  4. The break-even where points differ.
  5. The APR, identified as a comparison tool with its assumptions.
  6. What is a lender charge and what is a third-party or prepaid item.
  7. For any adjustable or non-amortizing feature: the worst-case path, not only the initial payment.
  8. PITI, not principal and interest alone.

6.3 The features that require a plain-language explanation

Any feature that changes the payment or the balance in a way the initial figure does not show:

FeatureWhat must be said
Adjustable rateIndex, margin, caps, and the worst-case payment
Interest-only periodPrincipal is not retired, and the payment recalculates over a shorter remaining term
BalloonThe amount due at maturity and that refinancing depends on conditions then
Negative amortizationThe balance can grow while payments are made, and a recast can raise the payment sharply
Temporary buydownThe payment after it ends, with equal prominence
Prepayment penaltyThat it exists, what triggers it, and what it costs
Mortgage insuranceThat it protects the lender, what it costs, and whether and how it ends
ImpoundsThat the payment includes taxes and insurance and can change when they do

6.4 The questions that produce a fitting recommendation

Before presenting anything, the originator should know:

  • How long does the borrower expect to hold the property and the loan? This decides points, buydowns, and hybrid terms.
  • What payment is he comfortable with, as distinct from what he can qualify for?
  • What is his tolerance for payment change?
  • What cash does he have, beyond the down payment?
  • What is the property, and how will it be occupied?
  • What does he expect to happen — income change, a sale, a move?

The answers are recorded, because they are what makes a later presentation defensible.

6.5 The recurring failure

Not that a licensee computed something wrong. That a licensee presented the product the borrower could be approved for as though it were the product that fit him — and the borrower could not tell the difference.

The controls are simple: ask the holding-period question, present the worst case alongside the best, present PITI, present alternatives on a common basis, and record what was presented and what was decided.

6.6 What the file must show

  • The borrower's stated objectives and constraints, with dates.
  • The products presented, with the figures as presented.
  • The assumptions underlying each figure.
  • Every feature requiring a plain-language explanation, and that it was given.
  • The comparison as presented, on a common basis.
  • The borrower's decision, and any instruction departing from the recommendation.
  • Referrals made — to a tax professional, to counsel — and the response.

6.7 The test

Reconstructability: could a person who was not there determine what the borrower was shown, on what assumptions, and what he decided?

If a comparison in the file cannot be reproduced from the figures it contains, it is not a record of advice. It is a marketing document that happens to be in a loan file.

6.8 A worked product presentation

The borrower. Purchasing a primary residence at 720,000 with fifteen percent down. Employed on salary for nine years, stable. Two children, ages 4 and 7. He says he expects to stay "probably forever, but who knows." Reserves after closing: about four months of expenses. He mentions his brother-in-law told him adjustable loans are "how you actually save money."

Three structures are available, and Section 6.2's standard requires all three on a common basis.

What is held constant: the same loan amount, the same assumed closing date, the same horizon for total cost, and the same treatment of costs paid versus financed.

What is shown for each: rate, payment, worst-case payment where the payment can change, mortgage insurance where the down payment triggers it, total cost over the stated horizon, and every feature that changes the obligation.

The plain-language explanations Section 6.3 requires, each with its number:

On the fixed structure: the payment does not change; the mortgage insurance applies and here is what ends it and when.

On the adjustable structure: the rate is fixed for the initial period and then can change on a schedule, by a limited amount each time, to a stated maximum — and at that maximum the payment is this figure, which is the number the presentation exists to convey.

On the balloon structure: the payment is based on a longer schedule and the entire remaining balance is due on a date. The borrower must repay, refinance, or sell by then, and none of those is guaranteed to be available.

The suitability facts, from Section 6.4, and what they indicate.

"Probably forever, but who knows." The most common answer, and the least useful as stated. The follow-up is what makes it useful: what would cause you to move? A job change, a school change, a family need. A borrower with two young children and a nine-year employment history is not a short-horizon borrower, which weighs against paying for a rate that is fixed for a period shorter than his likely holding period.

Four months of reserves. Thin against a payment that can rise. This is a fact about payment-shock tolerance, and it is not a function of income size.

The brother-in-law. Not a reason for anything, and not a thing to argue with either. The response is the presentation: here is what the adjustable does under its worst case, here is what the fixed costs to avoid that, and the decision is yours.

What the broker does not do. Recommend a product, tell the borrower the adjustable is "safe because you'll refinance," present the initial payment as the payment, or characterize the fixed structure as expensive without showing what it buys. Section 6.1's boundary is that the conclusion is the borrower's, and Section 6.5's recurring failure is the presentation that made it for him.

What the file shows afterward, per Section 6.6: the three structures on a common basis with worst cases, the explanations given, the suitability questions asked and answered, and the borrower's selection with its date. Section 6.7's test applied: could a reviewer reconstruct the presentation without the broker present?

6.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to present two products on a common basis, list the features requiring plain-language explanation, and state what the file must show.

Key terms

TermDefinition
Primary marketWhere loans are originated, between lender and borrower.
Secondary marketWhere existing loans are bought and sold. Supplies liquidity so credit does not depend on one lender's balance sheet.
Standards flow backwardLenders originate to standards that make loans saleable — which is why a requirement can exist for investor reasons rather than credit reasons.
Mortgage-backed securityA pooled, securitized interest in loans, sold to investors.
Conforming loanOne meeting the purchasing standards of the enterprises that buy loans, including area size limits.
Non-conformingJumbo, non-QM, portfolio, or private. Not improper — just not saleable into standard channels, generally more expensive and sometimes the only option.
Servicing rightA separately tradable right. Owner and servicer can differ and both can change.
Mortgage bankerFunds loans with its own or warehouse funds, frequently selling them.
Mortgage brokerArranges loans; does not lend its own funds. A licensee must not describe a broker as the lender.
Warehouse lineShort-term credit used to fund loans before sale. How a non-depository funds at closing.
Correspondent lendingOriginating and funding in one's own name to another lender's guidelines, then selling to that lender.
Table fundingA loan closing in one party's name funded by another at closing. Its treatment and disclosure are compliance questions.
Conventional loanNot insured or guaranteed by a government agency.
Mortgage insuranceCommonly required below a down payment threshold. Protects the lender, paid by the borrower.
Government-backed structureAn agency insures or guarantees the lender. The government is not the lender, the loans bear ordinary interest, and they are not limited to new construction or first-time buyers.
FHAAgency-insured lending with lower down payments, upfront and annual mortgage insurance, property condition requirements, and area loan limits.
VAAgency-guaranteed lending for eligible borrowers, often with no down payment, no monthly mortgage insurance, a funding fee with exemptions, and a notice of value.
Property condition requirementsCommon to government programs. A closing-probability question for a seller — never translated into a preference against buyers using those programs.
Silent second / shared appreciationAssistance that is a real obligation. Present what it costs and requires, not only what it provides.
Index and marginThe published measure the rate follows; and the fixed amount added, set at origination.
CapsPeriodic limits at a single adjustment; a lifetime limit on total movement; sometimes an initial cap and a floor.
Fully indexed rateIndex plus margin today — the rate a discounted start rate will move toward.
Refinance riskThe exposure created by a balloon or a maturing structure: the paths all depend on conditions at maturity.
Rate lockA fixed rate for a period. Not a guarantee the loan will close, and its terms belong in writing before reliance.
Temporary buydownA reduced payment for an initial period. The payment after it ends is disclosed with equal prominence.
OccupancyOwner-occupied, second home, or investment. A material fact the lender relies on, and misstating it is fraud regardless of affordability.
Business purposeA loan made primarily for business, commercial, agricultural, or investment purposes, resting on the actual purpose and surrounding facts.
Business-purpose certificationRecords the borrower's statement. Does not establish the fact.
The two directions of errorTreating a consumer loan as business-purpose, which strips protections; and treating an investment loan as exempt from everything, which sweeps in requirements that still apply.
Common-basis presentationThe standard for comparing products. A comparison omitting a material difference misleads even when every number is accurate.
ReconstructabilityCould a person who was not there determine what the borrower was shown, on what assumptions, and what he decided.

Practice problems

Problem 1

An originator complains to his manager that an underwriter is demanding a documentation item that "makes no sense — the borrower has 40% equity and eight months of reserves, he obviously qualifies."

Explain why the requirement may exist anyway.

Solution. Underwriting standards flow backward from the secondary market. Lenders originate to standards that make loans saleable, because a lender who can sell a loan recovers its capital and can lend again — which is what the secondary market supplies and why mortgage credit is not limited by any single lender's balance sheet.

So the question is not only whether this borrower will repay. It is whether the loan will meet the purchaser's requirements, and a documentation item can exist because an investor requires it rather than because the underwriter doubts the borrower.

Two related facts worth knowing: standards change, sometimes quickly, because investor appetite changes; and "but he obviously qualifies" is not an argument that reaches the requirement.

If the loan genuinely cannot meet conforming standards, the alternative is a non-conforming channel — portfolio, non-QM, or private. Non-conforming does not mean improper; it means not saleable into standard channels, generally more expensive, and sometimes the only workable option.

Problem 2

A borrower tells an originator at a brokerage, "So you're the bank — you decide, right?" The originator says yes for simplicity. The firm arranges loans and does not fund them.

Assess, and state the consequences of the misstatement.

Solution. The statement is false and it misleads the borrower about three things at once.

A mortgage banker funds the loan; a mortgage broker arranges it. A broker does not lend its own funds, does not underwrite, and is not the lender of record — the funding lender is.

What the borrower now misunderstands: who decides — the lender underwrites, not the broker; who is paid and how — a broker's compensation is disclosed and is a distinct compliance subject; and who holds his file and his information.

A licensee must not describe the firm as a lender if it is a broker. The broker's actual value proposition is access and fit — multiple lenders' menus rather than one — and its compliance exposure is correspondingly about what was represented, what was disclosed, and how compensation worked.

If the borrower asks how a non-depository funds anything, the answer is a warehouse line — short- term credit a mortgage banker uses to fund before selling — which is a different arrangement from what this firm does.

Problem 3

Four statements made in one conversation: "FHA is a government loan, so the government is lending you the money"; "VA loans are only for first-time buyers"; "these programs are basically for new construction"; and "the mortgage insurance protects you if you can't pay."

Correct each.

Solution. All four are wrong, and the last is the one that changes what the borrower thinks he is buying.

The government is not the lender. Government-backed programs share a structure: an agency insures or guarantees the lender against certain losses, reducing risk and supporting terms — notably lower down payments. Private lenders make the loans, and the loans bear interest on ordinary terms.

Not first-time buyers. VA eligibility is based on service, established by a certificate of eligibility, and the entitlement can be restored and reused — a question for the VA and the lender, not the licensee's to compute.

Not new construction. Neither program is restricted to it.

Mortgage insurance protects the lender. The borrower pays for it and receives access to financing at a lower down payment in exchange. Borrowers consistently get this backwards, and correcting it is part of presenting the product honestly. Note also that FHA's structure — an upfront amount plus an annual amount collected monthly — differs from conventional mortgage insurance and can behave differently over the life of the loan, while VA typically carries a funding fee with exemptions rather than monthly insurance.

Problem 4

A seller has two offers at the same price, one from a buyer using an FHA loan. The listing agent tells the seller to take the other because "FHA buyers are a hassle." The property has a failing roof and peeling exterior paint.

Separate what is legitimate from what is not.

Solution. There is a legitimate fact here and an illegitimate translation of it.

Legitimate: government programs commonly carry property condition requirements, and a property with deferred maintenance may not satisfy them. A failing roof is exactly the kind of condition that can stop such a loan. That is a closing-probability question, and a seller is entitled to weigh probability of closing alongside price.

Not legitimate: "FHA buyers are a hassle" converts a property-condition fact into a preference against buyers using a program. That is a categorical judgment about people rather than an assessment of this property against this program's requirements, and it raises the fair lending and fair housing issues developed in Lesson 14.

The correct presentation is neutral and specific: this property has conditions that may not satisfy the program's requirements, here is what that means for the probability and timing of closing, and here is what repair or a different structure would change. The seller decides.

Problem 5

A 5/6 hybrid: 6.0% start rate, margin 2.75%, index at 4.50%, caps 2/1/5, balance $500,000. The originator tells the borrower "the start rate is great and rates should come down before it ever adjusts."

Compute the honest presentation and assess the statement.

Solution. Fully indexed rate today: 4.50 + 2.75 = 7.25%. The start rate is below it, which means that even with no market movement at all the rate moves up at the first adjustment — the single most important fact in this conversation, and the one the originator did not mention.

The worst-case path: first adjustment limited by the 2% initial cap → 8.0%. Subsequent adjustments limited by the 1% periodic cap. Lifetime ceiling 6.0 + 5 = 11.0%.

Payments on $500,000: roughly $2,998 at 6.0%; $3,619 at 8.0%; $4,672 at the 11.0% ceiling.

That table is the honest presentation. A borrower who has seen the worst case and accepted it has made a decision. One who was told rates should come down has been given a prediction stated as certainty, on which he may accept a payment he cannot otherwise afford — and it is the sentence behind a large share of adjustable-rate complaints.

Rates are never predicted. They respond to broad capital market conditions and are set by no single institution. And the rate at adjustment is index plus margin within the caps — not the lender's discretion and not the borrower's credit at that time.

Problem 6

A borrower is offered a temporary buydown reducing the payment for the first two years, on a loan with an interest-only period and a balloon at year seven. He says he will "just refinance before any of that matters." His rate lock expires in eleven days and the file is missing two conditions.

Identify every exposure and what must be presented.

Solution. Four exposures, and the borrower's plan depends on all of them going well.

The temporary buydown: the payment after it ends must be presented with equal prominence to the initial payment. A borrower who budgeted to the first-year payment and never registered the third-year payment has been sold rather than advised.

The interest-only period: principal is not retired, so at the end the payment recalculates to amortize the full original balance over the remaining, shorter term. The increase is larger than borrowers expect.

The balloon: a large sum due at maturity, with only three real paths — refinance, sell, or pay — and all three depend on conditions at maturity, including his credit, the property's value, and whether credit is available. "I'll just refinance" assumes a market, and that is refinance risk.

The lock: it fixes a rate for a period and is not a guarantee the loan will close. He needs in writing what rate and points are locked, for how long, what happens if the loan does not close in time, whether an extension is available and at what cost, and what voids it. A lock that expires because the file moved slowly is a foreseeable event, not an accident — and two outstanding conditions with eleven days left is exactly that situation.

Problem 7

A branch manager instructs an originator to process a loan as business-purpose on a fourplex the borrower will occupy, "since it's an income property," and to have the borrower sign the business- purpose certification. The file also contains a lease on the subject property dated a month before the application.

Assess both, and state which is different in kind.

Solution. The instruction inverts the analysis and the certification does not fix it.

Consumer residential mortgage requirements — including the MLO endorsement requirement and much of the federal disclosure regime — attach to consumer-purpose loans secured by a dwelling. A borrower occupying one unit points hard toward consumer purpose, and "it's an income property" is not the test. The determination rests on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts, considering what the proceeds fund, the borrower's relationship to the property and the activity, and the transaction's overall character.

A signature records the borrower's statement; it does not establish the fact — and a file built around a certification the surrounding facts contradict is visible to any examiner who reads the occupancy line.

The lease is different in kind. It is not a missing document or a late delivery: the file itself contains the evidence contradicting a material representation to the lender. The response is escalation, not a judgment call about whether it matters or whether the borrower could qualify either way.

The originator declines, does not transmit the file, and escalates above the manager. Following the instruction while noting it was directed documents that he knew — and misstating occupancy is loan fraud regardless of affordability, because the misstatement is about obtaining terms on a false representation of the risk being priced.

Problem 8

An originator presents one product: a 30-year fixed at 6.25%, principal and interest of $2,398, "with no points." He does not ask how long the borrower plans to stay, does not mention taxes and insurance, and does not present the 15-year or the buydown alternatives the lender offers. The borrower is a physician relocating on a two-year contract.

Identify the failures and state what the file must show.

Solution. The recurring failure in this lesson: presenting the product the borrower could be approved for as though it were the product that fit him — and the borrower could not tell the difference.

The holding-period question was never asked, and it is the one that decides points, buydowns, and hybrid terms. A borrower on a two-year contract is precisely the case where a break-even analysis matters and where a hybrid or a no-point structure may fit better than a long fixed term.

The payment quoted was P&I, not PITI. A borrower quoted principal and interest and later shown the full housing payment will feel misled — and in California the property tax line is most often understated, because a buyer's taxes reset on the change in ownership rather than tracking the seller's bill.

Alternatives were not presented on a common basis. A comparison must carry the same amount, term, and structure or state the differences; the note rate, payment, points, and lender charges separately; the break-even where points differ; the APR identified as a comparison tool with its assumptions; what is a lender charge versus a third-party or prepaid item; and the worst-case path for any adjustable or non-amortizing feature.

What the file must show: the borrower's stated objectives and constraints with dates; the products presented with the figures as presented; the assumptions underlying each; that every feature requiring plain-language explanation received one; the comparison on a common basis; the borrower's decision; and any referrals made and the response.

The test is reconstructability. If a comparison cannot be reproduced from the figures it contains, it is not a record of advice — it is a marketing document that happens to be in a loan file.

Chapter summary

The secondary market supplies liquidity, and underwriting standards flow backward from it — which is why a requirement can exist for investor reasons rather than credit reasons.

Conforming, jumbo, non-QM, portfolio, and private describe saleability, not propriety.

A banker funds; a broker arranges. Never describe a broker as the lender, because it misleads the borrower about who decides, who is paid, and who holds the file.

Government-backed means insured or guaranteed, not government-lent. The loans bear ordinary interest, are not limited to first-time buyers or new construction, and mortgage insurance protects the lender.

Property condition requirements are a closing-probability fact — never translated into a preference against buyers using a program.

An adjustable rate is index plus margin within caps. Compute the fully indexed rate, present the worst-case path, and never predict rates.

Interest-only, balloon, and temporary buydown structures each hide a later payment. Present it with equal prominence, and name refinance risk rather than assuming a market.

A rate lock is not a guarantee the loan will close, and its terms belong in writing before reliance.

Occupancy is a material fact and misstating it is fraud regardless of affordability. Learn the patterns, and treat a file containing its own contradiction as an escalation rather than a judgment call.

A business-purpose certification records a statement; the actual purpose governs — and the error runs in both directions, with the more serious one stripping protections the borrower was entitled to.

Route genuinely close classification questions before the file is built around an answer.

Present on a common basis, explain every feature that changes the payment or the balance, quote PITI, and ask the holding-period question first.

The file must let someone who was not there reconstruct what was shown, on what assumptions, and what was decided.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify the source and channel involved and what the borrower must be told about the firm's role, classify the loan's purpose and occupancy and state the facts your classification rests on, present every product discussed on a common basis with the figures and assumptions shown, compute the fully indexed rate and worst-case path for any adjustable feature and the payment following any buydown or interest-only period, identify every feature requiring a plain-language explanation and state what you would say, identify anything in the file that contradicts a representation and what you would do about it, state what you would decline to conclude or predict, and list what the file must contain for the presentation to be reconstructable. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A borrower who owns four rental houses wants a loan to buy a fifth rental property. The originator normally works with residential owner-occupied products and tells the borrower he will 'just use the standard consumer loan process, it's simpler.' What is wrong with that approach?

  1. A. A loan for an investment purchase is generally a business-purpose loan rather than a consumer loan, so a different disclosure and compliance framework and different products apply — the classification must be determined by the loan's purpose, not by convenience.
  2. B. Nothing is wrong, since the borrower is an individual and the collateral is residential property.
  3. C. The only problem is that investment loans carry higher rates, which must be disclosed.
  4. D. The only problem is that the borrower already owns four properties, which disqualifies him.

Answer: A. Purpose determines classification, and consumer-purpose and business-purpose loans sit under different regimes with different disclosures and products. The borrower being an individual and the collateral being residential do not make it consumer credit, and pricing and property count are separate questions.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What distinguishes the primary mortgage market from the secondary market?

  1. A. The primary market is where loans are originated to borrowers; the secondary market is where those existing loans are bought and sold among investors.
  2. B. The primary market handles first liens and the secondary market handles second liens.
  3. C. The primary market serves owner-occupants and the secondary market serves investors buying property.
  4. D. The primary market is regulated by states and the secondary market is unregulated.

Answer: A. Origination versus trading of existing loans is the distinction. It is unrelated to lien position, to who occupies the property, or to the presence of regulation.

2. How does a depository lender differ from a nondepository mortgage lender?

  1. A. A depository funds loans partly from customer deposits it holds; a nondepository has no deposits and funds through warehouse lines, sales into the secondary market, or investor capital.
  2. B. A depository lends only for owner-occupied property while a nondepository lends only for investment property.
  3. C. A depository originates loans while a nondepository only services them.
  4. D. A depository is regulated while a nondepository is not.

Answer: A. The funding source is the distinction. Both types originate, both may lend on various property types, and both are subject to regulation, though by different regulators.

3. What generally characterizes a government-backed loan program compared to a conventional loan?

  1. A. A government agency insures or guarantees the lender against certain losses, which supports terms such as lower down payments for qualifying borrowers.
  2. B. The government lends the money directly to the borrower.
  3. C. The loan carries no interest for qualifying borrowers.
  4. D. The loan may be used only for newly constructed homes.

Answer: A. The agency's role is insurance or guaranty to the lender, which reduces lender risk and supports more accessible terms. The government is not the lender, the loans bear interest, and they are not limited to new construction.

4. What is the essential feature of an adjustable-rate mortgage?

  1. A. The interest rate changes over the loan's life according to a specified index plus a margin, within any caps stated in the note.
  2. B. The payment amount is fixed while the term lengthens or shortens with rate changes.
  3. C. The rate is set by the lender's discretion at each adjustment date.
  4. D. The rate is fixed for the first year and then becomes permanently fixed at a market rate.

Answer: A. Index plus margin, subject to caps, is the mechanism. The payment typically changes with the rate, adjustments are not discretionary, and the rate continues to adjust rather than becoming permanently fixed.

5. What should drive a product recommendation to a borrower?

  1. A. The borrower's financial circumstances, plans, and tolerance for payment change, evaluated against the product's terms and risks.
  2. B. The product that produces the highest compensation for the originator.
  3. C. The product the borrower's neighbor or family member used successfully.
  4. D. The product with the lowest initial monthly payment.

Answer: A. Suitability turns on the borrower's own circumstances and the risks he would carry. Originator compensation, anecdote, and the lowest teaser payment each substitute something else for that analysis.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. Why does the secondary market influence what loan products a borrower can obtain?

  1. A. Because originators generally must be able to sell the loans they make, so investor requirements shape which products and borrower profiles are available.
  2. B. Because the secondary market sets the interest rate each borrower is charged.
  3. C. Because the secondary market approves each individual borrower's application.
  4. D. Because loans that cannot be sold are prohibited from being made.

Answer: A. Salability drives product availability, which is why investor guidelines feel like rules to a borrower. The secondary market neither prices individual loans, underwrites individual borrowers, nor prohibits portfolio lending.

2. A borrower wants the lowest possible payment for the first five years and plans to sell in year four. What is the sound approach?

  1. A. Present the products that fit that horizon along with the risks if the plan changes, and document what was explained, since plans change more often than borrowers expect.
  2. B. Recommend the product with the lowest initial payment, since it matches his stated plan.
  3. C. Recommend a long fixed-rate loan regardless, since it is always the safest choice.
  4. D. Decline to advise, since product selection is the lender's decision.

Answer: A. Matching the product to the stated horizon is appropriate, but the plan may not hold — so the risks and the record of the discussion matter. Neither blindly minimizing the payment nor defaulting to the most conservative product is advice, and the originator does have a role.

3. What characterizes a portfolio loan?

  1. A. The lender keeps the loan on its own books rather than selling it, which allows more flexible underwriting but concentrates the risk with that lender.
  2. B. The loan is secured by a portfolio of several properties at once.
  3. C. The loan is sold into the secondary market immediately after closing.
  4. D. The loan is originated by a broker rather than by a lender.

Answer: A. A portfolio loan is defined by the lender retaining it. Multi-property collateral, immediate sale, and broker origination describe other things entirely.

4. Why does owner-occupancy status matter to a loan's terms and compliance treatment?

  1. A. It affects risk pricing, program eligibility, and which consumer protection requirements apply, which is why occupancy misrepresentation is treated as a serious matter.
  2. B. It affects only the property tax treatment of the purchase.
  3. C. It determines whether the loan may be secured by a deed of trust.
  4. D. It affects only whether the borrower may rent the property later.

Answer: A. Occupancy drives pricing, eligibility, and which protections attach — which is exactly why misstating it is fraud rather than a technicality. It is not merely a tax or a security-instrument question.

5. A borrower asks why two lenders quoted materially different rates for the same loan. What is the accurate explanation?

  1. A. Pricing reflects each lender's cost of funds, risk appetite, investor requirements, margins, and the specific loan characteristics, so quotes legitimately differ.
  2. B. One lender must be quoting improperly, since rates are set uniformly.
  3. C. The difference reflects only the originator's compensation.
  4. D. The difference means one lender has not yet underwritten the file.

Answer: A. Rates are set by each lender within its own economics and risk view, so differences are normal. Uniform pricing, compensation alone, and incomplete underwriting do not explain ordinary quote variation.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 05

Application, borrower information, and qualification

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the application workflow, identify what constitutes an application, and explain what taking one triggers.
  • Collect and document income, asset, and liability information accurately, and identify what must be verified rather than accepted.
  • Explain how credit history and capacity are assessed and what a licensee may and may not say about credit.
  • Apply the occupancy and property purpose determination and recognize the patterns that contradict a stated purpose.
  • Compute debt-to-income ratios correctly and explain what they measure without stating thresholds as rules.
  • Handle adverse information honestly, and build an application record that is accurate and reconstructable.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: the application workflow and borrower information55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: credit, capacity, occupancy, and purpose50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: debt-to-income analysis and record accuracy45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Loan application workflow

1.1 The sequence

StageWhat happens
InquiryThe consumer contacts the firm; general information is exchanged
PrequalificationAn informal assessment on stated information
PreapprovalA lender review of supporting information, subject to conditions
ApplicationThe formal submission that triggers disclosure obligations
ProcessingDocuments collected, third-party reports ordered, the file assembled
UnderwritingThe credit decision, with conditions
Approval or denialThe decision, with adverse action requirements where applicable
Closing and fundingLessons 09 through 11

1.2 The three levels of assessment

Borrowers, sellers, and new licensees conflate these constantly, and the distinctions are practical rather than academic.

BasisWhat it establishesWhat it does not
PrequalificationLargely stated informationA rough borrowing rangeVerification of anything
PreapprovalLender review of supporting informationA likely amount, subject to conditionsA commitment to lend
Loan commitmentUnderwriting completeSubstantially more certaintyImmunity from changed circumstances

None guarantees funding. All remain contingent on the property, the appraisal, and the borrower's circumstances holding through funding.

A licensee who tells a borrower he is "approved" when a preapproval was issued has misdescribed the file's status, and the borrower will make an offer on that description.

1.3 What constitutes an application

This is the operative compliance question in the section, because taking an application triggers obligations — disclosure delivery timing, adverse action requirements, and the MLO endorsement requirement itself.

Under the federal framework, an application is generally understood to exist when the creditor has received the information it needs to evaluate the request — conventionally described as six items: the consumer's name, income, Social Security number to obtain a credit report, the property address, an estimate of the property's value, and the loan amount sought.

Two consequences licensees must understand:

  1. An application can exist before anyone completes a form. Collecting the six items in a conversation and an email exchange can constitute an application, and the disclosure clock does not wait for a signature.
  2. Structuring to avoid the trigger is a compliance problem, not a technique. Deliberately withholding a request for one of the items in order to delay disclosures is exactly the conduct the definition was written against.

Whether a particular set of facts constitutes an application is a compliance question the firm must answer with a written policy, not one an originator resolves case by case.

1.4 What taking an application triggers

  • Disclosure delivery within defined periods, developed in Lessons 07 and 09.
  • Adverse action obligations if the request is denied, developed in Lesson 06.
  • Record retention for the application and the file.
  • Government monitoring information collection where applicable, developed in Lesson 07.
  • The MLO endorsement requirement, since taking a residential mortgage loan application for compensation is what the endorsement covers.

1.5 The uniform application

Residential applications are generally taken on a standardized form capturing borrower information, employment, income, assets, liabilities, the property, the loan, declarations, and demographic information.

Three disciplines about completing it:

Every item is answered. A blank is ambiguous, and an ambiguous application is one nobody can later show was accurate.

The borrower's information is the borrower's statement. A licensee who fills in an answer the borrower did not give has misattributed a representation the lender will rely on.

Estimates are identified as estimates. A value estimate and a documented value are different things, and a file that does not distinguish them cannot be reconstructed.

1.6 Withdrawal and incomplete applications

An application may be withdrawn by the borrower or may become incomplete where requested information is not supplied. Each carries its own treatment under the adverse action framework, and recording which occurred, when, and on what communication is what makes the treatment defensible.

An application quietly abandoned and never dispositioned is a file with a gap in it, and it is the kind an examiner samples.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish the three assessment levels, state what constitutes an application and what it triggers, and explain why structuring to avoid the trigger is a problem.

2. Income, asset, and liability information

2.1 The three categories

CategoryWhat it establishes
IncomeCapacity to repay
AssetsFunds to close, reserves, and the source of both
LiabilitiesExisting obligations competing with the new payment

Each is verified rather than accepted, and the verification is what distinguishes an application from a conversation.

2.2 Income

What is generally documented: wage and salary income; self-employment income; bonus, commission, and overtime; retirement and Social Security; rental income; investment income; and other recurring receipts.

The recurring analytical questions:

Is it stable? Income that has recently begun, or that fluctuates, is assessed differently from steady salary. The lender's concern is whether it will continue.

Is it continuing? Income with a known end — a contract, a benefit with a termination date, a temporary assignment — is treated differently.

Is it documented? Stated income that cannot be documented is not income for underwriting purposes, whatever its reality.

Is it gross or net? Ratios use gross income, and a borrower who reports take-home pay has given a different number than the one the analysis needs.

2.3 Self-employment and variable income

The area where files most often go wrong, and where an originator's care matters most.

Self-employment income is typically established from tax returns and business documentation over a period, with adjustments — which means the figure the borrower thinks of as his income and the figure underwriting uses can differ substantially, in either direction.

Commission and bonus income is generally averaged over a period, and a borrower whose commission fell this year cannot be assessed on last year's figure alone.

Rental income is generally established from leases and tax returns, with a vacancy factor applied — so a borrower quoting gross rents is quoting a number that will be reduced.

A licensee who quotes a borrower a qualifying amount based on the borrower's own description of his self-employment income, without documentation, has set an expectation the file may not support. The honest position is that the figure is preliminary until the documents are reviewed.

2.4 Assets

What is documented: deposit accounts, investment accounts, retirement accounts, proceeds from a sale, gift funds, and business funds where permitted.

Two questions attach to every asset:

Is it there? Documented by statements, generally covering a period rather than a single day.

Where did it come from? This is sourcing, and it is what a large recent deposit triggers.

2.5 Large deposits and sourcing

A deposit inconsistent with the borrower's documented income requires explanation, and the reason is substantive rather than bureaucratic.

An undisclosed loan deposited as though it were savings is a hidden obligation that undermines the entire capacity analysis. The ratios computed on the borrower's documented debts would be wrong.

Legitimate sources are documented and accepted: a sale, a bonus, a tax refund, a transfer between the borrower's own accounts, a documented gift.

A gift and a loan are treated differently, which is why a gift generally requires documentation that it is a gift with no repayment expected.

What a licensee must never do: advise a borrower to deposit funds earlier so they "season," to break a deposit into smaller amounts, or to characterize a loan as a gift. Each is a suggestion to defeat the verification, and the last is a misrepresentation to the lender.

2.6 Liabilities

What is captured: installment debts, revolving accounts, other mortgages, student loans, alimony and child support, and obligations that will survive closing.

The recurring issues:

Debts not on the credit report. A private loan, a family obligation, an obligation guaranteed for someone else. The borrower is asked, and the answer belongs on the application.

Debts being paid by someone else. A car loan a business pays, an obligation a former spouse was ordered to pay. The treatment is an underwriting question, and the documentation requirement is real.

Debts about to be incurred. A borrower planning to finance furniture or a vehicle before closing is planning to change the analysis, and Section 5 addresses it.

Contingent liabilities. A co-signed obligation is an obligation, whatever the arrangement between the parties.

2.7 What a licensee does with the information

Collects it accurately, records what the borrower said, and identifies what has been documented and what has not.

Does not decide what qualifies, compute what the underwriter will accept, tell a borrower which debts "won't count," or omit something because it seems immaterial.

The application is a set of representations the lender relies on in pricing risk. Completeness is not a courtesy to the underwriter; it is the accuracy of the representation.

2.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to name what is verified in each category, explain why a large deposit requires sourcing, and state what a licensee must never suggest about deposits.

3. Credit history and capacity

3.1 What credit information does

Credit history supports an assessment of the borrower's willingness and demonstrated ability to repay obligations. It sits alongside capacity — the income-and-obligations analysis of Section 5 — and collateral.

The conventional framing is the three C's: credit, capacity, and collateral. Some add capital — the borrower's own funds in the transaction — and conditions, the economic and transactional context.

3.2 What a credit report contains

Identifying information; accounts with balances, payment history, and status; public record and collection information where reported; and inquiries.

Three things a licensee should understand about the data:

It can be wrong. Errors occur, and the borrower has rights to dispute them under the framework Lesson 07 develops.

It is a snapshot. A report pulled today reflects what was reported through a date, and lenders commonly re-check before funding.

Inquiries are visible. A borrower shopping with several lenders will show several inquiries, and the treatment of multiple mortgage inquiries within a window is a scoring question rather than a licensee's to explain in detail.

3.3 Permissible purpose and authorization

A consumer report may be obtained only for a permissible purpose, and in this context that means the borrower's transaction.

Two disciplines:

Obtain and document authorization. Pulling a report without one is a problem regardless of intention.

Do not pull a report for a purpose other than the transaction. Curiosity, a favor, or evaluating someone who is not an applicant are not permissible purposes.

3.4 What a licensee may and may not say about credit

May: explain what a credit report contains and that lenders use it; explain that scores exist and are produced by models; explain that the borrower has rights to obtain and dispute report information; and tell the borrower what the report actually shows.

May not: predict a score; tell a borrower what score he "needs," which states a threshold as a rule; promise that a particular action will raise a score; advise on repairing or disputing specific items as a strategy; or tell a borrower to close or open accounts to improve his position.

The last two are where originators most often exceed the line, because the advice feels helpful and the borrower is asking for it. Credit counseling is a distinct service, and telling a borrower to dispute accurate information is telling him to file a false dispute.

3.5 Adverse credit information

Late payments, collections, charge-offs, judgments, foreclosures, short sales, and bankruptcies each carry their own treatment, and waiting periods and requirements vary by program.

The originator's job with adverse information is to surface it early and document the explanation. A borrower with a five-year-old bankruptcy has a file that can be assembled; the same borrower whose bankruptcy surfaces at underwriting has a file that stalls.

The letter of explanation is a standard mechanism: the borrower explains the circumstance in his own words. It is the borrower's statement, and a licensee who drafts it for him has authored a representation the borrower will sign.

3.6 Capacity, briefly

Capacity is the income-and-obligations analysis of Section 5, and it interacts with credit: strong credit does not cure inadequate capacity, and strong capacity does not cure a pattern of nonpayment.

Compensating factors — reserves, a low loan-to-value, a long tenure, a modest payment increase — may support a file that is weak on one dimension. Whether they do is an underwriting determination, and a licensee who tells a borrower his reserves "will make up for" a credit issue has made it.

3.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what a credit report contains and its limits, explain permissible purpose, and identify what a licensee may not say about credit.

4. Occupancy and property purpose

4.1 Why the determination carries so much

Occupancy — owner-occupied, second home, or investment — affects pricing, program eligibility, and which consumer protections apply.

It is therefore a material fact the lender relies on, and misstating it is loan fraud.

Property purpose — consumer versus business — determines which body of requirements attaches, as Lesson 04 developed.

4.2 The determination is factual

Occupancy is not a box the borrower selects. It is a fact about what will happen, and the application asks the borrower to represent it.

What supports the representation: the borrower's current residence and its disposition; the distance to employment; the property's configuration; the presence or absence of leases; the borrower's stated plans and their plausibility; and, on a refinance, how the property has actually been used.

4.3 The patterns that contradict a stated occupancy

PatternWhat it suggests
A "primary residence" the borrower will not move intoOccupancy misrepresentation
A second home in the same city as the primary residenceInvestment property described otherwise
A lease on the subject property dated before the applicationThe file contains its own contradiction
A borrower who cannot describe the property's location relative to his workA straw or absentee arrangement
Multiple simultaneous "primary residence" applicationsCoordinated misrepresentation
Rental income from the subject property on the borrower's tax returns, on an owner-occupied refinanceThe stated use is contradicted by the borrower's own filings
A borrower who asks what occupancy "gets the best rate"Selection by pricing rather than by fact

The lease and the tax return are different in kind from the others. They are not ambiguities to be resolved by asking — the file contains the evidence contradicting a material representation, and the response is escalation rather than a judgment call.

4.4 The request an originator will receive

A borrower says: "Can we put it down as owner-occupied? The rate is better and I can afford either payment anyway."

The answer is no, and the reasoning must be stated because the borrower's framing is the wrong one.

Affordability is beside the point. The misstatement is not about whether he will pay. It is about obtaining terms on a false representation of the risk the lender is pricing.

Decline plainly, explain why, and record the loan as it actually is. And note that the request itself belongs on the report-promptly list — not because the borrower is necessarily dishonest, but because the file now has a known pressure point on it.

4.5 Legitimate changes of intent

A borrower's plans can genuinely change: a job relocation, a family change, a property that turns out not to work.

A change of intent after closing is not fraud. A misrepresentation at application is. The distinction is what the borrower intended when he made the representation, and the file should record the facts as they stood then.

Where intent changes during the transaction, the application is corrected and the lender told. A licensee who learns before closing that the borrower will not occupy and says nothing has adopted the misstatement.

4.6 Property type and use

Beyond occupancy, the property's type and use drive eligibility and pricing: single-family, condominium, planned development, two-to-four units, manufactured housing, mixed use, and unique or non-conforming properties.

Two recurring issues:

Condominium and planned development eligibility depends on project characteristics — owner-occupancy ratios, budget and reserves, litigation, and concentration — and a project can be ineligible even where the borrower is strong.

Unpermitted space and conversions affect value, insurability, and program eligibility. A licensee who lets unpermitted square footage enter the file as living area has introduced an inaccuracy that flows into the appraisal and the loan amount.

4.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why occupancy is material, recognize the contradiction patterns, respond correctly to the request, and distinguish a change of intent from a misrepresentation.

5. Debt-to-income analysis

5.1 The two ratios

RatioFormula
Front-end (housing)Housing expense ÷ gross monthly income
Back-end (total debt)Total monthly obligations ÷ gross monthly income

Housing expense conventionally means PITI — principal, interest, taxes, and insurance — plus association dues and mortgage insurance where applicable.

Total obligations add the other recurring monthly debts.

5.2 A worked computation

Gross monthly income $9,000. Proposed PITI $2,520 (P&I $1,880, taxes $410, hazard $110, mortgage insurance $120); association dues $0. Car payment $480; student loan $300; credit card minimums $120.

Front-end: 2,520 ÷ 9,000 = 28.0% Back-end: (2,520 + 480 + 300 + 120) ÷ 9,000 = 3,420 ÷ 9,000 = 38.0%

5.3 The errors that produce wrong ratios

  1. Using net income. Ratios use gross. A borrower reporting take-home pay produces a ratio that is wrong in the borrower's favor.
  2. Quoting P&I instead of PITI. Omitting taxes, insurance, and mortgage insurance understates the housing ratio substantially — and in California the tax line is most often understated, because a buyer's taxes reset on the change in ownership rather than tracking the seller's bill.
  3. Omitting association dues on a condominium or planned development.
  4. Omitting debts that will survive closing.
  5. Using a payoff assumption that has not been arranged.
  6. Averaging variable income incorrectly, or using a peak year.

Reasonableness check: a 28% front-end on a $9,000 income implies a housing payment near $2,520. If the computed ratio implies a payment that does not resemble the loan being discussed, something is wrong.

5.4 Thresholds

Thresholds vary by program, by compensating factors, and over time.

A licensee computes and explains the ratios, and never states a threshold as a rule.

Telling a borrower he "qualifies easily because 38% is under the 43% limit" does two things wrong at once: it states a threshold as a fixed rule, and it makes an underwriting determination the licensee is not authorized to make. A borrower who hears it writes an offer.

5.5 Residual income and the limits of ratios

Some programs consider residual income — what remains after housing, debts, and living expenses — which can produce a different assessment for a borrower with a high income and a high ratio, or the reverse.

Ratios are a screen, not a judgment. They do not capture household size, geographic cost differences, income stability, or reserves. Underwriting considers more, which is why a file that "passes the ratios" can still be declined and one that does not can still be approved with compensating factors.

5.6 What changes a ratio after application

The events that jeopardize an approval, which belong in a written note to the borrower at application rather than being discovered later:

Borrower actionEffect
Opening new credit, financing furniture or a vehicleChanges the debt-to-income analysis the approval rested on
Changing or leaving a jobEmployment is a condition; a change may end the approval
Large unexplained depositsRequires sourcing; may look like undisclosed borrowed funds
Moving money between accountsComplicates asset verification
