Paying off debt with funds needed to closeReduces verified cash to close
Missing a payment on any obligationAffects credit at the re-check
Co-signing for someone elseAdds a contingent liability

A short written note at application — do not open credit, change jobs, or move large sums without telling us first — prevents more failed transactions than any other single communication an originator sends.

5.7 The three numbers

What the borrower can borrow — the lender's number. What cash is available — down payment, closing costs, reserves, moving costs, and the immediate costs of occupancy. Borrowers routinely plan to the down payment and forget the rest. What the borrower is willing to pay monthly — frequently lower than the first, and the number that should drive the search.

Where they conflict, the conflict is the conversation — held early and deliberately, rather than discovered at the closing table.

5.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to compute both ratios, name the six errors that produce wrong ones, and state why a licensee never quotes a threshold.

6. Adverse information and accurate records

6.1 The standard

The application is a set of representations the lender relies on in pricing risk. Its accuracy is not a courtesy to the underwriter — it is the representation itself.

Everything in this section follows from that.

6.2 What must never happen to an application

  • Altering a date, an amount, or an answer the borrower gave.
  • Omitting a debt, an obligation, or a property the borrower disclosed.
  • Recording income that has not been represented and cannot be documented.
  • Characterizing a loan as a gift, or a business-purpose loan as consumer, or the reverse, to fit a product.
  • Completing an item the borrower did not answer, in the borrower's voice.
  • Drafting a letter of explanation and presenting it as the borrower's statement.
  • Backdating anything.

These are misrepresentations to a lender, and most of them are committed in a moment of helpfulness on a file that "would qualify anyway."

6.3 The instruction an originator will receive

A manager says: move the job change date earlier so the employment history reads better, and leave off the small consumer debt — it will not affect the ratios anyway.

Refuse. Do not transmit the file. Escalate to the responsible broker.

Two justifications will be offered and neither works. That the ratios would pass anyway — if that were true the alteration was unnecessary, and it was still made. And that the manager directed it — following an improper instruction and documenting that it came from someone else does not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.

6.4 Handling adverse information

Surface it early. A bankruptcy, a foreclosure, a collection, a gap in employment, a recent job change, a debt not on the report — each is easier to address at application than at underwriting.

Document the explanation in the borrower's words, dated.

Never characterize the outcome. "That won't be a problem" is an underwriting conclusion, and a borrower who hears it stops looking at alternatives.

Never advise concealment. A borrower who asks whether he has to mention something is asking a question with one answer.

6.5 Corrections

Where an error is discovered — by anyone, at any stage — it is corrected immediately, in writing, to everyone who received the original, and before anyone acts on it if that is still possible.

The instinct to wait and see whether it matters is the instinct that converts a mistake into a misrepresentation. An error you know about and leave uncorrected is no longer an error.

Corrections are made visibly, with the original preserved and the change attributable. A record that can be silently altered is not a record.

6.6 What the file must contain

  • The application as taken, with the date, and every subsequent version.
  • What the borrower stated and what has been documented, distinguished.
  • Every document collected, with its source and date.
  • The credit authorization.
  • Explanations of adverse information, in the borrower's words, dated.
  • The disclosures delivered — what, to whom, when, by what method, with evidence.
  • Every communication material to a term or a decision.
  • Corrections issued, with the originals retained.
  • Anything the originator declined to do, and the escalation.

6.7 The test

Reconstructability: could a person who was not there determine what the borrower represented, what was documented, what was disclosed and when, and on what basis the file moved forward?

A file that passes that test survives an examination even where it contains a problem. A file that does not fails even where it contains none, because nobody can show what happened.

6.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to list what must never happen to an application, state the correct response to an improper instruction, and describe what the file must contain.

Key terms

TermDefinition
PrequalificationAn informal assessment on stated information. Verifies nothing.
PreapprovalA lender review of supporting information, subject to conditions. Not a commitment to lend.
Loan commitmentUnderwriting complete. More certainty, not immunity from changed circumstances.
Application (the six items)Name, income, Social Security number, property address, an estimate of value, and the loan amount sought. Can exist before any form is completed.
Structuring to avoid the triggerDeliberately withholding a request for one item to delay disclosures. The conduct the definition was written against.
What an application triggersDisclosure timing, adverse action obligations, retention, monitoring information collection, and the MLO endorsement requirement.
Incomplete versus withdrawnDifferent dispositions with different treatment. Record which occurred, when, and on what communication.
Gross incomeWhat ratios use. A borrower reporting take-home pay has given a different number.
Stability and continuanceWhether income has a track record and whether it will continue. The two analytical questions applied to every income source.
SourcingDocumenting where funds came from. What a large deposit inconsistent with documented income triggers.
Undisclosed loanFunds deposited as though savings. A hidden obligation that undermines the entire capacity analysis.
Gift versus loanTreated differently. A gift generally requires documentation that no repayment is expected.
Contingent liabilityA co-signed obligation is an obligation, whatever the arrangement between the parties.
Three C'sCredit, capacity, collateral — with capital and conditions sometimes added.
Permissible purposeThe only basis on which a consumer report may be obtained. Authorization is obtained and documented.
Letter of explanationThe borrower's statement in his own words. A licensee who drafts it has authored a representation the borrower will sign.
Compensating factorsStrengths that may support a weak dimension. Whether they do is an underwriting determination.
OccupancyOwner-occupied, second home, or investment. A material fact the lender relies on; misstating it is fraud regardless of affordability.
File-contradicts-itself patternA lease dated before the application, or rental income on the tax returns for an owner-occupied refinance. Escalation, not a judgment call.
Change of intentA genuine change after closing is not fraud; a misrepresentation at application is. Where intent changes during the transaction, the application is corrected and the lender told.
Project eligibilityCondominium and planned development characteristics — occupancy ratios, budget and reserves, litigation, concentration — that can make a project ineligible even for a strong borrower.
PITIPrincipal, interest, taxes, insurance — plus dues and mortgage insurance. What the housing ratio uses, not P&I.
Front-end / back-end ratioHousing ÷ gross income; total obligations ÷ gross income.
Residual incomeWhat remains after housing, debts, and living expenses. Considered by some programs, and a reminder that ratios are a screen rather than a judgment.
The start-of-file warningThe written note about credit, employment, and moving funds. Prevents more failed transactions than any other single communication.
The three numbersWhat he can borrow, what cash exists, and what he is willing to pay monthly — the third being the one that should drive the search.
Correction obligationImmediately, in writing, to everyone who received the original, before reliance. Made visibly, with the original preserved.
ReconstructabilityCould a person who was not there determine what was represented, documented, disclosed, and decided.

Practice problems

Problem 1

An originator has, over two emails and a phone call, obtained a prospect's name, income, Social Security number, property address, an estimate of value, and the requested loan amount. He has not sent a form. His manager says the disclosure clock does not start "until she signs the application," and suggests holding off on asking for the property address on future files "so we get more time."

Assess both.

Solution. An application likely already exists, and no form was needed. Under the federal framework an application is generally understood to exist when the creditor has the information needed to evaluate the request — conventionally the six items, all of which he has. The disclosure clock does not wait for a signature.

The manager's suggestion is worse than a misunderstanding. Deliberately withholding a request for one of the items in order to delay disclosures is structuring to avoid the trigger — exactly the conduct the definition was written against, and a compliance problem rather than a technique.

Taking an application triggers more than disclosure timing: adverse action obligations if the request is denied, record retention, government monitoring information collection where applicable, and the MLO endorsement requirement itself.

Whether a particular set of facts constitutes an application is a compliance question the firm must answer with a written policy — not one an originator resolves case by case, and certainly not one a manager resolves by adjusting what gets asked.

Problem 2

A borrower shows a preapproval letter and tells his agent he is "approved." The originator confirms it. The letter states no income or asset documentation was reviewed, lists six outstanding conditions, and expires in nine days.

Correct the description and state what the letter establishes.

Solution. A preapproval is not an approval, and neither is a commitment to fund.

Prequalification rests on largely stated information and establishes a rough range while verifying nothing. Preapproval is a lender review of supporting information establishing a likely amount subject to conditions — not a commitment to lend. A loan commitment follows completed underwriting and provides substantially more certainty, and still not immunity from changed circumstances.

None guarantees funding. All remain contingent on the property, the appraisal, and the borrower's circumstances holding through funding.

This particular letter establishes very little. Nothing was documented, six conditions remain, and it expires in nine days — and the seller's agent will read it exactly that way.

A licensee who tells a borrower he is "approved" has misdescribed the file's status, and the borrower will write an offer on that description.

Problem 3

A self-employed borrower says his income is "about $18,000 a month." His returns show substantially less after adjustments. He also has $52,000 that appeared in his checking account three weeks ago. His brother lent it to him for the down payment, and he asks whether he should have deposited it sooner "so it seasons," or split it into smaller amounts.

Address the income and every part of the deposit question.

Solution. On income: the figure is preliminary until the documents are reviewed, and the originator should have said so before quoting anything. Self-employment income is typically established from tax returns and business documentation over a period, with adjustments — which means the number the borrower thinks of as his income and the number underwriting uses can differ substantially, in either direction. Quoting a qualifying amount from the borrower's own description sets an expectation the file may not support.

On the deposit: it must be sourced, and the source is the problem. A deposit inconsistent with documented income triggers sourcing for a substantive reason — an undisclosed loan deposited as though it were savings is a hidden obligation that undermines the entire capacity analysis, because the ratios computed on his documented debts would be wrong.

A gift and a loan are treated differently. This is a loan from his brother, and it is a liability.

Both suggestions must be declined plainly. Advising him to deposit funds earlier so they "season," or to break a deposit into smaller amounts, is advising him to defeat the verification — and characterizing the loan as a gift would be a misrepresentation to the lender. The correct path is to disclose the loan, document its terms, and let underwriting treat it as what it is.

Problem 4

A borrower asks his originator what credit score he needs, whether disputing three accurate late payments would help, whether closing two old cards would raise his score, and whether his $80,000 in reserves will "make up for" the collection on his report.

Answer each.

Solution. All four are outside the line, and the originator should say so rather than guessing helpfully.

"What score do I need" states a threshold as a rule. Requirements vary by program, by compensating factors, and over time. A licensee explains that scores exist and are produced by models — and does not predict one or name a number the borrower will rely on.

Disputing accurate information is filing a false dispute. Advising it is not a service. What a licensee may do is explain that the borrower has rights to obtain and dispute report information, and tell him what the report actually shows.

Closing accounts is credit strategy advice. Promising that a particular action will raise a score is a prediction about a model, and credit counseling is a distinct service.

The reserves question asks for an underwriting determination. Compensating factors — reserves, a low loan-to-value, long tenure, a modest payment increase — may support a file weak on one dimension, but whether they do is underwriting's call. Telling him his reserves will make up for the collection makes it for them, and he will stop considering alternatives.

What the originator does instead: surface the collection now, get the explanation in the borrower's own words and dated, and let underwriting decide. Early is cheap; at underwriting it stalls the file.

Problem 5

A borrower says: "Can we put it down as owner-occupied? The rate's better and I can afford either payment anyway." The subject property is a rental in a city three hours from his job, his tax returns show rental income from it, and there is a lease in the file dated a month before the application.

Respond, and identify what is different in kind here.

Solution. The answer is no, and his framing is the wrong one.

Affordability is beside the point. Occupancy affects pricing, program eligibility, and which consumer protections apply, which makes it a material fact the lender relies on. The misstatement is not about whether he will pay — it is about obtaining terms on a false representation of the risk the lender is pricing. That is loan fraud.

Decline plainly, explain why, and record the loan as it actually is. The request itself belongs on the report-promptly list — not because he is necessarily dishonest, but because the file now has a known pressure point on it.

The lease and the tax returns are different in kind from the rest. The distance from his job and the "rate's better" framing are facts to weigh. The lease dated before the application and the rental income on his own filings are not ambiguities to resolve by asking — the file contains the evidence contradicting a material representation. The response is escalation, not a judgment call about whether it matters.

Worth distinguishing: a genuine change of intent after closing is not fraud; a misrepresentation at application is. And where intent changes during the transaction, the application is corrected and the lender told — a licensee who learns before closing that the borrower will not occupy and says nothing has adopted the misstatement.

Problem 6

Compute both ratios. Gross monthly income $9,000. P&I $1,880; property taxes $410; hazard $110; mortgage insurance $120; condominium dues $340. Car $480; student loan $300; card minimums $120. The originator computed a 21% front-end using P&I only, quoted the seller's current property tax figure, and told the borrower he "qualifies easily, well under the 43% limit."

Compute correctly and identify every error.

Solution. Housing expense is PITI plus dues and mortgage insurance: 1,880 + 410 + 110 + 120 + 340 = $2,860.

Front-end: 2,860 ÷ 9,000 = 31.8% — not 21%. Back-end: (2,860 + 480 + 300 + 120) ÷ 9,000 = 3,760 ÷ 9,000 = 41.8%.

Three errors. Quoting P&I instead of PITI understated the housing ratio by nearly eleven points. Omitting the condominium dues compounded it. And the California property tax figure is the one most often understated, because a buyer's taxes reset on the change in ownership rather than tracking the seller's bill — so $410 may itself be low, and the estimate belongs with the county assessor.

The qualifying statement is a fourth error and the most consequential. It states a threshold as a fixed rule and makes an underwriting determination the licensee is not authorized to make. Thresholds vary by program, by compensating factors, and over time — and a borrower who hears "qualifies easily" writes an offer.

Reasonableness check: a 21% front-end on $9,000 implies a housing payment near $1,890, which does not resemble the loan being discussed. That mismatch should have caught the error before the borrower did.

Problem 7

Three weeks into processing, a borrower finances $9,000 of furniture, moves $22,000 between accounts, pays off his car with part of his down payment funds, and co-signs a lease for his daughter. The originator learns all of it the week before closing.

Assess each and state what should have happened at application.

Solution. All five attack the file the approval rested on, and one of them is a liability the borrower would not have thought to mention.

Financing furniture changes the debt-to-income analysis. Moving $22,000 between accounts complicates asset verification and may require sourcing. Paying off the car with closing funds solves one ratio by breaking another — it reduces verified cash to close. Co-signing adds a contingent liability, and a co-signed obligation is an obligation whatever the arrangement between the parties.

Underlying all of it: an approval rests on the file as underwritten, and lenders commonly re-check credit and employment before funding. A credit report is a snapshot through a date.

What should have happened at application is a short written note: do not open credit, change jobs, or move large sums without telling us first. Also on that list: leaving a job and missing a payment on any obligation.

That single communication prevents more failed transactions than any other an originator sends — and sent at application it costs nothing, while learned the week before closing it costs the closing.

Problem 8

A branch manager tells an originator to move a job-change date three months earlier "so the employment history reads better," to leave off a $2,300 consumer debt that "won't affect the ratios anyway," and to write the letter of explanation for the borrower's old collection "since you know what underwriting wants to hear."

Respond to each, and state what does not protect him.

Solution. Refuse all three, do not transmit the file, and escalate above the manager.

Altering a date is changing a fact, not tidying. The application is a set of representations the lender relies on in pricing risk, and its accuracy is not a courtesy to the underwriter — it is the representation itself.

Omitting the debt is a misrepresentation, and the size does not matter. Note the self-defeating justification: if the ratios would pass anyway, the omission was unnecessary — and it was still made.

Drafting the letter of explanation is authoring a representation the borrower will sign. It is the borrower's statement, in his own words, dated. Writing what underwriting "wants to hear" is composing testimony.

What does not protect him: doing any of it and documenting that the manager directed it. Following an improper instruction and documenting that it came from someone else does not transfer responsibility for the act. It documents that you knew.

What the file should show instead: the application as taken with its date and every subsequent version; what the borrower stated and what was documented, distinguished; the credit authorization; the explanation in the borrower's words; the disclosures delivered with evidence; corrections issued with originals retained; and what he declined to do, and the escalation.

Chapter summary

Prequalification verifies nothing, preapproval is not a commitment, and no level guarantees funding.

An application exists when the six items are in hand — before any form is signed — and it triggers disclosure timing, adverse action obligations, retention, monitoring collection, and the endorsement requirement. Structuring to avoid the trigger is a compliance problem, not a technique.

Income is tested for stability, continuance, and documentation, and ratios use gross. Self-employment and variable income routinely differ from what the borrower believes, so nothing is quoted as final before the documents are read.

Every asset raises two questions: is it there, and where did it come from. An undisclosed loan deposited as savings is a hidden obligation that undermines the whole analysis, and advising a borrower to season, split, or recharacterize funds is advising him to defeat the verification.

Liabilities include what the report does not show — private loans, obligations others pay, and co-signed debts.

Credit is one of three C's, the report can be wrong and is a snapshot, and a report may be pulled only for a permissible purpose with documented authorization.

Never predict a score, name a required score, advise disputing accurate items, or promise that reserves will offset a weakness — the last is an underwriting determination.

Surface adverse information early and document the explanation in the borrower's own words.

Occupancy is a material fact and misstating it is fraud regardless of affordability. Learn the contradiction patterns, and treat a file containing its own evidence against a representation as an escalation.

A change of intent is not a misrepresentation — but where intent changes during the transaction, the application is corrected and the lender told.

Compute both ratios on PITI plus dues, using gross income, and never state a threshold as a rule. Ratios are a screen, not a judgment.

Send the written warning at application about credit, employment, and moving funds.

The application's accuracy is the representation. Alter nothing, omit nothing, author nothing in the borrower's voice, correct immediately and visibly — and build a file a person who was not there could reconstruct.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. State whether an application exists on the facts given and what that triggers, identify every item of income, asset, and liability information and state what must be documented rather than accepted, identify any deposit requiring sourcing and what you would ask, state the occupancy and purpose determination and the facts it rests on, identify anything in the file that contradicts a representation and what you would do about it, compute both ratios showing your components, identify every statement you would decline to make and why, draft the written warning you would send at application, and list what the file must contain for the application to be reconstructable. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A borrower tells the originator: 'Put down that I'll live in the property — I'll actually rent it out, but owner-occupied gets me a better rate. And leave off the car loan, I'm paying it off next month anyway.' The originator believes the borrower can afford the payment either way. What is the correct response?

  1. A. Refuse both requests, explain that occupancy and liabilities must be stated accurately because the lender relies on them, and record the loan as it actually is — misstating either is loan fraud regardless of whether the borrower could afford the payment.
  2. B. Record the occupancy as requested but include the car loan, since occupancy is the borrower's stated intention and intentions can change.
  3. C. Omit the car loan as requested but record the occupancy accurately, since a debt being paid off shortly is not a real obligation.
  4. D. Follow both instructions and note in the file that they came from the borrower.

Answer: A. Both requests ask the originator to misstate facts the lender relies on in pricing and approving the loan, which is fraud whether or not the borrower can afford the payment. A debt that exists at application is a liability until it is actually paid and documented, and recording that the borrower asked for the misstatement does not make it permissible.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What information does a loan application collect about the borrower's capacity?

  1. A. Income, employment, assets, and liabilities, which together support the analysis of whether the borrower can repay.
  2. B. Only the borrower's credit score, since it summarizes creditworthiness.
  3. C. Only the borrower's income, since the payment is made from income.
  4. D. The borrower's intended use of the property and nothing further.

Answer: A. Capacity analysis needs the full picture: what comes in, what is owed, and what reserves exist. A credit score measures history rather than capacity, and income alone ignores existing obligations.

2. What does a debt-to-income ratio measure?

  1. A. The borrower's recurring monthly obligations, including the proposed housing payment, as a percentage of gross monthly income.
  2. B. The borrower's total debt as a percentage of the property's value.
  3. C. The borrower's monthly savings as a percentage of income.
  4. D. The proposed loan payment as a percentage of the borrower's net worth.

Answer: A. The ratio compares recurring obligations to income. Debt against property value is loan-to-value, and neither savings rate nor net worth defines the ratio.

3. Why does the source of a borrower's down payment matter?

  1. A. Because lenders verify that funds are the borrower's own or a properly documented gift, since undisclosed borrowed funds create an unrecorded obligation and change the risk.
  2. B. Because the source determines the property's appraised value.
  3. C. Because only funds held for more than five years may be used.
  4. D. Because the source determines whether the loan may be sold in the secondary market.

Answer: A. An undisclosed loan for the down payment is a hidden liability that undermines the capacity analysis, which is why sourcing and documenting funds is standard. Value, arbitrary seasoning rules, and salability are not the reason.

4. What does a credit report contribute to the qualification analysis?

  1. A. A record of the borrower's history of meeting obligations, which informs the assessment of willingness and reliability alongside capacity.
  2. B. A determination of whether the borrower's income is sufficient.
  3. C. A verification of the borrower's employment and assets.
  4. D. An appraisal of the collateral securing the loan.

Answer: A. Credit history speaks to willingness to repay, which complements the capacity analysis drawn from income, assets, and liabilities. It verifies neither income, employment, assets, nor collateral.

5. How should an originator handle adverse information a borrower discloses, such as a past bankruptcy?

  1. A. Record it accurately and address it with documentation and explanation as the program requires, since concealing it would misrepresent the file.
  2. B. Omit it if enough time has passed that it no longer appears on the credit report.
  3. C. Omit it unless the lender specifically asks about it.
  4. D. Record it only if the borrower cannot provide a satisfactory explanation.

Answer: A. Accuracy is the obligation, and adverse facts are handled with documentation rather than omission. Neither the passage of time, the absence of a direct question, nor the quality of the explanation makes concealment acceptable.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A borrower is self-employed. What generally distinguishes the income analysis?

  1. A. Income is typically established from tax returns and business records over a period, with attention to stability and to the difference between gross receipts and net income.
  2. B. Self-employed income is disregarded and only assets may be counted.
  3. C. Self-employed income is verified by a letter from the borrower's accountant alone.
  4. D. Self-employed borrowers are evaluated only on credit history.

Answer: A. Documented returns over time, with net rather than gross income, is the standard approach. Self-employment does not disqualify income, and a single letter does not substitute for the underlying records.

2. A borrower's application lists a monthly income figure that does not match the pay documentation. What should the originator do?

  1. A. Resolve the discrepancy with documentation before the file proceeds, and correct the application to match what is verified.
  2. B. Use the higher figure, since the borrower knows his own income best.
  3. C. Use the lower figure, which is the conservative approach.
  4. D. Submit the file with both figures and let the underwriter decide.

Answer: A. Discrepancies are resolved with evidence, not by choosing a number. Passing an unreconciled conflict to the underwriter submits a file the originator knows to be internally inconsistent.

3. Why is a borrower's occupancy intent captured at application rather than assumed?

  1. A. Because occupancy affects pricing, program eligibility, and which consumer protections apply, so it is a material fact the lender relies on.
  2. B. Because occupancy determines who may hold title to the property.
  3. C. Because occupancy is required to be reported to the county assessor by the lender.
  4. D. Because occupancy determines the appraiser's choice of valuation approach.

Answer: A. Occupancy is material to the lender's decision, which is what makes misstating it fraud. It does not determine vesting, is not reported by the lender to the assessor, and does not drive the appraisal method.

4. A borrower asks the originator to 'estimate' his assets on the application because he has not gathered his statements yet. What is the sound approach?

  1. A. Record what can be supported and complete the item when the documentation arrives, rather than entering figures the borrower has not verified.
  2. B. Enter the borrower's estimate and correct it later if the statements differ.
  3. C. Leave the asset section blank until closing.
  4. D. Enter a conservative figure below the borrower's estimate to be safe.

Answer: A. An application states facts the lender relies on, so unverified estimates and invented conservative figures are both misstatements. Leaving the section blank stalls the file without resolving anything.

5. What is the significance of reserves in a qualification analysis?

  1. A. They measure the borrower's ability to continue paying if income is interrupted, which is a distinct risk factor from capacity at the moment of application.
  2. B. They determine the maximum loan amount the borrower may receive.
  3. C. They substitute for a down payment when the borrower lacks one.
  4. D. They are counted as income in the debt-to-income calculation.

Answer: A. Reserves address resilience after closing rather than capacity at closing. They neither cap the loan, replace the down payment, nor convert into income.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 06

Underwriting, collateral, and approval conditions

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the ability-to-repay requirement and the qualified mortgage framework at orientation depth.
  • Distinguish automated from manual underwriting and explain what an automated finding does and does not decide.
  • Explain the appraisal's role, appraiser independence, and the correct response to a low appraisal.
  • Describe title and hazard insurance requirements and identify what each does and does not cover.
  • Manage conditions and verifications, and explain why a prior-to-funding condition is not a formality.
  • Apply the adverse action requirements and explain what must happen when a request is denied, withdrawn, or incomplete.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: ability to repay and underwriting methods55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: collateral, title, and insurance50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: conditions, verification, and adverse action45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Ability-to-repay orientation

1.1 What underwriting is

Underwriting is the decision whether to extend credit on stated terms, made against the lender's guidelines and applicable law.

It is not a formality that follows a preapproval, and it is not something an originator performs. A licensee who tells a borrower what underwriting will do has made the decision without the authority to make it.

1.2 The ability-to-repay requirement

Federal law requires a creditor making a covered residential mortgage loan to make a reasonable and good faith determination, based on verified and documented information, that the consumer has a reasonable ability to repay the loan according to its terms.

Two features define it:

It is a determination, not a form. The creditor must actually consider the required factors and be able to show it.

It rests on verified and documented information. Stated information the creditor did not verify does not support the determination — which is why the verification discipline of Lesson 05 is a legal requirement rather than a processing preference.

1.3 The factors considered

In outline, the determination considers the consumer's:

Factor
Current or reasonably expected income or assets
Current employment status
The monthly payment on the covered transaction
The monthly payment on any simultaneous loan
The monthly payment for mortgage-related obligations
Current debt obligations, alimony, and child support
The monthly debt-to-income ratio or residual income
Credit history

Two of these are the ones files most often miss. A simultaneous loan — a second recorded at the same closing — must be considered, and mortgage-related obligations means taxes, insurance, assessments, and dues, which is why the housing figure is PITI rather than principal and interest.

1.4 The payment used

For adjustable and non-amortizing structures, the payment used in the determination is not necessarily the initial payment. The framework requires consideration of a payment computed on defined assumptions — which is why a product with a discounted start rate does not qualify a borrower on that start rate.

A licensee who tells a borrower the initial payment is what he must qualify on has described a different loan.

1.5 Qualified mortgages, in outline

A qualified mortgage is a category of loan meeting defined requirements — including limits on certain features and on points and fees, and requirements about how the payment is computed — that provides the creditor a degree of protection regarding the ability-to-repay determination.

Features generally inconsistent with the category include negative amortization, interest-only periods, balloon payments in the ordinary case, and terms exceeding a defined length.

Two points for a licensee:

Non-QM is not improper. It means the loan does not meet the category's requirements, which generally makes it more expensive and sometimes makes it the only workable option for a legitimate borrower.

Whether a particular loan is a qualified mortgage is a compliance determination, and the points and fees limit is calculated by rule rather than by intuition — which matters directly to a broker, because broker compensation can count toward it. Lesson 09 develops that.

1.6 Exclusions

Certain transactions fall outside the ability-to-repay framework — including, in outline, business-purpose loans and certain other categories.

That is precisely why the Lesson 04 classification discipline matters. A loan misclassified as business-purpose is a loan for which the required determination may never have been made, and the borrower was stripped of a protection he was entitled to. The certification does not fix it; the actual purpose governs.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what the ability-to-repay determination requires, name the factors most often missed, and explain why a discounted start rate does not qualify a borrower.

2. Automated and manual underwriting

2.1 Automated underwriting

Automated systems evaluate a file against programmed criteria and return a finding or recommendation, together with the documentation the finding requires.

What an automated finding does: applies consistent criteria quickly, identifies the documentation level required, and tells the originator what the file needs.

What it does not do:

A finding is not an approval. It is a recommendation based on the data entered, and it is conditioned on that data being verified.

Three consequences licensees must hold:

  1. Garbage in, garbage out. A favorable finding produced from an income figure that documentation does not support is worth nothing, and it will reverse when the documents arrive.
  2. The finding is re-run. Data changes as the file is verified, and a re-run can return a different recommendation.
  3. The underwriter still underwrites. The finding directs the documentation; a human confirms the file matches it.

"The system approved it" is not a defense for a file whose data was wrong, and an originator who enters an optimistic figure to get a finding has produced an answer to a question nobody asked.

2.2 Manual underwriting

An underwriter evaluates the file directly against guidelines. It applies where a file is outside automated parameters, where the program requires it, and where compensating factors need human assessment.

Manual underwriting is not a lesser process. It frequently applies to files that are strong in unusual ways — substantial reserves with thin credit, or documented income of a kind a system handles poorly.

2.3 Compensating factors

Strengths that may support a file weak on one dimension: substantial reserves, a low loan-to-value, a long tenure in employment or residence, a modest payment increase over current housing cost, demonstrated ability to carry a similar payment, and limited other debt.

Whether a compensating factor supports a particular file is an underwriting determination.

An originator who tells a borrower his reserves "will make up for" a credit issue has made it — and the borrower stops considering alternatives on the strength of it.

2.4 Exceptions

Lenders sometimes grant exceptions to guidelines. Three things a licensee should understand:

They are the lender's to grant, on the lender's criteria, and they are not obtained by pressure.

They are documented, with the rationale, because an examiner will ask why this file was treated differently.

Exception patterns are a fair lending issue. Where exceptions are granted more readily to some applicants than others without a documented neutral basis, the pattern is exactly what fair lending examinations look for. Lesson 14 develops it.

2.5 What the originator contributes to underwriting

Accurate data at the front. Every hour spent verifying before submission is returned in conditions not raised.

Complete documentation matched to the finding.

Honest presentation of weaknesses, with explanations documented in the borrower's own words.

Prompt, complete condition responses, addressed in Section 5.

What the originator does not contribute: advocacy that misdescribes the file, pressure for an exception, or a characterization of the borrower's likelihood of approval to the borrower.

2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what an automated finding is and is not, explain why "the system approved it" fails, and state who decides whether a compensating factor applies.

3. Appraisal and collateral review

3.1 What the appraisal is for

The lender obtains an appraisal to measure its collateral risk — what could be recovered if the loan is not repaid.

Lenders lend against the lower of the appraised value and the purchase price.

That single sentence explains every consequence of a low appraisal, and it is worth memorizing in exactly that form. On a refinance there is no purchase price, so value is the appraised value — which is why a refinance is more exposed to the appraisal outcome and why cash-out availability is not knowable until it arrives.

3.2 Appraiser independence

A licensee may provide genuinely relevant information through the proper channel — sales the licensee believes relevant, information about condition and improvements, a copy of the contract.

A licensee may not communicate a target.

"The deal dies without another $25,000" is precisely the communication independence rules exist to prevent, and a value that moves after that conversation is unreliable for the purpose the appraisal serves.

The distinction is between supplying information and supplying a target — and requests to "take another look" that arrive with a number attached are the pattern to refuse, including when the request comes from your own borrower or your own manager.

Appraiser independence requirements also govern who may order and communicate with the appraiser, and firms implement them through defined channels precisely so that individual originators are not the point of contact.

3.3 Valuation review

Lenders review appraisals for completeness, support, and reasonableness — through desk or field review, automated tools, or a second appraisal where required.

A review that questions an appraisal is not an accusation. It is the lender testing whether the collateral conclusion is supported, which is the same discipline the appraisal itself applies to comparable selection.

3.4 The reconsideration process

Where an originator or a borrower believes an appraisal is materially wrong, lenders provide a reconsideration of value process.

How it is done correctly:

  • Through the lender's defined channel, not by contacting the appraiser directly.
  • With relevant sales the appraiser may not have considered, identified with data.
  • With factual corrections — a bedroom miscounted, a permitted addition omitted, a condition misdescribed.
  • Without a target number.

What is not a reconsideration: an assertion that the value is wrong because the contract price is higher, or because the transaction will fail without a different number.

3.5 The low appraisal

The buyer's options are practical rather than automatic: bring additional funds, renegotiate the price, negotiate another resolution, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed.

What does not happen automatically: the price does not adjust to the appraised value by operation of any loan program, the loan is not denied, and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right.

Where an appraisal contingency has been removed, the practical options remain but the contractual rights are limited — and whether the borrower may cancel and what happens to a deposit is a legal question for counsel, not for the licensee.

3.6 The borrower's copy

The borrower is entitled to receive a copy of the appraisal and other written valuations developed in connection with the application, under the framework Lesson 07 develops.

Delivery is evidenced, and a file that cannot show when the valuation reached the borrower has a gap in exactly the place an examiner looks.

3.7 Other collateral considerations

ConsiderationWhy it matters
Property typeSingle-family, condominium, planned development, two-to-four units, manufactured, mixed use — each with its own eligibility
Project eligibilityCondominium and planned development characteristics can make a project ineligible even for a strong borrower
ConditionDeferred maintenance, health and safety items, and unpermitted work can stop a loan under program requirements
Unpermitted spaceCannot be counted as living area without disclosure of its status, and it affects value, insurability, and eligibility
Legal nonconformityA use lawful when established that no longer conforms carries its own treatment
Environmental and hazard exposureContamination, mapped hazard zones, and insurability
Access and utilitiesParticularly on rural property — legal access, water source, septic

3.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the lower-of-value-or-price rule, distinguish supplying information from supplying a target, and describe a correct reconsideration request.

4. Title insurance and hazard insurance

4.1 Two different insurances

Title insuranceHazard insurance
CoversDefects in titlePhysical loss or damage
LooksBackward — defects already existing in the record or chainForward — future events
PremiumGenerally paid once, at closingRecurring
Lender's interestLender's policy insuring the lien and its priorityMortgagee clause naming the lender

Borrowers conflate them constantly, and a licensee who cannot separate them will not be able to explain why both are required.

4.2 The lender's title policy

The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority. The owner's policy insures the borrower's interest.

They insure different interests, which is why both commonly exist — and why a buyer who declines an owner's policy because "there's a title policy on the loan" has not economized on a duplicate. He has left his own interest uninsured.

4.3 Exceptions, exclusions, requirements

The three categories a licensee must distinguish on a preliminary report:

CategoryWhat it is
ExceptionAn item the policy will not insure against
ExclusionA category the policy form does not cover at all — governmental regulation, eminent domain, matters created by the insured
RequirementSomething the insurer needs before issuing — a reconveyance, a resolution, evidence of authority

Requirements are the items with deadlines attached, and they are the ones that delay closings.

Three responses wrong in every case: treating an item as routine because most properties have one; asking title to "remove" an exception; and predicting an easement's or restriction's effect on the borrower's plans.

4.4 What the title work must resolve

For a lender, the operative questions are who owns it, what encumbers it, and where will our lien sit.

The recurring items:

An unreleased deed of trust the borrower says was paid. A recorded reconveyance must be obtained — payment does not clear the record; the document does — and obtaining one from a lender that has merged or ceased to exist can take weeks.

A judgment against a similarly named person. Routed to title, resolved by a statement of information, and never assumed away.

Mechanic's lien exposure from recent work. Priority may relate back to when work commenced, so a lien recorded later can outrank the new deed of trust — which is why the intake question is whether work was recently done and everyone is paid.

An existing second on a refinance. A subordination agreement may be required, and it is that lienholder's decision with counsel — never "standard."

Authority requirements. Trustee evidence, corporate resolutions, powers of attorney — each a requirement with a deadline.

A lis pendens. A recorded notice of pending litigation affecting title, and a serious cloud.

4.5 Endorsements

Lenders commonly require endorsements extending or modifying coverage for particular risks — including matters relating to surveys, environmental protection liens, and specific encumbrances.

A licensee should know endorsements exist and are ordered, and should not represent what any particular endorsement covers.

4.6 Hazard insurance

Lenders require hazard coverage naming the lender under a mortgagee clause, in an amount and with terms the program requires.

What a licensee must confirm: coverage is in force at closing, the amount satisfies the requirement, the mortgagee clause is correct, and the premium is paid or escrowed.

Force-placed coverage. Where a borrower's policy lapses, the lender may place coverage and charge the borrower — typically at a far higher cost and protecting only the lender's interest. This is a real consequence of a lapse, and borrowers should hear it.

4.7 Availability, and why it fails transactions

In mapped fire and flood areas, availability and cost of hazard insurance have become a common cause of failed transactions in California, and the failure is usually discovered late because borrowers treat insurance as a formality.

Insurance is a first-week item in a mapped hazard area, not an administrative closing task. A borrower who learns in week one that coverage will cost far more than assumed can act. A borrower who learns it two days before closing generally cannot.

Flood insurance carries its own requirement where the property is in a designated special flood hazard area and the loan is federally related, and the determination is made by a defined process.

4.8 Other required coverages

Depending on the property and program: condominium master policy review and any required walls-in coverage; earthquake coverage where required or elected; rent loss coverage on income property; and liability coverage where the program requires it.

4.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish the two insurances, distinguish exceptions from requirements, name what title work must resolve, and explain why hazard insurance is a first-week item.

5. Conditions and verification

5.1 What a condition is

A condition is a requirement that must be satisfied before the loan proceeds to the next stage. Approvals are commonly conditional, and the conditions are the work.

TypeWhen it must be satisfied
Prior to documentBefore loan documents are drawn
Prior to fundingBefore the lender releases funds
At fundingConcurrently
Post-closingAfter funding, typically documentation cleanup

5.2 Conditions are not formalities

An unsatisfied prior-to-funding condition means the loan does not fund, whatever the schedule says and whoever has already scheduled movers.

An originator who describes conditions to a borrower as "just paperwork" has set an expectation the file cannot meet — and has removed the borrower's motivation to respond quickly.

5.3 The categories

CategoryExamples
Income and employmentVerification of employment, paystubs, returns, a written explanation of a gap
AssetsStatements, sourcing of a deposit, gift documentation
CreditExplanation of a derogatory item, evidence of a payoff, a dispute resolution
PropertyAppraisal conditions, repairs, a certification of completion, project documentation
TitleReconveyance, subordination, authority evidence, resolution of a lien
InsurancePolicy, mortgagee clause, flood determination, evidence of premium
ComplianceSigned disclosures, a corrected document, evidence of timing
Verbal verification of employmentCommonly required shortly before funding

5.4 The re-verification problem

An approval rests on the file as underwritten, and lenders commonly re-verify credit and employment before funding.

That is why the events of Lesson 05 matter so much: new credit, a job change, large unexplained deposits, moving money, paying off debt with closing funds, and missed payments each can undo an approval after it was granted.

The written warning at application — do not open credit, change jobs, or move large sums without telling us first — prevents more failed closings than any other communication an originator sends.

5.5 Managing conditions

Read the condition as written. Half of condition responses fail because the response addressed something adjacent.

Respond completely. A partial response restarts the cycle and consumes days that a lock does not have.

Track them with owners and dates. Each condition has one person responsible and a date.

Escalate early. A condition that cannot be satisfied is a problem on the day it is identified, not on the day it is due — and there is usually an alternative if there is time to find one.

Never satisfy a condition with something other than what it asks for, and never represent that a condition is satisfied when it is not.

5.6 What must never happen to a condition

  • Altering a document to satisfy a condition.
  • Backdating anything.
  • Submitting a document the originator knows to be inaccurate.
  • Representing that a verbal verification occurred when it did not.
  • Signing on a borrower's behalf.
  • Telling a borrower a condition is satisfied to relieve pressure.

Each is a misrepresentation, and each occurs on files that would probably have closed anyway — which is what makes them so costly.

5.7 The lock and the timeline

Conditions consume the days a rate lock provides. A borrower needs in writing what is locked, for how long, what happens if the loan does not close in time, whether an extension is available and at what cost, and what voids it.

A lock that expires because the file moved slowly is a foreseeable event, not an accident.

5.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the condition types, explain why a prior-to-funding condition is not a formality, describe how conditions are managed, and state what must never be done to satisfy one.

6. Approval, denial, and adverse action

6.1 The dispositions

DispositionWhat it is
ApprovalThe credit decision to extend, subject to conditions
CounterofferAn offer on different terms than requested
DenialA refusal to extend credit on the terms requested
WithdrawalThe applicant withdraws the request
IncompleteThe applicant does not supply information after a request

Each carries its own treatment, and recording which occurred, when, and on what communication is what makes the treatment defensible.

6.2 Adverse action

Adverse action includes a denial or revocation of credit, a change in terms unfavorable to the applicant, or a refusal to grant credit in substantially the amount or on substantially the terms requested.

The requirement, in outline: an applicant against whom adverse action is taken must receive notice, within a defined period, containing either a statement of the specific reasons or a disclosure of the right to obtain them — together with the other content the rule requires, including information about the credit reporting agency where a consumer report was used.

6.3 The specific reasons

The reasons stated must be the actual, specific reasons — not a general reference to a policy or a check-box that does not describe what happened.

The requirement exists so an applicant learns something usable. A denial reason of "does not meet our standards" tells the applicant nothing and does not satisfy the purpose.

Where a consumer report contributed, additional content is required, including the agency's identity and a statement that the agency did not make the decision and cannot supply the reasons.

6.4 The counteroffer

Where a creditor offers different terms and the applicant does not accept, the treatment depends on the framework and on how the offer and the response were handled.

A licensee should understand that a counteroffer is a defined event with consequences, not an informal conversation — and should route the disposition question rather than deciding it.

6.5 Withdrawal and incompleteness

A withdrawal is the applicant's act, and it is recorded with the date and the communication.

An incomplete application arises where requested information is not supplied, and the framework prescribes how it may be treated — including notice requirements in defined circumstances.

An application quietly abandoned and never dispositioned is a file with a gap in it, and it is exactly the kind an examiner samples. "The borrower stopped responding" is not a disposition; a documented notice and a recorded outcome is.

6.6 What a licensee does with a denial

Deliver it promptly and accurately. A denial delayed while an originator looks for an alternative is a compliance problem that helps no one.

Do not soften the reason. Telling a borrower he was denied "because of the appraisal" when he was denied for income is a misstatement he will act on — and the notice will say otherwise.

Do not editorialize about the decision. "They're being unreasonable" is a characterization the borrower will repeat.

Do explain what a licensee legitimately can: what the notice says, that he may request the specific reasons where the notice discloses that right, that he may obtain his consumer report from the agency named, and that other lenders and programs exist.

Do not promise another lender will approve him.

6.7 Fair lending in the underwriting context

Underwriting is where fair lending exposure concentrates, because it is where discretion operates.

Three practices constrain it, developed fully in Lesson 14:

Consistent application of criteria, so a file's treatment does not depend on who handled it.

Documented exceptions with a neutral basis, because an exception pattern granted more readily to some applicants is precisely what a fair lending examination looks for.

Outcome review — examining approval, denial, pricing, and exception patterns rather than intentions. Individual decisions rarely reveal anything; patterns do.

6.8 The file at disposition

Whatever the outcome, the file should show: the application and its versions; what was verified and how; the underwriting decision and its basis; every condition and its resolution; the disposition, its date, and the notice delivered with evidence; and any explanation given to the borrower.

A denied file needs a complete record as much as a funded one — arguably more, because a denial is the disposition an applicant is most likely to question.

6.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the dispositions, state what adverse action requires, explain why a generic reason fails, and describe how a denial is communicated.

Key terms

TermDefinition
UnderwritingThe decision whether to extend credit on stated terms, against guidelines and law. Not performed by an originator.
Ability to repayA reasonable and good faith determination, based on verified and documented information, that the consumer can repay according to the loan's terms.
Simultaneous loanA second recorded at the same closing, which must be considered in the determination.
Mortgage-related obligationsTaxes, insurance, assessments, and dues — why the housing figure is PITI.
The payment usedFor adjustable and non-amortizing structures, computed on defined assumptions — so a discounted start rate does not qualify the borrower.
Qualified mortgageA category meeting defined requirements, including limits on features and on points and fees, providing the creditor a degree of protection.
Non-QMOutside the category. Not improper — generally more expensive, and sometimes the only workable option.
Automated findingA recommendation based on the data entered, conditioned on verification. Not an approval, and re-run as data changes.
Garbage in, garbage outA favorable finding from unsupported data is worth nothing and reverses when documents arrive. "The system approved it" is not a defense.
Compensating factorsStrengths that may support a weak dimension. Whether they do is an underwriting determination.
ExceptionA departure from guidelines granted by the lender, documented with its rationale — and exception patterns are a fair lending issue.
Lower of value or priceWhat lenders lend against. On a refinance, value is the appraised value.
Appraiser independenceSupply information, never a target — including at your own borrower's or manager's request.
Reconsideration of valueThe lender's defined channel for challenging an appraisal, with relevant sales and factual corrections, and without a target number.
Borrower's copy of the valuationDelivered and evidenced.
Title exception / exclusion / requirementA risk not insured; a category outside the policy; and something the insurer needs before issuing. Requirements carry the deadlines.
Owner's versus lender's policyDifferent interests, which is why both exist — and declining the owner's policy leaves the borrower uninsured.
ReconveyanceThe recorded release. Payment does not clear the record; the document does.
Mechanic's lien relation-backPriority may run from when work commenced, so a later-recorded lien can outrank the new deed of trust.
Mortgagee clauseThe provision naming the lender on the hazard policy.
Force-placed coverageCoverage the lender places after a lapse, typically far more expensive and protecting only the lender.
Insurance as a first-week itemIn mapped hazard areas, availability and cost are a common cause of failed transactions — discovered late because borrowers treat it as a formality.
ConditionA requirement satisfied before the loan proceeds. Prior to funding means the loan does not fund without it.
Re-verificationCredit and employment commonly re-checked before funding, which is why post-approval borrower conduct undoes approvals.
Rate lock expiryA foreseeable event when the file moves slowly, not an accident.
Adverse actionDenial, revocation, an unfavorable change in terms, or refusal to grant credit substantially as requested. Requires notice with specific reasons or the right to obtain them.
Specific reasonsThe actual reasons. A generic reference to standards does not satisfy the purpose.
Withdrawal versus incompleteThe applicant's act; versus a failure to supply requested information. Different treatment, and "stopped responding" is not a disposition.
Outcome reviewExamining approval, denial, pricing, and exception patterns rather than intentions.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A borrower is offered a 5/6 hybrid with a 6.0% start rate, a 2.75% margin, and an index at 4.50%. The originator tells him he qualifies "on the 6% payment." The file also includes a simultaneous second recorded at closing, and the housing figure used omits the $340 condominium dues.

Identify each error.

Solution. Three errors, and each understates the obligation the determination must consider.

The start rate does not qualify him. The ability-to-repay framework requires the payment to be computed on defined assumptions for adjustable and non-amortizing structures — and here the fully indexed rate is already 4.50 + 2.75 = 7.25%, above the start rate, so even with no market movement the payment rises. Telling him he qualifies on the 6% payment describes a different loan.

The simultaneous loan must be considered. A second recorded at the same closing is one of the factors, and it is among the two files most often miss.

Mortgage-related obligations include dues. That is why the housing figure is PITI plus dues and mortgage insurance, not principal and interest — the other commonly missed factor.

Underlying all three: the determination must be reasonable and good faith, based on verified and documented information, and the creditor must be able to show it actually considered the required factors. It is a determination, not a form.

Problem 2

An originator enters an optimistic self-employment income figure to obtain a favorable automated finding, planning to "true it up when the returns come in." When the underwriter questions the file he says the system approved it.

Assess.

Solution. A finding is not an approval. It is a recommendation based on the data entered, conditioned on that data being verified — and it identifies the documentation the file needs rather than deciding the credit question.

Garbage in, garbage out. A favorable finding produced from an income figure documentation does not support is worth nothing, and it will reverse when the documents arrive. The finding is also re-run as data changes during verification, so the optimistic entry buys nothing except a borrower expectation that will be broken.

"The system approved it" is not a defense for a file whose data was wrong. The underwriter still underwrites; the finding directs the documentation and a human confirms the file matches it.

What the originator should have contributed instead: accurate data at the front — every hour spent verifying before submission is returned in conditions not raised — complete documentation matched to the finding, and honest presentation of the weakness with the borrower's explanation documented in his own words.

Problem 3

An appraisal comes in $30,000 below the contract price. The originator emails the appraiser three sales he believes were overlooked, notes that the roof was replaced last year and was not mentioned, and adds: "We need $920,000 to make this work — can you take another look?" His borrower and his branch manager both asked him to.

Separate what is permitted from what is not, and describe the correct process.

Solution. The email mixes something permitted with something prohibited, and the prohibited part contaminates the rest.

Permitted: supplying genuinely relevant information through the proper channel — sales the licensee believes relevant, information about condition and improvements, a copy of the contract. The three sales and the roof replacement are exactly that, and the roof is a factual correction if the report omitted a permitted improvement.

Prohibited: "We need $920,000." That is a target, and a value that moves after that conversation is unreliable for the purpose the appraisal serves. Requests to "take another look" that arrive with a number attached are the pattern to refuse — including when they come from your own borrower and your own manager.

The correct process is a reconsideration of value through the lender's defined channel, not a direct email to the appraiser. Appraiser independence requirements govern who may order and communicate with the appraiser, and firms implement defined channels precisely so individual originators are not the point of contact.

And what is not a reconsideration: an assertion that the value is wrong because the contract price is higher, or because the transaction fails without a different number.

Problem 4

The borrower asks what happens now that the appraisal is low, whether the price "automatically drops," whether he can demand a second appraisal, and — since he waived the appraisal contingency — whether he can cancel and get his deposit back.

Answer each.

Solution. Lenders lend against the lower of appraised value and purchase price, so the loan amount is computed on the appraised value. On a refinance there would be no price and value would be the appraisal alone.

His options are practical rather than automatic: bring additional funds, renegotiate the price, negotiate another resolution such as a credit or a term change, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed.

What does not happen automatically: the price does not adjust to appraised value by operation of any loan program; the loan is not denied; and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right.

On the waived contingency: that is a legal question and the originator must not answer it. The practical options remain, but the removed contingency limits his contractual rights, and whether he may cancel and what happens to the deposit turns on the contract's terms and the circumstances. Recommend counsel before he decides to stop performing.

Separately, confirm the borrower received his copy of the appraisal and that delivery is evidenced — a file that cannot show when the valuation reached him has a gap exactly where an examiner looks.

Problem 5

A refinance file shows an unreleased 2016 deed of trust the borrower says was paid, a judgment against a similarly named person, an existing second, and a $180,000 renovation completed four months ago with an unpaid contractor dispute. The preliminary report arrived on day eleven of a fourteen-day lock.

Handle each, and identify what went wrong before any of it.

Solution. The timing failure came first, and it made everything else harder. The preliminary report belongs at the front of the queue, because requirements carry the deadlines and some take weeks.

The 2016 deed of trust requires a recorded reconveyance. Payment does not clear the record; the document does — the borrower's recollection is not that document — and obtaining one from a lender that has merged or ceased to exist can take weeks.

The judgment goes to title, resolved through a statement of information. Never assumed away.

The existing second likely requires a subordination agreement, because paying off and re-recording the first would otherwise move the second into first position. That is the second lienholder's decision with counsel — never "standard."

The renovation is the exposure a mortgage licensee must recognize. Mechanic's lien priority may relate back to when work commenced, so a lien recorded next month can outrank the new deed of trust — and lien rights arise from work, not from a contract with the owner, so subcontractors the borrower never met can have them. Surface it to escrow, title, and counsel now.

And a lock that expires because the file moved slowly is a foreseeable event, not an accident.

Problem 6

A property is in a mapped fire hazard severity zone. The originator plans to have the borrower obtain insurance quotes "once we're through underwriting." Separately, the borrower's existing policy on another property lapsed and he asks why his servicer charged him $4,100 for coverage.

Assess both.

Solution. The insurance plan is the single most preventable failure in California mortgage practice right now. In mapped fire and flood areas, availability and cost of hazard insurance have become a common cause of failed transactions — and the failure is discovered late precisely because borrowers and originators treat insurance as a formality.

Insurance is a first-week item in a mapped hazard area, not an administrative closing task. A borrower who learns in week one that coverage will cost far more than assumed can act — restructure, renegotiate, or walk. One who learns it two days before closing generally cannot.

The file must also confirm coverage is in force at closing, that the amount satisfies the program, that the mortgagee clause is correct, and that the premium is paid or escrowed. And where the property is in a designated special flood hazard area on a federally related loan, flood insurance carries its own requirement determined by a defined process.

The $4,100 is force-placed coverage. Where a policy lapses, the lender may place coverage and charge the borrower — typically at far higher cost, and protecting only the lender's interest. That is a real consequence of a lapse, and it is worth telling every borrower at closing rather than letting them discover it.

Problem 7

Four days before funding, three conditions remain: a verbal verification of employment, sourcing of a $14,000 deposit, and a signed corrected disclosure. The borrower is unreachable, movers are booked, and the branch manager suggests marking the verbal verification complete since "we spoke to them last month" and having the originator sign the disclosure correction on the borrower's behalf.

Respond.

Solution. Refuse both suggestions, and treat the conditions as what they are.

An unsatisfied prior-to-funding condition means the loan does not fund, whatever the schedule says and whoever has booked movers. Describing conditions to a borrower as "just paperwork" is what produced this situation — it removed his motivation to respond quickly.

The verbal verification is commonly required shortly before funding precisely because an approval rests on the file as underwritten and lenders re-verify employment before funding. A verification from last month is not the condition. Representing that a verbal verification occurred when it did not is a misrepresentation.

Signing on the borrower's behalf is a misrepresentation and is never available.

The deposit still requires sourcing, because an undisclosed loan deposited as savings is a hidden obligation that would make the ratios wrong.

What should happen: escalate today rather than on the due date — a condition that cannot be satisfied is a problem on the day it is identified, and there is usually an alternative if there is time. Reach the borrower through every channel, tell him plainly that funding depends on these three items, and address the lock consequences honestly.

Problem 8

A file is denied for insufficient documented income. The originator tells the borrower it was "the appraisal," delays the notice a week while shopping the file to two other lenders, sends a notice saying only "does not meet our credit standards," and never dispositions a second application from another borrower who stopped responding two months ago.

Identify every failure.

Solution. Four failures, and each is independently a problem.

Misstating the reason. Telling him it was the appraisal when he was denied for income is a misstatement he will act on — he may pay for a second appraisal or renegotiate a price for no reason — and the notice will say otherwise, so he will also learn the originator misled him.

Delaying the notice. Adverse action notice must go out within a defined period. A denial delayed while an originator shops the file is a compliance problem that helps no one, and it does not become acceptable because the motive was to find a solution.

The generic reason fails the requirement's purpose. The notice must contain either the actual, specific reasons or a disclosure of the right to obtain them — "does not meet our credit standards" tells the applicant nothing usable. Where a consumer report contributed, additional content is required, including the agency's identity and a statement that the agency did not make the decision and cannot supply the reasons.

The abandoned application is a fourth failure. "The borrower stopped responding" is not a disposition. An application may be treated as incomplete under a prescribed framework, including notice requirements in defined circumstances — and an application quietly abandoned and never dispositioned is exactly the file an examiner samples.

What the originator may legitimately tell the borrower: what the notice says, that he may request the specific reasons where the notice discloses that right, that he may obtain his report from the agency named, and that other lenders and programs exist. He may not editorialize about the decision or promise another lender will approve him — and a denied file needs a complete record as much as a funded one.

Chapter summary

Underwriting is a decision an originator does not make, and telling a borrower what underwriting will do makes it.

Ability to repay is a determination on verified and documented information, considering factors that include the simultaneous loan and mortgage-related obligations — and for adjustable structures, a payment computed on defined assumptions rather than a discounted start rate.

Qualified mortgage is a category with feature and points-and-fees limits, and non-QM is not improper. Business-purpose exclusions are why the classification discipline matters — a misclassified loan may be one for which the determination was never made.

An automated finding is a recommendation on the data entered, not an approval. "The system approved it" is not a defense, and compensating factors and exceptions are the lender's determinations — with exception patterns a fair lending issue.

Lenders lend against the lower of value or price. Supply an appraiser information, never a target, use the reconsideration channel, and evidence the borrower's copy.

Nothing about a low appraisal is automatic, and the deposit question on a waived contingency is legal.

Title and hazard insurance cover different things and run in different directions. Distinguish exceptions, exclusions, and requirements — which carry the deadlines — and order the report first.

Payment does not clear the record; a reconveyance does. Recent construction raises relation-back exposure, and a refinance with an existing second usually needs a subordination.

Insurance is a first-week item in mapped hazard areas, and force-placed coverage is the real consequence of a lapse.

Conditions are the work, not formalities. Read them as written, respond completely, assign owners and dates, escalate early — and never alter, backdate, sign for a borrower, or represent a condition satisfied when it is not.

Re-verification before funding is why post-approval conduct undoes approvals, and the written warning at application is the cheapest prevention available.

Adverse action requires timely notice with the actual specific reasons or the right to obtain them. Deliver it promptly, state the real reason, editorialize about nothing, and disposition every application — because "stopped responding" is not a disposition and a denied file needs as complete a record as a funded one.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment.
