Appraisal, title, escrow, and settlement

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Explain appraiser independence, who may order and communicate, and what a licensee may and may not send.
  • Read a valuation critically and request a reconsideration correctly.
  • Read a preliminary report, distinguish exceptions from requirements, and route each item.
  • Explain escrow's neutrality and what escrow instructions do and do not govern.
  • Read a settlement statement and reconcile it against what was disclosed and agreed.
  • Describe recording, funding, and document custody, and what each accomplishes.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: appraiser independence and valuation review55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: title exceptions and escrow50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: settlement statements, recording, and custody45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Appraisal independence

1.1 Why independence exists

An appraisal exists to measure the lender's collateral risk. A value that moves because someone needed it to move measures nothing, and the transaction, the lender, and any investor who buys the loan all rely on a number that is no longer an opinion.

Independence requirements exist to keep the people with an interest in the outcome away from the person forming the opinion.

1.2 The core rule

A licensee may provide genuinely relevant information through the proper channel. A licensee may not communicate a target.

Permitted — informationProhibited — a target
Sales the licensee believes relevant, with data"We need $920,000"
Information about condition, permitted improvements, and features"The deal dies without another $25,000"
A copy of the contract"Can you take another look?" with a number attached
Factual corrections — a miscounted bedroom, an omitted additionAny statement of the value required

The distinction is between supplying information and supplying a target — and a request to reconsider that arrives with a number attached is the pattern to refuse, including when it comes from your own borrower, your own agent, or your own manager.

1.3 Who may order and communicate

Independence requirements govern who may select, order, and communicate with the appraiser, and firms implement them through defined channels precisely so that individual originators are not the point of contact.

Common structures include an appraisal management company or an internal function separated from production. The separation is the control, and routing around it — by calling the appraiser, by suggesting an appraiser, or by having someone else make the call — defeats it.

1.4 Coercion and its softer forms

The prohibition reaches more than an explicit demand.

Also prohibited in substance: conditioning payment on a value; withholding payment for a value the requester dislikes; implying future assignments depend on the outcome; providing an anticipated or target value with the order; and selecting an appraiser because of a history of favorable values.

The last one is the subtlest and the most common. A firm that steers work toward appraisers who "understand the market" has built coercion into its ordering pattern without anyone saying anything prohibited.

1.5 The borrower's copy

The borrower is entitled to receive copies of appraisals and other written valuations developed in connection with the application — promptly upon completion or a defined period before consummation, whichever is earlier — with notice of the right early in the process.

Delivery is evidenced. A file that cannot show when the valuation reached the borrower has a gap exactly where an examiner looks.

1.6 Appraisal bias

Valuation is a judgment, and judgment is where bias operates. Concerns about appraisal bias — including in the treatment of neighborhoods and of the people occupying properties — are a recognized issue receiving increased federal and California attention.

The structural control is objective, market-derived support. A derived adjustment can be examined; an impression cannot. Comparable selection, adjustment derivation, and neighborhood description are each places where a stated basis constrains discretion.

Where a licensee believes an appraisal reflects bias: escalate to the broker and follow the lender's reconsideration process. Do not confront the appraiser, and do not advise the borrower that he has a claim — that is a legal conclusion. Lesson 14 develops the framework.

1.7 What a licensee never does

  • Order or select the appraiser where the firm's structure assigns that elsewhere.
  • Contact the appraiser directly where the channel is defined.
  • Send a target, in any form.
  • Suggest which comparables to use as a way of steering the conclusion.
  • Tell a borrower what the value "should" come in at.

1.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the information-versus-target distinction, name the softer forms of coercion, and state what a licensee does when an appraisal appears biased.

2. Valuation review

2.1 What the lender does with the report

Lenders review appraisals for completeness, support, and reasonableness — through desk or field review, automated tools, or a second appraisal where required.

A review that questions an appraisal is not an accusation. It is the lender testing whether the collateral conclusion is supported — the same discipline the appraisal itself applies to comparable selection.

2.2 Reading a report critically

An originator is not an appraiser and does not re-value the property. What an originator can do is read for factual accuracy and internal consistency, which is a different and legitimate exercise.

What to checkWhy
Property factsBedroom and bath count, square footage, lot size, garage, year built
Permitted additionsAn omitted permitted addition is a factual gap
Condition descriptionAgainst what the file and the borrower say
Occupancy notedAgainst the file's representation
Comparable dates and distancesWhether they are recent and within a defensible market area
Adjustment directionAdjustments are made to the comparable, never the subject
Net versus gross adjustmentA small net can conceal a large gross, and reliability tracks gross
Whether the conclusion followsWhether the reconciliation explains the weighting

2.3 The direction of adjustment

Worth stating because it is the mechanic most often misread:

Adjustments are made to the comparable, never to the subject. If the comparable is superior, its price is adjusted downward; if inferior, upward.

Comparable better, subtract.

An originator who sees adjustments running the other way is looking at either an unusual presentation or an error, and it is worth asking through the proper channel.

2.4 What a low value means

Lenders lend against the lower of the appraised value and the purchase price.

On a refinance there is no purchase price, so value is the appraised value — which is why a refinance is more exposed to the appraisal outcome and why cash-out availability is not knowable until the appraisal arrives.

The borrower's options are practical rather than automatic: bring additional funds, renegotiate the price, negotiate another resolution, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed.

What does not happen automatically: the price does not adjust to the appraised value by operation of any program, the loan is not denied, and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right.

Where an appraisal contingency has been removed, the practical options remain but the contractual rights are limited — and whether the borrower may cancel and what happens to a deposit is a legal question for counsel.

2.5 The reconsideration of value

Done correctly:

  • Through the lender's defined channel, never by contacting the appraiser.
  • With relevant sales the appraiser may not have considered, identified with data rather than asserted.
  • With factual corrections — a miscounted room, an omitted permitted addition, a misdescribed condition.
  • Without a target number.

What is not a reconsideration: an assertion that the value is wrong because the contract price is higher, or because the transaction fails without a different number.

2.6 Property condition findings

Appraisals frequently identify condition items, and program requirements can make some of them conditions to funding — health and safety items, a failing roof, missing systems, or incomplete construction.

Two practical consequences:

A property with deferred maintenance may not satisfy a program's requirements, which is a closing-probability fact rather than a preference — and never translated into a preference against buyers using a program.

Repairs and reinspection take time, which puts them among the slow items rather than the closing items.

2.7 Other valuation products

Automated valuation models, broker price opinions, and desk reviews each have defined uses and limits, and whether a particular product may be relied on for a particular purpose is a program and compliance question.

A licensee should not describe one as equivalent to an appraisal, and should not obtain one to test a value before ordering the appraisal in a way that would defeat the independence structure.

2.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to read a report for factual accuracy, state the adjustment direction rule, explain what a low value produces, and describe a correct reconsideration request.

3. Title exceptions and liens

3.1 What the preliminary report is

A preliminary report reports the condition of title as shown in the records and states the terms on which the title insurer would be willing to issue a policy, including its exceptions.

Three things it is not: a guarantee that title is clear; the policy itself; or a survey — it addresses record title, not the physical property.

3.2 The three categories

CategoryWhat it is
ExceptionAn item the policy will not insure against
ExclusionA category the policy form does not cover at all — governmental regulation, eminent domain, matters created by the insured
RequirementSomething the insurer needs before issuing

Requirements are the items with deadlines attached, and they are what delays closings.

Three responses wrong in every case: treating an item as routine because most properties have one; asking title to "remove" an exception; and predicting an easement's or restriction's effect on the borrower's plans.

3.3 What the lender needs answered

Who owns it, what encumbers it, and where will our lien sit.

3.4 The recurring items and their routing

ItemHandling
An unreleased deed of trust the borrower says was paidA recorded reconveyance must be obtained. Payment does not clear the record; the document does — and obtaining one from a lender that merged or ceased to exist can take weeks
An existing second on a refinanceA subordination agreement is generally required, because paying off and re-recording the first would otherwise move the second into first position. That is the second lienholder's decision with counsel — never "standard"
A judgment against a similarly named personRouted to title and resolved through a statement of information. Never assumed away
Recent constructionMechanic's lien priority may relate back to when work commenced, so a lien recorded later can outrank the new deed of trust — and rights arise from work, not from a contract with the owner
A lis pendensA recorded notice of pending litigation affecting title. A serious cloud; route to counsel
Property tax delinquencyThe tax lien generally takes priority regardless of when it attached
Authority requirementsTrustee evidence, corporate resolutions, powers of attorney — each a requirement with a deadline
Easements and CC&RsObtain the underlying documents; they can prevent what the borrower intends

3.5 The mechanic's lien question at intake

Has any work been done on this property recently, by whom, and is everyone paid?

A borrower who renovated last spring with an unresolved contractor dispute has a title problem that has not appeared yet — and a lender has a priority problem. Lenders on construction and recently improved property require indemnities, title endorsements, and evidence of payment for exactly this reason.

Whether a particular lien is valid or timely is a legal question. The licensee's contribution is timing: a defect surfaced at intake is a condition; the same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

3.6 The policies

The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority. The owner's policy insures the borrower's interest.

They insure different interests, which is why both commonly exist — and a borrower who declines an owner's policy because "there's a title policy on the loan" has left his own interest uninsured.

Endorsements extend or modify coverage for particular risks. A licensee should know they exist and are ordered, and should not represent what any particular endorsement covers.

3.7 What title insurance does not cover

Zoning and governmental regulation. Physical condition. Boundary location under a standard policy — the survey exception. Matters the insured created or agreed to. Matters known to the insured and not disclosed. Anything the policy excepted.

A borrower asks whether a fence is on the line and is told the title report "came back clean." That answer is wrong. The report addresses record title, and boundary location is precisely what the standard policy excepts. A survey answers it.

3.8 Order it first

The preliminary report and its underlying documents belong at the front of the queue, with the association documents and the hazard-area insurance quotes.

An exception discovered late — an easement across a building site, an unreleased lien requiring a document from a lender that no longer exists — takes time to resolve. A borrower who receives the report on day three has options; one who receives it on day twelve has a formality.

3.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish exceptions, exclusions, and requirements; route each recurring item; state the mechanic's lien intake question; and state what title insurance does not cover.

4. Escrow instructions and funds

4.1 What escrow is

Escrow is a neutral third party holding funds and documents under conditional delivery, authorized to act only according to the parties' mutual written instructions.

Two elements make an arrangement an escrow: a binding contract between the parties, and conditional delivery to a neutral holder.

4.2 Why it exists

Simultaneity. A buyer will not release funds before receiving title; a seller will not release title before receiving funds. Escrow breaks the impasse by having both go first to a neutral party, who releases to each only when the conditions are satisfied.

That single function explains every rule that follows.

4.3 Neutrality and what it forbids

Escrow mayEscrow may not
Follow mutual written instructionsAct on one party's instruction alone
Hold funds and documentsAdvise either party
Prepare and circulate documents per the instructionsDecide a dispute between the parties
Record and disburse when conditions are metRelease funds because one party asserts entitlement
Report status to both partiesTake a position on who is right

Where the parties disagree, escrow stops. And an agent's or an originator's confirmation is not a party's consent.

4.4 Instructions and the underlying agreement

Escrow's instructions implement the parties' agreement. Where they conflict, the agreement governs, and the discrepancy is reconciled by the parties in writing — not by escrow deciding and not by a licensee telling escrow which figure to use.

Instructions are amended the same way the agreement is: in writing, signed. An email from a licensee amends nothing.

4.5 The reconciliation nobody else performs

Nobody compares the escrow instructions and the closing figures against the loan terms and the disclosures line by line — escrow prepares from what it received, the lender reads its own documents, and the borrower reads a summary.

The originator's contribution at this stage is that reconciliation: loan amount, rate, term, payoffs, credits, compensation, prorations, and cash to close, against what was disclosed and agreed.

A discrepancy found the day before closing is a problem. The same discrepancy found after disbursement is a dispute.

4.6 Funds

Funds to close must arrive in a form and by a time the closing requires, and cleared rather than merely deposited.

Payoff demands are obtained by escrow from each lienholder and state what satisfies the obligation — including accrued interest to the payoff date and other amounts owed under the note. They are routinely more than the last statement balance, and routinely a surprise to a borrower nobody warned.

Prorations allocate continuing charges at the ownership boundary, and escrow computes the operative figures — a licensee explains the concept and checks that an estimate is in the right range.

4.7 Trust funds

Where funds pass through the brokerage rather than directly to escrow, they are trust funds: separated from the firm's own funds, recorded by beneficiary, and handled timely.

A check held in a desk drawer over a weekend is a trust fund handling problem, whatever the intention.

4.8 Selection and referral

Selection of escrow is negotiable between the parties and is often addressed in the purchase agreement.

A licensee must not accept anything of value for directing settlement business. Referrals are ordinary; payment for them is prohibited, and disclosure does not cure it.

Where the firm has an ownership interest, that is an affiliated business arrangement — permitted subject to disclosure with an estimate at or before referral, no required use, and no thing of value beyond a return on ownership.

4.9 Wire fraud

The highest-risk moment in the transaction is when funds move.

  1. Warn in writing at application — wire instructions will never change by email; verify by voice at an independently obtained number.
  2. Treat any change as presumptively fraudulent until verified through a channel the attacker does not control.
  3. Never verify using a number from the email carrying the instructions.

Report any incident or near-miss to the broker immediately, whether or not funds moved.

4.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what makes an arrangement an escrow, state what neutrality forbids, explain what governs a conflict between instructions and the agreement, and state the wire fraud protocol.

5. Settlement statements

5.1 What the statement does

The settlement statement — and for a consumer mortgage, the Closing Disclosure — shows each party's debits and credits and the resulting cash position.

It is the arithmetic of the transaction, and it is the last place a discrepancy can be caught cheaply.

5.2 The structure

SideTypical entries
Borrower/buyer debitsPurchase price, closing costs the borrower pays, prorated items reimbursed to the seller
Borrower/buyer creditsDeposit, loan proceeds, seller credits, prorated items owed by the seller
Seller debitsLoan payoffs, compensation, seller-paid costs, credits to buyer, prorated items owed, liens satisfied
Seller creditsSale price, prorated items prepaid

The reliable check: the price is a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer; the deposit and the loan proceeds are credits to the buyer. Everything else follows from asking who benefits and who pays.

On a refinance there is no seller side — the statement shows the new loan proceeds against the payoff, costs, prepaids, and any cash to or from the borrower.

5.3 Prorations

Continuing charges are allocated at the ownership boundary.

Seller prepaid beyond the boundary → seller credited, buyer debited. Charge accrued, or money held for the buyer's period → seller debited, buyer credited.

Taxes $7,300 annually, paid through June 30; closing May 31; 365-day basis; day of closing to the buyer. Buyer's period May 31–June 30 = 31 days. 7,300 ÷ 365 = $20.00/day × 31 = $620.00 credited to the seller.

Three conventions change the answer and must be read rather than assumed: the day-count basis, who receives the day of closing, and the fact that California's property tax year does not align with the calendar year.

5.4 The lines an originator reconciles

LineAgainst
Loan amount, rate, termThe lock and the approval
Points and lender chargesThe Loan Estimate, within tolerance
Third-party chargesThe estimate and their tolerance category
Prepaid interestThe actual disbursement date
Escrow depositsThe program requirement and the actual tax and insurance figures
PayoffsThe payoff demands, good through the disbursement date
CreditsWhat was agreed and disclosed
CompensationWhat was disclosed — the reconciliation firms skip
ProrationsThe convention stated and the boundary used
Cash to closeThe whole statement

5.5 Tolerances at the statement

The final charges are where the tolerance framework of Lesson 09 becomes concrete.

Zero tolerance charges generally may not increase. Ten percent category totals may not exceed the estimate by more than ten percent. Unlimited charges may vary, subject to a real good faith standard.

Where a tolerance is exceeded without a valid changed circumstance, a cure is owed — refunding the excess within a defined period with a corrected disclosure. A cure is a remedy, not a business decision.

5.6 Explaining the statement to a borrower

What a licensee does: walk the borrower through what each category is, distinguish lender charges from third-party charges and prepaids, explain that prepaids are amounts he would owe anyway, and identify anything that changed from the estimate and why.

What a licensee does not do: describe a fee as "standard," explain a lender's charge as though qualified to, or minimize a change the borrower is entitled to understand.

A borrower surprised at the table is a borrower who was not told, and the surprise is almost always avoidable — most of it is prepaids and escrow deposits nobody explained.

5.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to place entries on the correct side, compute a proration in both directions, list the lines an originator reconciles, and explain a statement to a borrower.

6. Recording, funding, and document custody

6.1 The four events, in order

#EventWhat happens
1SigningDocuments are executed. The transaction is not closed
2FundingThe lender releases proceeds, subject to its conditions
3RecordingThe deed and security instrument are recorded, giving constructive notice
4DisbursementEscrow disburses once recording is confirmed

Recording precedes disbursement deliberately — it prevents a gap in which money has moved but the interests are not of record.

6.2 Recording order and priority

Where multiple instruments record, the order establishes lien priority.

An out-of-sequence recording can place a new lender behind an interest it was to precede — which is why closing is sequenced rather than simultaneous, and why this is not a clerical preference.

The exceptions from Lesson 03 still apply: property tax liens generally take priority regardless of timing, and mechanic's lien priority may relate back to when work commenced.

6.3 Rescindable transactions

On a transaction carrying a right of rescission — in outline, certain transactions secured by the consumer's principal dwelling, notably a refinance with a different lender, and not a purchase-money loan on the dwelling being acquired — funds are not disbursed until the rescission period expires.

Each consumer entitled to rescind must receive the required notices, and the period runs from the later of consummation, delivery of the notice, or delivery of the material disclosures — so a defective or undelivered notice can extend it.

A refinance closing is therefore not a purchase closing, and a borrower expecting funds at signing should have been told in advance.

6.4 Funding conditions

Prior-to-funding conditions are not formalities. An unsatisfied one means the loan does not fund, whatever the schedule says.

The recurring final-stage items: the verbal verification of employment; a final credit re-check; evidence of insurance in force with the correct mortgagee clause; the payoff demand good through the disbursement date; and confirmation that funds to close have arrived and cleared.

6.5 Constructive notice

Recording gives constructive notice to the world — a recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so the law treats everyone as knowing it.

Inquiry notice is the one that surprises lenders, because nothing was recorded: an occupant who is not the record owner, rent paid to a third party, visible recent construction. A party may be charged with what an investigation would have revealed — and it threatens bona fide encumbrancer status, which requires taking for value, in good faith, and without notice.

6.6 Document custody

After recording, the original recorded instruments are returned as directed, and the note is delivered to the lender or its custodian.

Two points a licensee should understand:

The note is the instrument that carries the debt, and its custody matters — which is why lenders and investors use custodians and why an original's whereabouts is not a clerical question.

The recorded instruments come back weeks later, and a borrower asking why he does not have his deed yet is asking a reasonable question with an ordinary answer.

6.7 Confirming closing to the borrower

When funding and recording are confirmed, tell the borrower in writing, with the date and what it means.

What a borrower needs to know at that point: that the loan funded and recorded, and on what dates; when the first payment is due — remembering that interest is paid in arrears, so it is generally not the following month; where to send it, and that servicing may transfer; what his escrow account covers and that the payment can change when taxes or insurance do; and where his documents will come from and roughly when.

6.8 The file at closing

  • The final Closing Disclosure and its delivery evidence.
  • The signed note and security instrument.
  • The settlement statement and the reconciliation performed against the disclosures.
  • Payoff demands and evidence of payoff.
  • Evidence of insurance with the correct mortgagee clause.
  • The title policy or commitment to issue.
  • Funding and recording confirmations, with dates.
  • Compensation disclosed and received, reconciled.
  • Any cure issued, with its corrected disclosure.

6.9 The test

Reconstructability: could a person who was not there determine what was disclosed, what was agreed, what was charged, when funds moved, and on what basis?

A file that passes survives an examination even where it contains a problem. A file that does not fails even where it contains none.

6.10 Checkpoint

You should be able to sequence the four events and explain the ordering, describe how a rescindable closing differs, distinguish constructive from inquiry notice, and state what the file must show at closing.

Key terms

TermDefinition
Appraiser independenceRequirements keeping people with an interest in the outcome away from the person forming the opinion.
Information versus targetRelevant sales, condition information, the contract, and factual corrections are permitted. Any statement of the value required is not — including at your own borrower's or manager's request.
Defined channelWho may select, order, and communicate with the appraiser. The separation is the control, and routing around it defeats it.
Soft coercionConditioning or withholding payment on a value, implying future assignments depend on it, providing a target with the order, and selecting appraisers with a history of favorable values.
Valuation copiesProvided promptly upon completion or a defined period before consummation, whichever is earlier, with early notice — and delivery evidenced.
Adjustment directionMade to the comparable, never the subject. Comparable better, subtract.
Gross versus net adjustmentA small net can conceal a large gross, and reliability tracks gross.
Lower of value or priceWhat lenders lend against. On a refinance, value is the appraised value, so cash-out availability is unknown until it arrives.
Reconsideration of valueThrough the lender's channel, with relevant sales and factual corrections, and without a target.
Preliminary reportA report of record title stating the terms on which a policy would issue. Not a guarantee, not the policy, not a survey.
Exception / exclusion / requirementA risk not insured; a category outside the policy; and something needed before issuing. Requirements carry the deadlines.
ReconveyanceThe recorded release. Payment does not clear the record; the document does, and obtaining one can take weeks.
Subordination on a refinanceGenerally required where a second exists, because the new first would otherwise record behind it. The second lienholder's decision with counsel — never "standard."
Statement of informationThe confidential form letting title distinguish the parties from similarly named people in the records.
Mechanic's lien relation-backPriority may run from when work commenced, and rights arise from work rather than from a contract with the owner.
Lis pendensA recorded notice of pending litigation affecting title. A serious cloud.
Owner's versus lender's policyDifferent interests, which is why both exist — declining the owner's policy leaves the borrower uninsured.
What title does not coverZoning and regulation, physical condition, boundary location under a standard policy, matters the insured created or concealed, and anything excepted.
EscrowA neutral holder acting only on mutual written instructions, existing to solve simultaneity.
Escrow neutralityHolds, does not advise, does not decide. Where the parties disagree, escrow stops, and a licensee's confirmation is not a party's consent.
Instructions versus agreementInstructions implement the agreement; where they conflict the agreement governs, reconciled by the parties in writing.
Payoff demandWhat satisfies the obligation, including accrued interest to the payoff date and other amounts under the note — more than the last statement.
Proration directionPrepaid beyond the boundary credits the seller; accrued or held for the buyer's period debits the seller.
Settlement statement checkPrice is a seller credit and a buyer debit; deposit and loan proceeds are buyer credits.
The originator's reconciliationLoan terms, charges, prepaids, escrows, payoffs, credits, compensation, prorations, and cash to close — against what was disclosed and agreed. Nobody else does it.
CureRefunding a tolerance excess within a defined period with a corrected disclosure. A remedy, not a business decision.
The four eventsSigning, funding, recording, disbursement — with recording before disbursement deliberately, and recording order establishing lien priority.
Rescindable closingFunds wait for the period to expire; each entitled consumer receives the notice; the period runs from the later of defined events.
Constructive versus inquiry noticeKnowledge charged from the record; versus knowledge charged from facts that would prompt investigation — which threatens bona fide encumbrancer status.
Document custodyThe note goes to the lender or its custodian; recorded instruments return weeks later.
Interest in arrearsWhy the first payment is generally not due the month after closing.

Practice problems

Problem 1

An appraisal comes in $30,000 low. The originator emails the appraiser directly with three sales he believes were overlooked, notes that a permitted addition was omitted from the report, and adds: "We need $920,000 to make this work." His borrower and his manager both asked him to send it. His firm uses an appraisal management company.

Separate what is permitted from what is not, and state the correct process.

Solution. Two of the three contents are permitted; the third contaminates the message; and the channel was wrong regardless.

Permitted — information: relevant sales identified with data, and a factual correction such as an omitted permitted addition. Those are exactly what a reconsideration is built from.

Prohibited — a target. "We need $920,000" is the communication independence rules exist to prevent, and a request to reconsider that arrives with a number attached is the pattern to refuse — including when it comes from your own borrower and your own manager.

The channel is the control. Independence requirements govern who may select, order, and communicate with the appraiser, and firms use an appraisal management company or a separated internal function precisely so individual originators are not the point of contact. Emailing the appraiser directly defeats the separation, even with a message containing only permitted content.

Correct process: a reconsideration of value through the lender's defined channel, with the sales and the factual correction, and no number. And what is not a reconsideration: an assertion that the value is wrong because the contract price is higher or because the transaction fails without a different number.

Problem 2

A branch manager notices that two appraisers "always come in short" and directs the ordering desk to route work toward three others who "understand this market." He also proposes paying the appraisal invoice only after the report is reviewed, and including an "estimated value" field on the order form.

Assess each practice.

Solution. All three are coercion in substance, and the first is the subtlest and most common.

Selecting appraisers because of a history of favorable values builds coercion into the ordering pattern without anyone saying anything prohibited. The appraisers are never told what to conclude; they are simply selected for having concluded favorably before — and the effect on the population of reports is the same as an instruction.

Conditioning payment on the review is withholding payment based on a value, which is prohibited in substance whatever the stated rationale.

An "estimated value" field on the order is providing a target with the order — the target arrives before the work begins rather than after.

Why it matters beyond compliance: an appraisal exists to measure the lender's collateral risk, and a value that moves because someone needed it to move measures nothing. The lender, the transaction, and any investor who buys the loan all rely on a number that has stopped being an opinion.

Escalate to the broker. This is a firm-level practice, not an individual file question.

Problem 3

A refinance borrower wants $150,000 cash out and has been told by his originator that it "shouldn't be a problem." The appraisal returns below expectations. The borrower asks whether the price adjusts, whether he can demand a second appraisal, and — since he waived his contingency on a separate purchase — whether he can cancel that one and recover his deposit.

Address each.

Solution. The first error was the assurance. On a refinance there is no purchase price, so value is the appraised value — which makes a refinance more exposed to the appraisal outcome than a purchase, and means cash-out availability is not knowable until the appraisal arrives. "Shouldn't be a problem" was a prediction about someone else's independent opinion.

Lenders lend against the lower of appraised value and purchase price, so on the purchase the loan is computed on the appraisal.

The price does not adjust automatically by operation of any program, the loan is not denied, and no one is entitled to a second appraisal as of right. His practical options are to bring funds, renegotiate, negotiate another resolution, or cancel if a contingency permits and its procedure is followed.

The waived contingency question is legal and must not be answered. The practical options remain, but the removed contingency limits his contractual rights, and whether he may cancel and what happens to the deposit turns on the contract's terms and the circumstances. Recommend counsel before he stops performing.

Also confirm he received his copy of the appraisal and that delivery is evidenced.

Problem 4

A refinance preliminary report arrives on day eleven of a fourteen-day lock. It shows an unreleased 2016 deed of trust the borrower says was paid, an existing second, a judgment against a similarly named person, and a lis pendens. The borrower also mentions a $180,000 renovation finished four months ago with an unpaid contractor.

Route each and identify the first failure.

Solution. The timing failure came first and made everything harder. The preliminary report and its underlying documents belong at the front of the queue, because requirements carry the deadlines and several here take weeks. A borrower who receives it on day three has options; on day eleven he has a formality.

The 2016 deed of trust requires a recorded reconveyance. Payment does not clear the record; the document does — the borrower's recollection is not that document — and obtaining one from a lender that merged or ceased to exist can take weeks.

The existing second requires a subordination agreement, because paying off and re-recording the first would otherwise move the second into first position. That is the second lienholder's decision with counsel — never "standard."

The judgment goes to title, resolved through a statement of information. Never assumed away.

The lis pendens is a serious cloud — a recorded notice that pending litigation may affect anyone acquiring an interest. Route to counsel immediately.

The renovation is the exposure a mortgage licensee must recognize. Mechanic's lien priority may relate back to when work commenced, so a lien recorded next month can outrank the new deed of trust — and rights arise from work, not from a contract with the owner, so subcontractors the borrower never met can have them. A defect surfaced at intake is a condition; the same defect surfaced after funding is a loss.

Problem 5

A borrower asks whether the neighbor's fence encroaches, is told the title report "came back clean," and declines an owner's policy because "there's already a title policy on the loan." He also asks what the "requirements" section means, since the exceptions looked more important.

Correct all three.

Solution. "Clean" answers a question he did not ask. A preliminary report addresses record title — what the records show about ownership and encumbrances. It is not a survey, and the standard policy excepts matters a survey would disclose. Nothing in the report speaks to where the fence is. A survey does.

Also outside coverage: zoning and governmental regulation, physical condition, matters the insured created or agreed to, matters known and not disclosed, and anything excepted.

Declining the owner's policy is not economizing on a duplicate. The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority; the owner's policy insures his interest. They insure different interests, which is why both exist — and declining leaves his own interest uninsured.

The requirements are the more urgent section, not the less. An exception is a risk the policy will not insure against; an exclusion is a category outside the policy entirely; a requirement is something the insurer needs before issuing — a reconveyance, a resolution, authority evidence. Requirements carry the deadlines, and they are what delays closings.

Problem 6

The day before recording, the buyer emails escrow instructing it to hold back $4,000 from the seller's proceeds for a repair the seller promised verbally. The seller knows nothing about it. The originator emails escrow confirming the request is legitimate, and separately tells escrow to use the loan amount from the approval rather than the lower figure in the escrow instructions.

Assess.

Solution. Escrow stops on the first, and the second is not the originator's to direct.

A change to disbursement requires mutual written instructions. One party cannot redirect funds; and escrow may not simply disburse in full either, since that also acts on one side's position once a genuine dispute is raised. Escrow holds, does not advise, and does not decide — and where the parties disagree, it stops.

The originator's confirmation supplies nothing. An originator is not a party, and a licensee's confirmation is not a party's consent. The parties resolve it in writing and the resolution reaches escrow as a mutual instruction — and the job is to get that done before the closing date, not to argue with escrow about its role.

On the loan amount: escrow's instructions implement the parties' agreement, and where they conflict the agreement governs, reconciled by the parties in writing — not by escrow deciding and not by a licensee telling escrow which figure to use. Instructions are amended the way the agreement is: in writing, signed. An email from a licensee amends nothing.

What the originator should do is the reconciliation nobody else performs — compare the instructions and figures against the loan terms and disclosures, and raise the discrepancy immediately.

Problem 7

Reconcile a purchase settlement statement. Price $920,000; deposit $30,000; loan $736,000; annual taxes $7,300 paid by the seller through June 30 with a May 31 closing on a 365-day basis, day of closing to the buyer. The originator notices the compensation line shows $5,650 where the Loan Estimate disclosed $4,200, and an appraisal fee $200 above the estimate with no changed circumstance documented.

Place the entries, compute the proration, and address both discrepancies.

Solution. Placement: the price is a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer; the deposit and the loan proceeds are credits to the buyer. Everything else follows from asking who benefits and who pays.

Proration. The seller prepaid through June 30 but owns only through May 30. Buyer's period is May 31–June 30 = 31 days. 7,300 ÷ 365 = $20.00/day × 31 = $620.00 credited to the seller, debited to the buyer. Three conventions must be read rather than assumed: the day-count basis, who gets the day of closing, and the fact that California's tax year does not align with the calendar year.

The compensation discrepancy is the finding with the widest consequences — reaching the California mortgage loan disclosure statement, the federal disclosures, and potentially the points-and-fees calculation. Reconciling disclosed against received is the control firms skip, because one function prepares the disclosure and another receives the payment.

The appraisal fee is generally zero tolerance — a service the consumer could not shop for — so absent a valid changed circumstance it may not increase, and a cure is owed: refunding the excess within a defined period with a corrected disclosure. A cure is a remedy, not a business decision.

Both were caught the day before closing, which is the point. A discrepancy found then is a problem; found after disbursement it is a dispute.

Problem 8

A refinance borrower is told he is "clear to close," signs on Monday, and calls Wednesday angry that he has no money and no recorded deed. He also asks when his first payment is due, where to send it, why his payoff exceeded his statement by $6,400, and whether his payment can change since it is a fixed-rate loan.

Answer each.

Solution. "Clear to close" means the lender's conditions to document and fund are satisfied. It is not funding and not closing.

The four events, in order: signing — documents executed, the transaction is not closed; funding; recording, which gives constructive notice; and disbursement, after recording is confirmed — deliberately, so money does not move before the interests are of record. Recording order also establishes lien priority, which is why closing is sequenced rather than simultaneous.

His refinance is rescindable, and that is the real reason for the delay. On certain transactions secured by the principal dwelling — notably a refinance with a different lender — funds are not disbursed until the rescission period expires. Each entitled consumer must receive the notice, and the period runs from the later of consummation, delivery of the notice, or delivery of the material disclosures, so a defective notice extends it. He should have been told this before signing: a refinance closing is not a purchase closing.

His recorded documents come back weeks later, which is ordinary.

The payoff included accrued interest to the payoff date and other amounts owed under the note — routinely more than the last statement.

Interest is paid in arrears, so his first payment is generally not the following month. Servicing may transfer, so where to send it can change.

And yes, his payment can change even on a fixed-rate loan: the escrow account covers taxes and insurance, and a shortage after an increase produces a payment increase on a loan he believed was fixed.

Chapter summary

Independence exists because a value that moves because someone needed it to move measures nothing. Supply information, never a target, and use the defined channel — routing around it defeats the control.

Soft coercion counts, including selecting appraisers with a history of favorable values.

Read a report for factual accuracy and consistency, remembering that adjustments are made to the comparable and that reliability tracks gross adjustment.

Lenders lend against the lower of value or price, and on a refinance value is the appraisal. Nothing about a low value is automatic, and the deposit question on a waived contingency is legal.

Reconsider through the channel, with data and factual corrections, and without a number.

A preliminary report addresses record title. Distinguish exceptions, exclusions, and requirements — and requirements carry the deadlines. Order it first.

Payment does not clear the record; a reconveyance does. A refinance with a second usually needs a subordination, and recent construction raises relation-back exposure — so ask the intake question.

Title does not insure boundary location under a standard policy, and the owner's and lender's policies insure different interests.

Escrow solves simultaneity by being neutral. It acts only on mutual written instructions, advises no one, decides nothing, and stops where the parties disagree — and a licensee's confirmation is not a party's consent.

Instructions implement the agreement, and the agreement governs a conflict.

Nobody but the originator reconciles the closing figures against what was disclosed and agreed — including compensation, which is the reconciliation firms skip.

Prorations run in two directions, and three conventions change the answer.

Where a tolerance is exceeded without a valid changed circumstance, a cure is owed.

Signing, funding, recording, disbursement — with recording before disbursement deliberately, recording order setting priority, and funds waiting on a rescindable transaction.

Constructive notice comes from the record; inquiry notice comes from the ground and threatens bona fide encumbrancer status.

Confirm closing in writing with the first payment date, where to send it, that servicing may transfer, and that an escrowed payment can change — and keep a file someone who was not there could reconstruct.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Identify every appraisal communication described and classify it as permitted information or a prohibited target and state the channel you would use, read the valuation for factual accuracy and state what you would raise and how, distinguish the exceptions from the requirements on the report given and route each item with a deadline, state what escrow may and may not do on the facts and what governs any conflict between the instructions and the agreement, reconcile the settlement figures against what was disclosed and agreed and identify every discrepancy and the remedy owed, compute any proration with its convention stated, sequence the closing events and state whether the transaction is rescindable, and list what the file must show at closing. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. An originator is frustrated that an appraisal came in low. She calls the appraiser, says the transaction will die without another $25,000 of value, forwards three additional sales she selected, and asks him to 'take another look.' The appraiser revises the value upward. What is the correct assessment?

  1. A. Pressuring an appraiser toward a target value violates appraiser independence, and the fact that the value changed after the call makes the resulting appraisal unreliable — providing genuinely relevant additional data through the proper channel is legitimate, but stating the needed number is not.
  2. B. There is no problem, because the originator provided factual comparable sales rather than making up a value.
  3. C. There is no problem, because the appraiser exercised his own independent judgment in deciding to revise.
  4. D. The only problem is that the originator contacted the appraiser directly rather than through the lender.

Answer: A. The distinction is between supplying information and supplying a target. Naming the number the transaction needs is exactly the influence independence rules exist to prevent, and the appraiser's nominal independence does not cure a value that moved after being told what it had to be.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. Why is appraiser independence protected in mortgage lending?

  1. A. Because the lender and the secondary market rely on the valuation to measure collateral risk, and a value influenced by parties with an interest in closing is unreliable for that purpose.
  2. B. Because appraisers are prohibited from communicating with anyone involved in the transaction.
  3. C. Because independence determines which appraisal approach must be used.
  4. D. Because independence rules set the fee the appraiser may charge.

Answer: A. Reliability of the collateral measure is the reason. Appropriate communication is permitted through proper channels, and independence rules govern neither methodology nor fees.

2. What does the lender's title policy insure?

  1. A. The validity and priority of the lender's lien, up to the policy amount and subject to its exceptions and exclusions.
  2. B. The borrower's ownership interest in the property.
  3. C. The property's physical condition at the time of closing.
  4. D. The accuracy of the appraised value relied on by the lender.

Answer: A. A lender's policy insures the lien and its priority. Ownership is the owner's policy, and neither condition nor value is a title matter.

3. What is escrow's role in a mortgage transaction closing?

  1. A. To act as a neutral holder that receives funds and documents and disburses and records according to the parties' and the lender's instructions.
  2. B. To verify that the borrower qualifies for the loan.
  3. C. To approve the loan terms on the borrower's behalf.
  4. D. To determine which liens must be paid from the proceeds.

Answer: A. Escrow implements instructions neutrally. Qualification is underwriting, term approval is the parties', and which liens are paid is determined by the title work and the instructions rather than by escrow's own judgment.

4. Why does the lender require a title report before funding?

  1. A. To confirm what interests exist against the property and what must be cleared so its lien records in the required position.
  2. B. To confirm the property's square footage and physical characteristics.
  3. C. To confirm the seller's asking price is reasonable.
  4. D. To confirm the borrower's occupancy of the property.

Answer: A. Title work exists for lien position. Physical characteristics come from the appraisal, price from the contract, and occupancy from separate documentation.

5. What happens at funding in a typical purchase transaction?

  1. A. The lender releases the loan proceeds to escrow subject to its conditions, and after recording confirms the lien's position, escrow disburses.
  2. B. The borrower receives the loan proceeds directly and pays the seller.
  3. C. The lender records its deed of trust and then decides whether to release funds.
  4. D. Escrow disburses to all parties and then requests the loan proceeds from the lender.

Answer: A. Funds flow to escrow under conditions, recording establishes position, and disbursement follows. Proceeds do not pass through the borrower, and escrow does not disburse before it holds the funds.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. The appraisal identifies significant deferred maintenance affecting habitability. What is the likely underwriting consequence?

  1. A. The lender may condition the loan on repairs being completed or on a holdback, because the collateral's condition affects its value and marketability.
  2. B. The appraisal is disregarded because condition is the buyer's concern rather than the lender's.
  3. C. The loan amount is automatically reduced by the estimated repair cost.
  4. D. The lender must obtain a second appraisal from a different appraiser.

Answer: A. Condition affects the collateral, so the lender addresses it with conditions. It is not disregarded, not handled by an automatic reduction, and does not require a second appraisal.

2. The preliminary report shows an unreleased deed of trust from a loan the borrower says he paid off years ago. What must happen?

  1. A. A recorded reconveyance or other clearing document must be obtained, because the record still shows the lien regardless of whether the debt was paid.
  2. B. The borrower's statement that it was paid is sufficient for the lender.
  3. C. The new lender may record ahead of it because the underlying debt no longer exists.
  4. D. Title insurance will cover the item automatically without further action.

Answer: A. Priority is determined by the record, so an unreleased lien must be cleared of record. The borrower's recollection does not clear it, recording later does not leapfrog it, and the insurer will except rather than silently insure it.

3. Who selects the appraiser in a typical residential mortgage transaction, and why?

  1. A. The lender or an independent management process makes the assignment, so that parties with an interest in the transaction closing do not choose the valuer.
  2. B. The borrower, since the borrower pays the appraisal fee.
  3. C. The originator, who knows which appraisers work efficiently.
  4. D. The seller's agent, who has the best knowledge of the local market.

Answer: A. Separating selection from the interested parties is the structural protection for independence — which is exactly why neither the borrower's payment nor the originator's convenience determines the choice.

4. The settlement statement shows a payoff amount higher than the borrower expected. What is the most likely explanation?

  1. A. The payoff includes interest accrued to the payoff date and may include other amounts under the note, so it exceeds the principal balance alone.
  2. B. The escrow holder added a fee for processing the payoff.
  3. C. The lender is charging the borrower for the new loan's costs twice.
  4. D. The payoff figure is an error that should be recalculated by escrow.

Answer: A. A payoff is the balance plus accrued interest and any other amounts owed under the note, which is why it exceeds the principal. Escrow does not compute the payoff figure and would not recalculate the lender's demand.

5. Why must documents be recorded in the correct order at closing?

  1. A. Because recording order establishes lien priority, so an out-of-sequence recording can place the new lender behind an interest it was to be ahead of.
  2. B. Because the county requires documents to be submitted alphabetically.
  3. C. Because the order determines the effective date of the borrower's ownership.
  4. D. Because the order affects the transfer tax due on the transaction.

Answer: A. Sequence determines priority, which is the entire point of controlling it at closing. It does not affect submission formalities, the ownership date, or transfer tax.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 12

Private money, seller financing, and nontraditional transactions

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Describe private investor lending, the broker's duties to investors, and the requirements that attach to multi-lender arrangements.
  • Apply the business-purpose determination and explain what a borrower's certification does and does not establish.
  • Describe seller carryback financing, its documentation, and the risks each party carries.
  • Assess hard-money suitability and explain what a licensee must be able to show about product fit.
  • Assemble broker-arranged loan documentation that satisfies both the borrower and the investor sides.
  • Recognize usury exposure, identify when an exemption question arises, and route it correctly.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: private investor lending and business purpose55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: seller financing and hard-money suitability50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: documentation and usury exposure45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Private investor loans

1.1 What private money is

A loan funded by a private investor or group of investors rather than by an institutional lender, typically arranged by a broker who brings the borrower and the money together.

The broker's position is different from institutional origination in one decisive way:

The broker has duties to the investor as well as to the borrower — and the investor is relying on the broker's presentation of the loan, the collateral, and the borrower in a way an institutional underwriter never does.

1.2 Legitimate uses

Private money is not a lesser product. It exists because institutional channels cannot serve some transactions:

SituationWhy private money fits
Bridge financingA short gap between transactions that conventional timelines cannot serve
SpeedA transaction that cannot wait for institutional underwriting
Property conditionCollateral no conforming channel will accept
Unusual collateral or structureMixed use, unpermitted improvements, unusual parcels
Business-purpose transactionsWhere the consumer framework does not apply
Credit or documentation profileA legitimate borrower a conforming channel cannot document

The characteristics that follow: shorter terms, higher rates, more fees, greater emphasis on collateral than on income, and frequently a balloon.

1.3 The broker's duties on the investor side

The investor is a client too, and the duties are real.

Present the loan accurately. The borrower, the collateral, the position, the term, and the risks — without characterizing a weak file as strong.

Disclose what the broker knows. Including anything about the borrower, the property, or the transaction that a reasonable investor would want.

Disclose the broker's compensation and interest, including whether the broker or an affiliate has any interest in the transaction, the property, or the borrower.

Handle the funds as trust funds — Section 5.

Not represent an outcome. No projection of repayment, no assurance the collateral will hold value, and no statement that a loan is "safe."

1.4 What an investor must be told about the collateral

The value and its basis — an appraisal, and its date. Not the broker's estimate presented as a valuation.

The lien position, and what sits ahead of it.

The loan-to-value or combined loan-to-value, computed on the documented value.

The condition of the property, including anything that would affect a sale.

Title exceptions and requirements, including anything unresolved.

Occupancy, and any tenancy that would survive a foreclosure.

1.5 Multi-lender arrangements

Where a broker assembles more than one investor into a single loan, additional California requirements attach — including requirements about how the transaction is structured, documented, and serviced, and about the number of lenders and their interests.

A broker assembling investors into a single loan is operating inside a regulated structure, not merely finding money for a borrower — and whether a particular arrangement satisfies the requirements is a compliance and legal determination.

1.6 Threshold activity

Where a broker's private money activity exceeds defined volume or structural thresholds, further California requirements attach, including reporting.

An originator's contribution is accurate transaction records, because the reports are compiled from them — and because the thresholds are computed from activity nobody tracks by memory.

1.7 Servicing

Where a broker services a private money loan — collecting payments and remitting to investors — the funds collected are trust funds, and the servicing obligations of Lesson 13 apply.

Servicing a loan the broker arranged, for investors the broker recruited, on collateral the broker presented, concentrates every duty in this lesson in one firm. That is not prohibited, and it is why the documentation and the trust accounting must be exact.

1.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state why private money exists, name the broker's duties to an investor, list what an investor must be told about collateral, and explain what a multi-lender arrangement triggers.

2. Business-purpose lending

2.1 Why the classification carries so much

Consumer residential mortgage requirements — including the MLO endorsement requirement and much of the federal disclosure regime — attach to consumer-purpose loans secured by a dwelling. Loans made primarily for a business purpose are treated differently.

That makes the classification consequential, and it makes it a target for misuse — because a business-purpose classification removes obligations that a consumer classification imposes.

2.2 The determination

A loan is business-purpose when it is made primarily for a business, commercial, agricultural, or investment purpose rather than for personal, family, or household purposes.

The analysis considers, among other things: what the proceeds are actually used for; the borrower's relationship to the property and to the activity; whether the borrower is engaged in the business the loan supports; the property's use and occupancy; and the transaction's overall character.

The determination rests on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts.

2.3 What a certification does and does not establish

A borrower's signature on a business-purpose certification records his statement. It does not establish the fact.

A file assembled around a certification that the surrounding facts contradict is a file with a problem in it — visible to any examiner who reads the occupancy line, the stated use of proceeds, or a lease dated before the application.

The certification is evidence, and it is one piece of evidence among several. A file whose only support for the classification is the certification has not documented a determination; it has documented that someone signed a form.

2.4 The errors run in both directions

Treating a consumer loan as business-purpose. The more common error and the more serious one, because it strips the borrower of protections he was entitled to — the ability-to-repay determination, the disclosure regime, and the rescission right among them.

Treating every investment property loan as exempt from everything. This sweeps in requirements that still apply.

A business-purpose classification does not suspend fair lending obligations, licensing requirements that attach independently, fraud prohibitions, usury analysis, or the firm's own standards.

2.5 Where the line is genuinely hard

Some transactions are close, and pretending otherwise produces bad files:

  • A borrower refinancing a rental he once occupied.
  • A cash-out on a primary residence to fund a business.
  • A loan on a property with both a residence and a commercial use.
  • A fourplex the borrower will occupy — which points hard toward consumer purpose.
  • A borrower with one rental property versus one with twelve.
  • A construction loan on a property the borrower intends to occupy when finished.

The response to a genuinely close case is not to pick the classification that is convenient. It is to route it to compliance and, where necessary, counsel — before the file is built around an answer.

A file constructed on the wrong classification is expensive to unwind, because the disclosures, the licensing analysis, and sometimes the product all rest on it.

2.6 The instruction an originator will receive

A manager says: process it as business-purpose since it is an income property, and have the borrower sign the certification.

Decline, do not transmit the file, and escalate above the manager. "It's an income property" is not the test, the certification does not decide it, and following an improper instruction while noting that it was directed does not transfer responsibility for the act — it documents that you knew.

2.7 What still applies

Even on a properly classified business-purpose loan:

Still applies
Fair lending obligations
Licensing requirements that attach on their own terms
Fraud prohibitions and misrepresentation liability
California broker law — trust funds, records, advertising, supervision
Usury analysis, unless an exemption applies
Duties to investors where private money is involved
Honest presentation of terms and risks

2.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state the determination and what it rests on, state what a certification establishes, name both directions of error, and state the response to a close case and to an improper instruction.

3. Seller carryback financing

3.1 What it is

The seller finances all or part of the purchase price, taking a note secured by a deed of trust on the property sold.

Two common structures: a carryback second behind institutional first financing, and a carryback first where the seller finances the whole price.

3.2 Why it happens

For the buyer: access where institutional financing is unavailable or too slow, and sometimes better terms.

For the seller: a sale that would not otherwise close, a return on the carried amount, and potentially a different tax treatment — which is a question for a tax professional, not for a licensee.

3.3 What must be documented

ElementWhy
The noteAmount, rate, payment, term, maturity, late charge, default terms
The security instrumentRecorded, with the correct legal description
PriorityWhich position, and what sits ahead
PrepaymentWhether permitted and on what terms
Acceleration and alienationWhat triggers each
SubordinationWhether the seller has agreed to subordinate to future financing, and on what conditions
ServicingWho collects, where payments go, and how they are recorded
Insurance and tax obligationsAnd how the seller learns if they lapse
Default remediesAnd the procedure

3.4 The seller's risks

Priority risk. A carryback second is extinguished as a claim against the property by a senior foreclosure, leaving the seller with an unsecured claim subject to California's deficiency restrictions.

The subordination clause. An open-ended agreement to subordinate to future financing commits the seller to move behind loans that do not yet exist, on terms nobody has seen.

A seller who signs an instrument with an open-ended subordination clause has agreed to something he may not have understood, and it is the single most consequential provision in carryback documentation.

Payment and default risk. The buyer may not pay, and the seller's remedy is a foreclosure he must conduct.

Insurance and tax lapse, which impairs the collateral without the seller knowing unless he arranged to be told.

Waste and condition, since the seller's security is a property he no longer controls.

3.5 The buyer's risks

A balloon he must refinance, and refinancing depends on conditions at maturity — his credit, the property's value, and whether credit is available.

Terms he cannot evaluate, where the documentation was assembled informally.

A due-on-sale problem where an underlying loan's alienation clause is triggered by the transfer.

Servicing failures, where payments are made and not recorded.

3.6 The disclosure obligations

Where a licensee arranges a carryback in defined circumstances, California requires a disclosure statement to the parties covering the terms, the security, the parties' creditworthiness information, and other required particulars.

Two points:

It exists to give both parties information they cannot otherwise obtain — a seller carrying paper is extending credit and generally has none of the information a lender would have.

A licensee arranging a carryback without addressing it has left both parties in a transaction neither can evaluate.

3.7 What a licensee does and does not do

Does: identify that a carryback is being contemplated; explain the mechanics and the risks to each party in plain terms; ensure the disclosure obligations are addressed; recommend that each party obtain counsel and, for the tax questions, a tax professional; ensure the note and security instrument are prepared properly and recorded; and document what was explained and recommended.

Does not: draft the note and deed of trust from a form and call it done; advise on the tax treatment; predict whether the buyer will pay; characterize the arrangement as safe; or tell a seller that a subordination clause is standard.

Seller-carry documentation belongs with counsel. The provisions that matter — subordination, acceleration, alienation, prepayment, and remedies — are exactly the ones a form will not resolve for a particular transaction.

3.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to name what must be documented, state the seller's and the buyer's risks, identify the most consequential provision, and state what a licensee does and does not do.

4. Hard-money risk and suitability

4.1 What hard money is

Collateral-focused lending, typically short-term and higher-rate, where the underwriting emphasis is on the property rather than on the borrower's documented income.

It overlaps heavily with private money and is often the same transaction described from the pricing side rather than the funding side.

4.2 The characteristics

CharacteristicConsequence for the borrower
Higher rateMaterially higher carrying cost
Points and feesSubstantial, and frequently paid at closing from proceeds
Short termOften one to three years
Balloon at maturityRefinance, sell, or pay — all depending on conditions then
Lower loan-to-valueRequires more equity
Interest-only or partial amortizationLittle or no principal reduction
Prepayment provisionsMay penalize the exit the borrower is planning
Fast fundingThe reason many borrowers are there

4.3 The suitability question

A licensee is not an investment adviser and does not make a suitability determination in the sense a regulated adviser would. But the licensee must be able to show why this borrower is in this product, and the file must support it.

The question the file must answer: why is this borrower in a hard-money loan rather than a conventional one, and what is his exit?

Legitimate answers: speed a conventional channel cannot provide; collateral no conforming channel will accept; a business-purpose transaction outside the consumer framework; a documented credit or documentation profile; a defined bridge with a specific end.

Answers that are not answers: it was the product available; the borrower was in a hurry; conventional would have taken too long and nobody asked why the deadline existed; or the borrower said he would refinance.

4.4 The exit

Every short-term collateral loan is an exit plan wearing a loan's clothes, and the exit is where these transactions fail.

What must be examined and recorded:

  • What is the exit — sale, refinance, or a defined event?
  • What does it depend on — a permit, a market, a credit improvement, a buyer?
  • What happens if it does not occur on schedule?
  • Is there an extension provision, and at what cost?
  • Does a prepayment provision penalize the intended exit?

"I'll just refinance" assumes a market. All three balloon paths — refinance, sell, or pay — depend on conditions at maturity, and naming that assumption is the disclosure that matters.

4.5 The consumer-purpose problem

Where a hard-money loan is consumer-purpose and secured by a dwelling, the consumer framework applies in full — the ability-to-repay determination, the disclosure regime, and the rest.

Hard money is not a category that escapes the consumer framework. Business purpose is. Conflating the two is the mechanism by which consumer borrowers end up in loans for which no ability-to-repay determination was ever made.

And the ability-to-repay determination is precisely what a collateral-focused underwrite does not perform — which is why the classification cannot be a convenience.

4.6 Presenting hard money honestly

State the total cost, not only the rate: points, fees, and interest over the expected term.

State the maturity and the amount due.

State what happens if the exit does not occur, in plain terms.

Compare it to the alternative the borrower could obtain, if any, on a common basis — and if there is no alternative, say so and say why.

Do not present speed as free. It is purchased, and the price is the whole difference.

4.7 The patterns that should stop a file

  • A consumer-purpose borrower being routed to a business-purpose classification.
  • A borrower whose stated exit is a refinance he could not obtain today.
  • An owner-occupant on a short-term balloon with no documented exit.
  • A borrower who does not understand that the balance is due at maturity.
  • A loan sized to the collateral where the borrower cannot service the payment.
  • Equity-stripping indicators — a distressed owner, substantial equity, a loan he cannot repay, and a lender positioned to take the property.

The last is the pattern that produces the most serious enforcement in this area, and a licensee who sees it escalates rather than participating.

4.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what the file must show about product fit, examine an exit, explain why hard money does not escape the consumer framework, and name the patterns that should stop a file.

5. Broker-arranged loan documentation

5.1 Two sides to document

A broker-arranged private money loan has a borrower side and an investor side, and both must be documented.

Institutional origination has one client. This has two, with opposed interests on price and risk — which is why the documentation obligations are heavier rather than lighter.

5.2 The borrower-side file

Everything an institutional file requires, plus the disclosures the arrangement triggers:

  • The application and its versions, with what was stated and what was documented, distinguished.
  • The purpose determination and the facts supporting it — not merely the certification.
  • The appraisal or valuation, with delivery evidenced.
  • Title, with exceptions and requirements resolved.
  • Insurance evidence with the correct mortgagee clause.
  • Every disclosure owed, with delivery evidence — including the California mortgage loan disclosure statement, and the consumer disclosures where the loan is consumer-purpose.
  • The product-fit record — why this product, what the exit is, and what was explained.
  • Compensation disclosed and received, reconciled.
  • The note and security instrument as executed and recorded.

5.3 The investor-side file

ItemWhy
The loan presentation as givenWhat the investor actually relied on
The appraisal or valuation, with its date and basisNot the broker's estimate
The title report, exceptions, and requirementsIncluding anything unresolved
The lien position and what sits aheadComputed, not asserted
Loan-to-value on the documented valueThe exposure
Borrower information as presentedAnd what was verified
The broker's compensation and any interestIncluding affiliates
Servicing arrangementsWho collects, and how funds flow
The investor's instructionsSigned
Trust fund recordsReceipt, holding, and disbursement of the investor's funds

5.4 Investor funds are trust funds

From receipt until properly disbursed.

Separated from the broker's own funds. Recorded by beneficiary. Disbursed per the arrangement's terms and the investor's instructions. And returned where the transaction does not close rather than applied elsewhere.

Using one investor's funds to complete another transaction is conversion — however temporary, however well intentioned, and regardless of whether the money is replaced. Intent to replace is a description of the plan, not a defense.

Reconciliation compares three balances: the bank balance, the book balance, and the total of the individual beneficiary ledgers. Bank-to-book alone cannot detect money held for the wrong beneficiary, because the total is right the whole time.

5.5 Conflicts

Private money concentrates conflicts, and each requires disclosure before reliance:

  • The broker or an affiliate having an interest in the property, the borrower, or the loan.
  • The broker acting as principal — lending its own funds, or buying the note.
  • The broker servicing the loan it arranged, for investors it recruited.
  • Compensation from both sides.
  • A relationship with the borrower or the investor a party would want to know about.

A conflict is managed by disclosure that arrives before the party relies on the advice it affects — and a broker acting as a principal while an investor believes it is being advised has a serious problem.

5.6 What must never appear in an investor presentation

  • A projected return stated as a fact.
  • An assurance of repayment or of the collateral's value holding.
  • A characterization of the loan as "safe" or "secured" in a way implying no risk.
