  • A valuation the broker produced, presented as an appraisal.
  • A loan-to-value computed on an unsupported value.
  • An omission of what sits ahead of the position.

5.7 The reconstructability test

Could a person who was not there determine what the investor was told, on what basis, what the borrower was told, what was disclosed to each, and where every dollar went?

In private money that test is the whole compliance posture, because there is no institutional underwriter whose file substitutes for the broker's.

5.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to list what each side's file must contain, state the trust fund obligations for investor funds, name the conflicts requiring disclosure, and state what must never appear in an investor presentation.

6. Usury exemptions and legal referral

6.1 What usury is

Usury is charging interest above the maximum rate the law permits. California's usury framework establishes limits, with a substantial set of exemptions.

The consequences of a usurious loan are significant and are legal questions, which is why this section is about recognition rather than analysis.

6.2 Why it matters in private money specifically

Institutional lending sits comfortably inside exemptions. Private money frequently involves rates and fee structures near or above the limits, arranged by parties who may or may not fall within an exemption.

Usury is the risk that private money participants most often do not know they are running.

6.3 The exemption structure, in outline

California's framework provides exemptions of several kinds, including for certain classes of lenders, for loans arranged by a licensed real estate broker, and for other defined categories.

The broker-arranged exemption is the one that matters most in this course, and it carries requirements about what "arranged by" means and what the broker must actually do.

Whether an exemption applies to a particular transaction is a legal determination. It depends on the lender's status, the broker's actual role, the loan's characteristics, and the facts of the arrangement — and it is not established by writing "arranged by a licensed real estate broker" on a document.

6.4 What "arranged by" requires

The exemption depends on the broker having actually performed the arranging role, not on a nominal designation.

A broker whose name appears on a transaction it did not arrange has not created an exemption, and the arrangement raises a further question about why the designation was made.

This is the pattern to recognize: a lender who cannot lend at the rate proposed, and a broker's name added to the file. Escalate it.

6.5 What counts toward the rate

The analysis is not limited to the stated interest rate. Charges and structures can be treated as interest for the purpose, and the determination is legal.

Two consequences:

A loan whose stated rate sits below a limit can still be examined, where fees and structures are considered.

A licensee structuring fees to keep a stated rate low, while the economics sit elsewhere, has made a decision belonging to counsel — and the pattern is one that examiners and courts both recognize.

6.6 The referral discipline

Every usury question is a referral.

What a licensee may do: identify that a usury question is present; state that exemptions exist and that whether one applies depends on facts and status; ensure the question is routed before the loan is made; and document the referral.

What a licensee may not do: conclude that an exemption applies; state that the broker's involvement makes a loan exempt; compute whether a structure sits inside a limit; or reassure an investor or a borrower that a rate is permissible.

The cost of routing a usury question is a conversation. The cost of getting it wrong is the loan.

6.7 The other referrals in this lesson

Private money and nontraditional transactions concentrate questions outside the license:

QuestionReferral
Usury and exemptionCounsel
Whether a multi-lender structure satisfies the requirementsCompliance and counsel
Whether a transaction is consumer or business purpose, where closeCompliance and counsel, before the file is built
Seller carryback documentationCounsel for each party
Tax treatment of a carryback, an exchange, or interestA tax professional
Whether a subordination should be givenThe subordinating party's counsel
Whether a foreclosure or remedy is availableCounsel
Whether an investor arrangement implicates securities requirementsCounsel

That last row deserves naming. Arrangements pooling investor money can raise questions under securities law depending on their structure. A licensee who recognizes the question routes it; a licensee who assembles the structure without asking has answered it.

6.8 Where this lesson concentrates the risk

Private money, hard money, seller carrybacks, and business-purpose classification share four features that make them the highest-exposure area in this course:

  1. The consumer protections that constrain institutional lending are frequently absent or claimed to be.
  2. The broker owes duties to two sides with opposed interests.
  3. The documentation is assembled rather than standardized.
  4. The money frequently passes through the broker.

The controls are correspondingly simple and non-negotiable: classify purpose on the facts and route close cases before building the file; document product fit and the exit; present the loan to investors accurately and without projections; handle investor funds as trust funds with three-way reconciliation; disclose every conflict before reliance; route usury, securities, and structure questions to counsel; and keep a file that lets someone who was not there reconstruct what each side was told.

6.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what usury is and why private money runs the risk, explain what "arranged by" requires, state what a licensee may and may not say about exemptions, and name the referrals this lesson concentrates.

Key terms

TermDefinition
Private moneyA loan funded by private investors rather than an institution, arranged by a broker who owes duties to the investor as well as the borrower.
Legitimate usesBridge financing, speed, collateral no conforming channel accepts, unusual structures, business-purpose transactions, and documentable-profile borrowers.
Investor-side dutiesAccurate presentation, disclosure of what the broker knows, disclosure of compensation and interest, trust fund handling, and no representation of outcome.
Multi-lender arrangementMore than one investor in a single loan, triggering additional California requirements about structure, documentation, and servicing. A regulated structure, not merely finding money.
Business purposePrimarily business, commercial, agricultural, or investment — resting on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts.
Business-purpose certificationRecords the borrower's statement. Does not establish the fact, and a file supported only by it has documented a signature rather than a determination.
The two directions of errorTreating a consumer loan as business-purpose, which strips protections; and treating an investment loan as exempt from everything, which sweeps in obligations that still apply.
What still appliesFair lending, licensing, fraud prohibitions, California broker law, usury analysis, investor duties, and honest presentation.
Seller carrybackThe seller financing all or part of the price, taking a note secured by a deed of trust.
Subordination clause in a carrybackAn agreement to move behind future financing. The single most consequential provision, and never described as standard.
Carryback disclosure statementThe California requirement giving both parties information a seller extending credit otherwise has no way to obtain.
Hard moneyCollateral-focused, short-term, higher-rate lending — frequently the same transaction as private money described from the pricing side.
The product-fit questionWhy is this borrower in this product rather than a conventional one, and what is his exit? The file must answer it.
The exitSale, refinance, or a defined event — and all balloon paths depend on conditions at maturity. "I'll just refinance" assumes a market.
Hard money is not an exemptionBusiness purpose is the classification that removes the consumer framework; hard money is not. Conflating them is how consumer borrowers end up in loans with no ability-to-repay determination.
Equity strippingA distressed owner, substantial equity, a loan he cannot repay, and a lender positioned to take the property. Escalate; do not participate.
Two-sided documentationA borrower-side file and an investor-side file, because the arrangement has two clients with opposed interests.
Investor fundsTrust funds from receipt until properly disbursed — separated, recorded by beneficiary, disbursed per instructions, and returned if the transaction does not close.
ConversionUsing one investor's funds for another transaction. Intent to replace is a description of the plan, not a defense.
Three-way reconciliationBank, book, and beneficiary ledgers — because bank-to-book alone cannot detect money held for the wrong beneficiary.
Prohibited in an investor presentationA projected return as fact, an assurance of repayment or value, "safe," a broker valuation presented as an appraisal, an unsupported loan-to-value, or omitting what sits ahead.
UsuryCharging interest above the permitted maximum, with a substantial exemption structure — and consequences that are legal questions.
The broker-arranged exemptionDepends on the broker actually performing the arranging role. Not established by a designation on a document.
What counts toward the rateNot only the stated rate — charges and structures can be treated as interest, and the determination is legal.
Securities questionArrangements pooling investor money can raise securities issues depending on structure. Recognize and route; assembling without asking answers it.
Reconstructability in private moneyCould a person who was not there determine what each side was told, on what basis, and where every dollar went. There is no institutional file that substitutes for the broker's.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A broker assembles six investors to fund a single $1.4 million loan on a mixed-use property. He tells them the loan is "well secured at 55% loan-to-value," using his own estimate of value; does not mention a $310,000 first he is arranging simultaneously; deposits the investor funds into an account that also holds the firm's operating balance; and projects "a solid 11% return."

Identify every failure.

Solution. Six failures, and each maps to a distinct duty.

The value is the broker's estimate presented as a valuation. An investor must be told the value and its basis — an appraisal, with its date — not the broker's number.

The loan-to-value is therefore unsupported, and it must be computed on the documented value.

Omitting the senior lien is the most serious presentation failure. An investor must be told the lien position and what sits ahead of it. At 55% of an unsupported value with an undisclosed $310,000 first, the investors do not know what they own.

"A solid 11% return" is a projected return stated as fact, and the duty is explicit: no representation of outcome — no projection of repayment, no assurance the collateral holds value, and no statement that a loan is safe.

The deposit is commingling, complete on deposit. Investor funds are trust funds from receipt until properly disbursed — separated, recorded by beneficiary, and returned if the transaction does not close.

And six investors in one loan is a multi-lender arrangement, triggering additional California requirements about structure, documentation, and servicing. A broker assembling investors into a single loan is operating inside a regulated structure, and whether this one satisfies it is a compliance and legal determination.

Problem 2

A manager tells an originator to process a loan as business-purpose on a duplex the borrower will occupy, "since it produces income," and to have him sign the certification. The file also contains a lease on the subject property dated three weeks before the application.

Assess the instruction and the lease.

Solution. The instruction inverts the analysis, the certification does not fix it, and the lease is different in kind.

"It produces income" is not the test. A loan is business-purpose when made primarily for a business, commercial, agricultural, or investment purpose, and the analysis considers what the proceeds actually fund, the borrower's relationship to the property and the activity, the property's use and occupancy, and the transaction's overall character. A borrower occupying a unit points hard toward consumer purpose.

A signature records the borrower's statement; it does not establish the fact. A file supported only by the certification has documented a signature rather than a determination.

The consequence of getting it wrong here is the serious direction of the error: treating a consumer loan as business-purpose strips the borrower of protections he was entitled to — the ability-to-repay determination, the disclosure regime, and the rescission right among them.

The lease is the file contradicting itself. It is not a gap to fill — the file contains evidence contradicting a material representation.

Decline, do not transmit the file, and escalate above the manager. Following the instruction while noting it was directed does not transfer responsibility for the act — it documents that you knew.

Problem 3

A seller carries a $400,000 second behind institutional first financing. The documentation was assembled from a form. It contains an open-ended clause agreeing to subordinate to future financing, no requirement that the seller be notified if insurance or taxes lapse, and no servicing arrangement. Two years later the first forecloses.

Identify the seller's exposures and the provision that mattered most.

Solution. The subordination clause is the single most consequential provision in carryback documentation, and an open-ended one commits the seller to move behind loans that do not yet exist, on terms nobody has seen. A seller who signs it has agreed to something he may not have understood — and no licensee should ever describe it as standard.

Priority risk is what materialized. A carryback second is extinguished as a claim against the property by a senior foreclosure, leaving the seller an unsecured claim subject to California's substantial deficiency restrictions.

The other gaps compounded it. With no notification arrangement, insurance or tax lapse impairs the collateral without the seller knowing. With no servicing arrangement, payments may be made and not properly recorded. And the seller's security was a property he no longer controlled, exposing him to waste and condition risk.

What the licensee should have done: explain the mechanics and risks to each party in plain terms; ensure the California carryback disclosure statement obligations were addressed — they exist precisely because a seller extending credit has none of the information a lender would have; recommend counsel for each party and a tax professional for the tax questions; and document what was explained. Seller-carry documentation belongs with counsel — the provisions that matter are exactly the ones a form will not resolve.

Problem 4

An owner-occupant with damaged credit needs $180,000 against his home to pay medical debts. A hard-money lender will fund in eight days at 11.5% interest-only with 4 points and a two-year balloon. The originator plans to classify it business-purpose because the borrower also owns a small landscaping company, and notes the borrower "says he'll refinance when his credit recovers."

Assess.

Solution. This is a consumer-purpose loan on the facts, and the proposed classification is the mechanism by which the protections would disappear.

The proceeds fund personal medical debts, secured by his dwelling. Owning a business does not make a loan business-purpose — the analysis rests on what the proceeds actually fund and the transaction's character.

Hard money is not a category that escapes the consumer framework. Business purpose is. Conflating them is exactly how consumer borrowers end up in loans for which no ability-to-repay determination was ever made — and a collateral-focused underwrite is precisely the one that does not perform it.

The exit is not an exit. "He'll refinance when his credit recovers" is a refinance he could not obtain today, depending on conditions at maturity: his credit, the property's value, and whether credit is available. "I'll just refinance" assumes a market, and naming that assumption is the disclosure that matters.

The pattern to recognize: an owner-occupant on a short-term balloon with no documented exit, and — given substantial equity and a loan he may not be able to repay — the equity-stripping indicators that produce the most serious enforcement in this area.

Route the classification to compliance and counsel before the file is built around an answer.

Problem 5

A broker arranges a bridge loan for a builder: 12 months, 10.5%, 3 points, interest-only, funding in eleven days. The borrower is refinancing into construction financing already conditionally approved. The originator's file contains the application, the appraisal, and title.

Is this an appropriate use, and what is missing?

Solution. The use is legitimate and the file is incomplete.

Private money exists because institutional channels cannot serve some transactions, and speed — a transaction that cannot wait for institutional underwriting — is among the clearest legitimate uses. A builder bridging to conditionally approved construction financing is a defined bridge with a specific end, which is exactly what a documented exit looks like.

What is missing is the product-fit record. The file must answer: why is this borrower in this product rather than a conventional one, and what is his exit? Here the answers are good — speed, and a specific approved takeout — but they must be in the file, not in the originator's memory.

The exit examination is also missing: what the takeout depends on, what happens if it does not close on schedule, whether an extension provision exists and at what cost, and whether a prepayment provision penalizes the intended exit — which on a twelve-month loan a builder plans to exit early is a real question.

And the presentation must state total cost, not only the rate — 3 points plus twelve months at 10.5% — because speed is purchased, and the price is the whole difference.

Problem 6

A broker arranged a $600,000 private money loan and holds $600,000 of investor funds. The transaction is delayed. A different transaction closes Friday and is $95,000 short. The broker uses $95,000 of the first investors' funds, intending to replace it from the next funding. All investor funds sit in one account tracked by spreadsheet, reconciled monthly bank-to-book.

Assess.

Solution. Two violations, and the first is conversion.

Using one investor's funds to complete another transaction is conversion — using trust funds for a purpose other than the one for which they are held. However temporary, however well intentioned, and regardless of whether the money is replaced. Intent to replace is a description of the plan, not a defense. And where the first transaction does not close, the funds must be returned, not applied elsewhere.

The account arrangement is commingling if the firm's own funds are there, and in any case the records fail. Investor funds are trust funds from receipt until properly disbursed — separated, recorded by beneficiary, and disbursed per the arrangement's terms and the investors' instructions.

The reconciliation misses the balance that matters. It must compare the bank balance, the book balance, and the total of the individual beneficiary ledgers. Bank-to-book alone cannot detect money held for the wrong beneficiary, because the total is right the whole time — which is precisely the condition this account is now in.

Problem 7

An investor asks a broker whether a proposed loan is "safe," what return she can expect, and whether the broker has any interest in the transaction. The broker owns 20% of the borrowing entity, will service the loan, and is being paid by both the borrower and the investor.

Answer the investor's questions and address the conflicts.

Solution. Two of her three questions must be declined, and the third exposes three conflicts.

"Safe" may not be answered. The duties are explicit: no representation of outcome — no projection of repayment, no assurance the collateral will hold value, and no characterization of a loan as safe or as "secured" in a way implying no risk.

A projected return may not be stated as a fact. What she is entitled to is the loan's terms and the facts: the value and its basis, the lien position and what sits ahead, the loan-to-value on the documented value, the property's condition, title exceptions and requirements including anything unresolved, and occupancy including any tenancy that would survive a foreclosure.

Three conflicts require disclosure before she relies on anything: the broker's 20% interest in the borrowing entity; the broker servicing the loan it arranged for investors it recruited; and compensation from both sides.

A conflict is managed by disclosure that arrives before the party relies on the advice it affects — and a broker acting as a principal while an investor believes it is being advised has a serious problem. The 20% interest makes the broker something close to a principal on the borrower side while presenting the loan to the investor.

None of this is prohibited as such, which is the point: it is why the documentation and the trust accounting must be exact, and why the test is whether someone who was not there could reconstruct what she was told and on what basis.

Problem 8

A lender who cannot lend at 13% asks a broker to add its name to the file "so the loan is exempt." The broker also proposes moving part of the yield into a separately labeled fee to keep the stated rate at 9.9%, and is assembling twelve investors into a pooled fund to make several such loans.

Identify each issue and state what the broker must do.

Solution. Three legal questions, none of which the broker may answer, and one clear pattern.

The exemption is not created by a designation. California's usury framework has a substantial exemption structure, including for loans arranged by a licensed real estate broker — but that exemption depends on the broker actually performing the arranging role, not on a nominal designation. A broker whose name appears on a transaction it did not arrange has not created an exemption, and the request raises a further question about why the designation was wanted.

This is the pattern to recognize: a lender who cannot lend at the rate proposed, and a broker's name added to the file. Escalate it.

The fee restructuring is a decision belonging to counsel. The usury analysis is not limited to the stated rate — charges and structures can be treated as interest — so a loan whose stated rate sits below a limit can still be examined. A licensee moving yield into a fee label to keep a rate low has made a legal determination, and it is a pattern examiners and courts both recognize.

The pooled fund raises a securities question. Arrangements pooling investor money can raise issues under securities law depending on structure — and a licensee who recognizes the question routes it; one who assembles the structure without asking has answered it.

What the broker must do: route all three to counsel before the loans are made, document the referral, and decline the designation. The cost of routing a usury question is a conversation. The cost of getting it wrong is the loan.

Chapter summary

Private money exists for real reasons, and a broker arranging it owes duties to the investor as well as the borrower — accurate presentation, disclosure of what is known and of compensation and interest, trust fund handling, and no representation of outcome.

An investor must be told the value and its basis, the position and what sits ahead, the loan-to-value on documented value, condition, title, and occupancy.

Assembling investors into a single loan is a regulated multi-lender structure, and volume triggers further requirements.

Business purpose rests on the actual purpose and the surrounding facts. A certification records a statement and does not establish a fact, and the errors run both directions — with the serious one stripping protections the borrower was entitled to. Route close cases before the file is built.

A business-purpose classification suspends nothing else — fair lending, licensing, fraud, California broker law, usury, investor duties, and honest presentation all continue.

Seller carrybacks must be documented properly, and the open-ended subordination clause is the provision that matters most. Address the California disclosure obligations and send each party to counsel.

Hard money must answer the product-fit question and examine the exit, because every short-term collateral loan is an exit plan wearing a loan's clothes. Hard money does not escape the consumer framework — business purpose does, and conflating them is how consumer borrowers end up without an ability-to-repay determination.

Recognize the equity-stripping pattern and escalate rather than participate.

Document both sides. Investor funds are trust funds from receipt, conversion is conversion even when replaced, and reconciliation compares three balances.

Disclose every conflict before reliance, and never state a projected return as fact, assure repayment, call a loan safe, present a broker valuation as an appraisal, or omit what sits ahead.

Usury is the risk private money participants most often do not know they are running. The broker-arranged exemption depends on actually arranging, the analysis is not limited to the stated rate, and every usury question is a referral — as are securities, structure, carryback documentation, and tax questions.

In private money the file is the whole compliance posture, because there is no institutional underwriter whose record substitutes for the broker's.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Classify the loan's purpose and state the facts your determination rests on rather than the certification, identify every duty owed to any investor and state what must be presented and what may not, compute the position and loan-to-value on documented value and identify what sits ahead, answer the product-fit question and examine the stated exit including what it depends on and what happens if it fails, identify every conflict requiring disclosure and when it must be disclosed, state the trust fund handling required for any funds received and what reconciliation would detect a misapplication, identify every question you would route to compliance, to counsel, or to a tax professional and by what deadline, and state what the file must show for a person who was not there to reconstruct what each side was told. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A borrower who owns a landscaping business asks a broker to arrange a $200,000 private-money loan secured by a second lien on his home, to buy equipment for the business. The private investor wants a rate above the general usury limit and a one-year term with a balloon. The broker says usury is not a concern because 'private loans are exempt.' How should the situation be analyzed?

  1. A. The exemption commonly relied on is for loans made or arranged by a licensed real estate broker, which depends on the broker's actual role and licensure rather than on the loan being private — the classification also turns on the loan's purpose, and both should be confirmed with counsel before the terms are set.
  2. B. The broker is correct: loans funded by private investors rather than institutions are outside the usury limits.
  3. C. Usury limits never apply to loans secured by real property in California.
  4. D. The rate is permissible because the borrower is a business owner, which exempts all of his borrowing.

Answer: A. The exemption depends on the broker actually making or arranging the loan under a valid license, not on the funding source being private. Blanket statements that private loans, real-property loans, or business owners' loans are exempt each misstate the rule, and getting it wrong on a note that is already written is expensive.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What characterizes private money lending?

  1. A. Loans funded by individual or non-institutional investors, often underwritten primarily on the collateral, typically at higher cost and shorter term than institutional financing.
  2. B. Loans made by institutions to borrowers who do not qualify for conventional financing.
  3. C. Loans that are exempt from all disclosure and licensing requirements.
  4. D. Loans made without any security instrument recorded against the property.

Answer: A. Private capital, collateral-focused underwriting, and higher cost and shorter term are the hallmarks. Private funding does not remove disclosure or licensing obligations, and these loans are secured.

2. What is seller carryback financing?

  1. A. The seller extends credit to the buyer for part of the purchase price, taking a note secured by the property rather than receiving all cash at closing.
  2. B. The buyer assumes the seller's existing loan on the property.
  3. C. The seller pays a portion of the buyer's closing costs at settlement.
  4. D. The seller leases the property back from the buyer after closing.

Answer: A. A carryback is seller-extended credit secured by the property. Assumption, seller credits, and sale-leasebacks are all different arrangements.

3. What generally distinguishes a business-purpose loan from a consumer-purpose loan?

  1. A. The purpose for which the proceeds are used, which determines which consumer protection frameworks apply — not the type of collateral or whether the borrower is an individual.
  2. B. Whether the borrower is a business entity rather than a natural person.
  3. C. Whether the collateral is commercial rather than residential property.
  4. D. Whether the loan amount exceeds a stated threshold.

Answer: A. Purpose controls the classification. Entity status, collateral type, and loan size are common but unreliable proxies, and relying on them is how loans get misclassified.

4. What is the principal risk to a borrower in a short-term hard-money loan with a balloon?

  1. A. That the balloon comes due before the borrower can refinance or sell, exposing him to default and foreclosure on terms that leave little time to react.
  2. B. That the interest rate will adjust upward during the short term.
  3. C. That the lender may demand additional collateral during the term.
  4. D. That the loan cannot be prepaid before maturity.

Answer: A. Balloon risk is refinance-or-sell risk concentrated at a single date. Short-term hard-money loans are typically fixed for the term, and additional collateral demands and prepayment bars are not the characteristic hazard.

5. What documentation matters most in a broker-arranged private loan?

  1. A. Clear disclosure to both the borrower and the investor of the terms, the risks, the broker's role, and the broker's compensation.
  2. B. A verbal understanding between the parties, since private loans are negotiated individually.
  3. C. Documentation of the investor's net worth only.
  4. D. The borrower's credit report, which substitutes for other disclosures.

Answer: A. Both sides are relying on the broker, so both need the terms, risks, role, and compensation in writing. Verbal understandings, one-sided documentation, and a credit report do not discharge that.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A seller carrying back a note asks how he can reduce his risk. What is the sound guidance?

  1. A. Address the buyer's creditworthiness, the lien position of the carryback, the note's terms and remedies, and the documentation — and involve counsel, since the seller is now a lender.
  2. B. Rely on the property's value, since the seller can foreclose if the buyer defaults.
  3. C. Require the buyer to pay a larger down payment and treat that as sufficient protection.
  4. D. Structure the carryback as an unsecured personal loan for flexibility.

Answer: A. Becoming a lender means taking on credit, lien-position, and documentation risk together. Collateral value alone ignores position and cost of recovery, a down payment addresses only one dimension, and dropping the security makes matters worse.

2. A private investor asks the broker to guarantee the loan will perform. What should the broker say?

  1. A. That no one can guarantee borrower performance, and that the investor's protection comes from disclosed underwriting, lien position, and documentation rather than from a promise.
  2. B. That the loan will perform because it is secured by real property.
  3. C. That the broker will personally cover any shortfall to close the investment.
  4. D. That the investor should rely on the broker's track record with similar loans.

Answer: A. A performance guarantee is one no originator can honestly give, and offering a personal backstop or a track record in its place substitutes reassurance for the actual protections.

3. How should a broker treat a loan the borrower says is for 'business expansion' but which will actually pay off personal credit cards?

  1. A. As a consumer-purpose loan, because the actual use of proceeds controls the classification and the broker may not rely on a label that the file contradicts.
  2. B. As a business-purpose loan, since the borrower stated the purpose in writing.
  3. C. As a business-purpose loan, since the borrower operates a business.
  4. D. As whichever classification the funding investor prefers.

Answer: A. Actual use governs, which is why a written label the file contradicts does not protect anyone. Business ownership and investor preference are irrelevant to the classification.

4. What makes a balloon payment structure appropriate or inappropriate for a particular borrower?

  1. A. Whether the borrower has a realistic, evidenced path to repay or refinance by the maturity date, evaluated at origination rather than assumed.
  2. B. Whether the borrower is comfortable with the monthly payment amount.
  3. C. Whether the interest rate is lower than a fully amortizing alternative.
  4. D. Whether the balloon is disclosed in the loan documents.

Answer: A. Suitability turns on the exit, evidenced at origination. Payment comfort, a lower rate, and disclosure are all relevant but none of them answers whether the borrower can meet the balloon.

5. Why do nontraditional transactions warrant heightened documentation of the broker's advice?

  1. A. Because the terms are less standardized and the risks less familiar to the parties, so the record of what was explained is what shows the parties decided with the risks in front of them.
  2. B. Because nontraditional loans are prohibited unless documented in detail.
  3. C. Because investors require the documentation before funding.
  4. D. Because documentation converts the broker's role into that of a lender.

Answer: A. Unfamiliar, non-standard terms are where misunderstanding concentrates, which is why the advisory record matters most there. These loans are not prohibited, and documentation does not change the broker's role.

Mortgage Loan Brokering and Lending - Lesson Assignment 13

Servicing, payoff, default, and foreclosure

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Describe payment processing, servicing records, and what a servicing transfer obligates.
  • Explain escrow account administration, analysis, shortages, and why a fixed payment changes.
  • Explain the payoff demand, what it contains, and what clears the record when a loan is satisfied.
  • Describe delinquency, loss mitigation options, and what a licensee may and may not tell a distressed borrower.
  • Describe the nonjudicial foreclosure sequence and distinguish reinstatement from redemption.
  • Handle borrower communications and complaints through the defined procedures rather than informally.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: servicing records and escrow accounts55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: payoff, delinquency, and loss mitigation50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: foreclosure and borrower communication45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Payment processing and servicing records

1.1 What servicing is

Servicing is the administration of a loan after it funds — collecting payments, applying them, maintaining escrow accounts, remitting to the owner of the loan, handling payoffs, communicating with the borrower, and managing delinquency.

The servicer is not necessarily the owner of the loan, and neither is necessarily the party that originated it. All three can be different, and any of them can change.

A borrower confused about who owns his loan and who services it is asking a reasonable question with a genuinely complicated answer.

1.2 Why a mortgage licensee needs this

Three reasons:

Borrowers ask. A former borrower calls the person he knows — the originator — about a payment problem, an escrow increase, or a notice he received.

Brokers sometimes service. A broker who arranged a private money loan and collects payments for investors is servicing, and the obligations are real — including trust fund obligations.

Origination decisions become servicing consequences. An escrow estimate built on the seller's tax figure becomes a shortage; a product feature nobody explained becomes a complaint.

1.3 Payment application

Payments are applied in the order the note and the servicer's practice provide — typically to interest, principal, escrow, and then other amounts.

Two points that produce disputes:

Partial payments. A servicer's handling of a payment less than the full amount due is governed by the note and applicable requirements, and a borrower who assumes a partial payment cures a delinquency is frequently wrong.

Extra principal. A borrower sending more than the amount due may find it applied to the next installment rather than to principal, unless he directs otherwise. A borrower intending to reduce principal must say so, and telling him that in advance is worth more than explaining it afterward.

1.4 Servicing records

A servicer maintains a record of every receipt and every application, and the record is what answers a dispute about whether a payment was made, when, and how it was applied.

Where a broker services, the record obligations of Lesson 08 apply in full: complete records of receipts and disbursements, identifying whose funds they are, and retention for the required period.

Payments collected for an owner or investor are trust funds — separated, recorded by beneficiary, and disbursed per the arrangement's terms.

1.5 Servicing transfers

RESPA addresses transfers of servicing, including notice to the borrower and a period during which payments sent to the prior servicer are treated as timely.

The framework anticipates the confusion, which is why the protection exists. A borrower who sends a payment to the old servicer during that window has not defaulted.

What a borrower needs to know at a transfer: who is servicing now, where to send payments, whether anything else changes — the note's terms do not change on a servicing transfer — and what happens to his escrow account.

1.6 What a licensee tells a former borrower who calls

May: explain the difference between the owner and the servicer; explain that servicing transfers are ordinary and that the loan's terms do not change; explain what an escrow account is and why a payment can change; and direct him to his servicer, with the specific procedure to use.

May not: contact the servicer as though authorized without authority; interpret a notice he received; tell him whether he is in default; predict what the servicer will do; or advise him to stop paying.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish owner, servicer, and originator; explain partial payment and extra principal handling; and state what a servicing transfer does and does not change.

2. Escrow accounts

2.1 What an escrow account is

An escrow account — also called an impound account — is maintained by the servicer to pay property taxes and insurance, funded by an amount collected with each payment.

Its purpose is protective on both sides: the lender's collateral stays insured and free of tax liens, and the borrower spreads two large annual obligations across twelve payments.

2.2 Why the payment on a fixed-rate loan changes

The single most common servicing question, and one an originator can prevent.

A fixed-rate loan has a fixed principal and interest payment. The total payment is not fixed, because the escrow portion moves with the taxes and insurance it funds.

When taxes or insurance rise, the escrow portion rises — and where the account has fallen short, the borrower repays the shortage on top of the higher ongoing amount.

2.3 The California reassessment problem

This is where California originators create escrow shortages at scale.

A buyer's property taxes are based on a new base year value established on the change in ownership — not on the seller's bill. An estimate built from the seller's figure on a long-held property can be low by a multiple.

The result is predictable: the escrow account is underfunded from the first month, the analysis finds a shortage, and the borrower's "fixed" payment jumps in the first or second year.

A borrower told this at application accepts it. A borrower who discovers it in month fourteen files a complaint — and he is not wrong to be angry.

2.4 Escrow analysis

Servicers perform a periodic analysis comparing what the account collected against what it paid and will pay, producing a statement showing the new payment and the disposition of any shortage or surplus.

FindingWhat follows
ShortageThe account has less than required. Repaid over a period, or in a lump sum at the borrower's option, plus a higher ongoing amount
DeficiencyThe account is negative
SurplusThe account holds more than required. Refunded or applied, per the rules

RESPA limits the cushion a servicer may maintain, and governs the analysis and the statements provided.

2.5 Escrow waivers

Some programs permit a borrower to waive escrow and pay taxes and insurance directly, sometimes for a fee or at a specified loan-to-value.

What a borrower must understand before choosing it: he becomes responsible for paying two large obligations on time; failure to pay taxes or maintain insurance is a default under the security instrument even where payments are current; and the lender may force-place insurance at a far higher cost, protecting only the lender.

2.6 What a licensee explains at origination

Four things, in writing, at application:

  1. The payment includes taxes and insurance, and PITI is the number that matters — not principal and interest.
  2. In California the tax figure will be based on a new assessment, not the seller's bill, so the estimate is an estimate.
  3. The payment can change when taxes or insurance change, even on a fixed-rate loan.
  4. A supplemental tax bill will arrive after closing for the difference between the old and new assessed value for the remainder of the year — and it is usually not covered by the escrow account.

The supplemental bill is the surprise nobody warns about, and it arrives months after closing for an amount the borrower did not budget.

2.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a fixed-rate payment changes, describe the California reassessment problem, describe an escrow analysis, and list what to explain at origination.

3. Payoff demand and reconveyance

3.1 What a payoff demand is

A statement from the lienholder of what satisfies the obligation, good through a stated date.

3.2 What it contains, and why it exceeds the statement balance

Component
Unpaid principal balance
Accrued interest to the payoff date
Any prepayment charge, where the note provides one and it is permitted
Late charges and other amounts owed under the note
Fees for preparing the demand and for reconveyance, as permitted
Any advances the lender made — force-placed insurance, taxes paid

Interest is paid in arrears, and it accrues to the day of payoff. That is why a payoff is routinely more than the last statement balance — and why a payoff good through the 15th is wrong if the loan funds on the 20th.

Explaining this at the listing or the application prevents an unhappy conversation at closing, and it is one of the small things separating a licensee who prepared the client from one who did not.

3.3 The per diem and the good-through date

A demand states a per diem so the amount can be computed for a later date.

$412,000 at 6.25%, 365-day basis: 412,000 × 0.0625 ÷ 365 = $70.55 per day. Five days beyond the good-through date adds $352.75.

Escrow obtains and updates the demand, and a demand that expires before disbursement must be refreshed — an ordinary cause of a delayed closing.

3.4 Reconveyance

When the obligation is satisfied, the beneficiary directs the trustee to reconvey, and a reconveyance is recorded releasing the deed of trust.

Payment of the debt does not clear the record. The recorded document does.

Timelines apply to the delivery and recording of the release after payoff, and a borrower whose loan was paid years ago and whose title still shows the lien has a real problem that requires a document — not a recollection.

A licensee encountering an unreleased deed of trust on a preliminary report should treat it as a requirement with a deadline, because obtaining a reconveyance from a lender that has merged, been acquired, or ceased to exist can take weeks.

3.5 Partial reconveyance

In a blanket loan securing multiple parcels, a release clause permits individual parcels to be released as they are sold, on the terms the instrument states — typically a release price. A partial reconveyance effects that release.

3.6 Payoff versus assumption versus subordination

Three different things a borrower may confuse:

ActionWhat happens
PayoffThe obligation is satisfied and the lien released by reconveyance
AssumptionThe loan continues with a new borrower, generally requiring consent — and the seller remains liable without a novation
SubordinationThe lien remains and moves to a lower priority position

3.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a payoff exceeds the statement balance, compute a per diem extension, and state what clears a satisfied lien from the record.

4. Delinquency and loss mitigation

4.1 What default is

A failure to perform an obligation under the note or the security instrument. Non-payment is the common form, and the instrument creates others: failure to pay taxes, failure to maintain insurance, waste, and unauthorized transfer triggering the alienation clause.

Acceleration is what makes default consequential. Without an acceleration clause a lender could pursue only missed payments; with one, the entire balance becomes due.

4.2 The loss mitigation options, in outline

OptionWhat it is
ReinstatementCuring the arrearage and permitted costs, restoring the loan
Repayment planCuring the arrearage over time alongside regular payments
ForbearanceA temporary reduction or suspension, with the arrearage addressed afterward
ModificationA permanent change to the loan's terms
Short saleA sale for less than the balance, with lienholder approval
Deed in lieu of foreclosureA voluntary conveyance to the lender

4.3 What each carries that borrowers do not expect

Forbearance is not forgiveness. The suspended amounts are still owed, and how they are repaid at the end — lump sum, spread over payments, deferred to maturity, or capitalized — is the question that matters, and it must be in writing.

A modification changes the loan permanently, and may extend the term, capitalize arrears, or change the rate. Its credit and tax consequences are questions for other professionals.

A short sale requires every lienholder's approval, and a junior lienholder can defeat one. Its deficiency treatment depends on what the lienholders agree to.

A deed in lieu does not automatically extinguish junior liens, which is a common reason a lender declines one.

4.4 The California servicer requirements

California imposes borrower-protective requirements on servicers in the residential foreclosure context, including obligations around borrower contact before a notice of default, a single point of contact, and constraints on pursuing foreclosure while a complete loss mitigation application is pending.

The specifics are legal. A licensee's role is to know these protections exist and to route the borrower to counsel and to a HUD-approved housing counselor — because a borrower who does not know a protection exists cannot assert it.

4.5 What a licensee may and may not tell a distressed borrower

May: explain what the options are called and what each generally does; explain that a notice has deadlines and that the borrower should read it; explain that borrower protections exist in California; refer to counsel, to a HUD-approved housing counselor, and to a tax professional, in writing; and help him gather documents his servicer requests.

May not:

  • Predict whether any option will be approved.
  • Tell him whether he owes a deficiency — a legal question with significant consequences.
  • Characterize the credit consequences of a short sale, modification, or foreclosure.
  • Advise on the tax treatment.
  • Tell him to stop paying, which is advice with irreversible consequences.
  • Tell him a short sale "won't hurt as much."

4.6 Foreclosure rescue fraud

Distressed situations attract schemes, and California regulates foreclosure consulting and equity purchase specifically.

The patterns to recognize:

PatternWhat it is
Advance fees for loan modificationCollecting up front to obtain a modification, which California restricts
Equity strippingA transfer that moves the property away from a distressed owner with equity
Sale-leaseback with a repurchase optionPresented as a rescue; frequently a transfer the owner cannot undo
"Stop paying your lender and pay us instead"Diverts payments and accelerates the foreclosure
A transfer of title as a condition of helpThe owner ends up without the property
Instructions to avoid contact with the servicerRemoves the borrower's access to the protections above

A licensee who sees one of these escalates to the broker and does not participate, however the arrangement is framed and however genuinely the borrower needs help.

The advance fee point connects to Lesson 08: a fee collected before services are rendered is an advance fee, and California restricts advance fees for loan modification services specifically.

4.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the loss mitigation options and what each carries, state what California servicer protections exist in outline, list what a licensee may not tell a distressed borrower, and recognize rescue fraud patterns.

5. Nonjudicial foreclosure orientation

5.1 The two paths

NonjudicialJudicial
MechanismThe trustee's power of saleA court action
SpeedFasterSlower
CostLowerHigher
Deficiency judgmentGenerally not availableMay be available, subject to limits
Post-sale redemptionGenerally noneA statutory redemption period may apply

The trade-off is the point. A beneficiary proceeding nonjudicially gets speed and gives up the deficiency. In California residential practice, nonjudicial predominates.

5.2 The sequence, in outline

The process is statutory and its details are legal. In outline:

  1. Default occurs, and the beneficiary elects to proceed.
  2. Borrower contact requirements are satisfied where they apply.
  3. A notice of default is recorded, beginning the statutory period.
  4. A reinstatement period runs.
  5. A notice of sale is recorded, published, posted, and mailed, after the applicable period.
  6. The trustee's sale occurs, and title passes by trustee's deed.

5.3 Reinstatement and redemption

The distinction borrowers misunderstand most, and getting it wrong can cost someone their home.

Reinstatement: for a period, the borrower may cure by paying the arrearage and permitted costs — not the accelerated balance — and the loan is restored.

Redemption before sale: after the reinstatement window closes, the route is generally paying the full accelerated amount.

Those are materially different sums, and a licensee who tells a borrower he can "catch up any time before the sale" has conflated them.

5.4 The sale

The property is sold at a public auction conducted by the trustee. The beneficiary may credit bid up to the amount owed; other bidders pay in the form required.

Title passes by trustee's deed, and a buyer takes what the sale conveys — generally without the protections of an ordinary transaction, and subject to whatever senior interests survive.

5.5 What happens to junior liens

A senior foreclosure generally extinguishes junior liens as claims against the property, while the underlying debts may survive as personal obligations — subject to California's deficiency restrictions.

That is why priority matters and why junior lienholders monitor senior loans. A second wiped out by a first's foreclosure has lost its security entirely, whatever the merits of the debt.

A broker who arranged a second for an investor should have explained that exposure before the money was placed.

5.6 Deficiency

A deficiency is the shortfall where sale proceeds do not satisfy the debt. California restricts deficiency judgments substantially:

  • Generally unavailable after a nonjudicial sale, whatever the loan type.
  • Restricted for purchase money loans in defined circumstances — protection connected to the loan having been used to acquire the property.
  • Subject to limits even in judicial foreclosure, including valuation-based constraints.

Whether a deficiency is available in a specific case is a legal question with significant consequences — and it is exactly what a distressed borrower asks. The answer is a referral, not a reassurance.

5.7 Occupants after a sale

A purchaser at a trustee's sale takes subject to whatever occupancy rights exist, and removing an occupant is a legal process with its own requirements — including protections for tenants in defined circumstances.

Self-help is prohibited. Changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities is unlawful regardless of who now holds title.

5.8 Bankruptcy

A borrower's bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay halting collection and foreclosure activity.

Continuing collection or foreclosure activity after a filing can carry serious consequences. A licensee's role is recognition and immediate escalation — the analysis is entirely legal.

5.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to compare the two paths, outline the nonjudicial sequence, distinguish reinstatement from redemption, and state what happens to junior liens and to a deficiency.

6. Borrower communication and complaint handling

6.1 Why communication is a compliance subject

Because most servicing disputes are not about substance. They are about what the borrower was told, by whom, and when — and because the frameworks impose defined procedures that informal handling defeats.

6.2 The defined procedures

RESPA and its implementing rules provide procedures under which a borrower may submit:

ProcedurePurpose
Notice of errorAsserting the servicer made an error
Request for informationSeeking information about the loan

Both carry acknowledgment and response obligations with deadlines, and both are defeated when a borrower's concern is handled as a phone conversation nobody recorded.

A licensee's role is to recognize these as defined procedures with deadlines, tell the borrower they exist, and route him correctly — not to resolve a servicing dispute informally on his behalf.

6.3 Communicating with a distressed borrower

What helps:

  • Answer promptly. Silence reads as evasion and is what escalates a matter.
  • Say plainly what you can and cannot do, and why.
  • Give him the specific next step — the procedure, the party, the deadline.
  • Put referrals in writing, so he has them after the call.
  • Record what was said and when.

What does not help:

  • Reassurance you cannot support. "It'll be fine" is the sentence that produces the complaint.
  • Predictions about approval, timing, credit, or outcome.
  • Speculation about what the servicer or the lender is doing.
  • Criticism of the servicer, which he will repeat.

6.4 The referrals, in writing

For a distressed borrower, three referrals belong in writing and early:

  1. Counsel — for the legal consequences: deficiency, remedies, rights, and the effect of any document he is asked to sign.
  2. A HUD-approved housing counselor — for the process, and because the service is available to him.
  3. A tax professional — for the tax consequences of a short sale, modification, or forgiveness.

Early and in writing matters because a borrower under pressure does not retain a spoken referral, and because most of these questions have deadlines attached.

6.5 Handling a complaint

When a borrower alleges mishandling:

  1. Acknowledge promptly.
  2. Notify the broker immediately.
  3. Preserve everything — the file, the disclosures as delivered, communications, drafts, texts, and the advertising as it ran.
  4. Respond factually, without admitting or denying liability before the file has been reviewed.
  5. Offer nothing on your own initiative — no fee reduction, no credit.
  6. Report to the carrier where the matter could become a claim.

Why the wrong responses are wrong: an immediate detailed defense commits a position before anyone reviewed the file — and in a mortgage file, what was disclosed and when can be checked within minutes; an apology accepting fault may be treated as an admission and can compromise coverage; a fee reduction commits the firm and rarely ends the matter; and handling it quietly compounds the original problem with a supervision failure.

Deleting a record that reflects poorly is far worse than the record. It is generally discoverable anyway, and it changes the subject from professional judgment to integrity.

6.6 When a regulator makes contact

Notify the broker immediately. Preserve records. Do not respond independently or informally.

Cooperation is expected. Improvised cooperation without review is where licensees make statements they cannot support.

6.7 What the file must show

  • Every communication material to a term or a decision, with dates.
  • What the borrower was told and by whom.
  • Referrals made, to whom, and the borrower's response.
  • Documents delivered, with evidence of what, to whom, when, and by what method.
  • Anything the licensee declined to do, and the escalation.
  • Corrections issued, with the originals retained.

6.8 What origination owes servicing

The lesson's closing point, and the reason this material sits in an origination course:

Most servicing complaints are origination failures arriving late.

Servicing complaintOrigination failure
"My fixed payment went up"PITI never explained; California reassessment never mentioned
"I got a supplemental tax bill nobody told me about"Not explained at application
"My payoff was thousands more than my balance"Accrued interest never explained
"Nobody told me the balance was due at maturity"Balloon presented without its number
"My payment tripled after the fifth year"Fully indexed rate and worst-case path never shown
"I was told I could just refinance"A prediction stated as a plan
"I didn't know I had to pay my own taxes"Escrow waiver consequences never explained

Every one of them is preventable in a conversation that costs nothing at application.

6.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the defined procedures, describe how to communicate with a distressed borrower, state the complaint sequence, and connect a servicing complaint to its origination failure.

Key terms

TermDefinition
ServicingAdministration of a loan after funding — collection, application, escrow, remittance, payoffs, communication, and delinquency management.
Owner, servicer, originatorThree roles that can be three different parties, any of which can change.
Partial paymentHandled per the note and applicable requirements. A borrower who assumes it cures a delinquency is frequently wrong.
Extra principalMay be applied to the next installment unless the borrower directs otherwise. He must say so.
Servicing transferRequires notice, with a period in which payments to the prior servicer are treated as timely. The note's terms do not change.
Escrow (impound) accountServicer-maintained funding for taxes and insurance, protective on both sides.
Why a "fixed" payment changesPrincipal and interest are fixed; the escrow portion moves with the taxes and insurance it funds.
California reassessment problemA buyer's taxes rest on a new base year value set on the change in ownership, not the seller's bill — so an estimate from the seller's figure can be low by a multiple, producing a first-year shortage.
Escrow analysisThe periodic comparison producing a new payment and the disposition of a shortage, deficiency, or surplus. RESPA limits the cushion.
Escrow waiverThe borrower pays taxes and insurance directly. Failure to do so is a default even where payments are current, and force-placed coverage is far more expensive and protects only the lender.
Supplemental tax billThe post-closing bill for the difference between old and new assessed value for the remainder of the year — usually not covered by the escrow account.
Payoff demandWhat satisfies the obligation through a stated date: principal, accrued interest, any permitted prepayment charge, late charges, permitted fees, and lender advances.
Per diemThe daily interest figure allowing a demand to be extended. A demand expiring before disbursement must be refreshed.
ReconveyanceThe recorded release. Payment does not clear the record; the document does, and obtaining one can take weeks.
Partial reconveyanceRelease of an individual parcel under a blanket loan's release clause.
AccelerationOn default, the entire balance becomes due. What makes default consequential.
ReinstatementCuring the arrearage and permitted costs within the statutory window, restoring the loan.
Redemption before salePaying the full accelerated amount after the reinstatement window closes. A materially different sum.
ForbearanceA temporary reduction or suspension. Not forgiveness — how the suspended amounts are repaid is the question that matters, and it belongs in writing.
ModificationA permanent change to terms, with credit and tax consequences for other professionals.
Short saleA sale below the balance requiring every lienholder's approval — and a junior lienholder can defeat one.
Deed in lieuA voluntary conveyance that does not automatically extinguish junior liens.
California servicer protectionsBorrower contact before a notice of default, a single point of contact, and constraints on foreclosing while a complete application is pending. Know they exist; route the specifics.
Foreclosure rescue patternsAdvance fees for modification, equity stripping, sale-leaseback with repurchase, "pay us instead," title transfer as a condition of help, and instructions to avoid the servicer. Escalate; never participate.
Nonjudicial foreclosureSale under the power of sale. Faster and cheaper; generally no deficiency and no post-sale redemption.
Credit bidThe beneficiary's bid up to the amount owed at the trustee's sale.
Trustee's deedThe instrument conveying title after the sale, generally without an ordinary transaction's protections.
Junior lien extinguishmentA senior foreclosure generally wipes out junior liens as claims against the property, while the debts may survive personally.
DeficiencyThe post-sale shortfall. Substantially restricted in California, and always a legal question.
Automatic stayThe halt on collection and foreclosure activity generally triggered by a bankruptcy filing. Recognize and escalate immediately.
Notice of error / request for informationDefined RESPA procedures with acknowledgment and response deadlines. Defeated by informal handling.
The origination debtMost servicing complaints are origination failures arriving late.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A former borrower calls his originator eighteen months after closing. He received a letter from a company he has never heard of, does not know where to send his payment, sent an extra $500 last month that "disappeared," and says his fixed-rate payment went up by $310.

Address each.

Solution. Four ordinary servicing facts, and one of them is an origination failure.

The letter is a servicing transfer. The owner, the servicer, and the originator can be three different parties, and any of them can change. RESPA requires notice and provides a period in which payments sent to the prior servicer are treated as timely — the framework anticipates exactly this confusion. The note's terms do not change on a transfer.

The $500 was probably applied to the next installment. Extra funds may be applied that way unless the borrower directs otherwise — he must say he wants it applied to principal. Telling a borrower that at closing is worth more than explaining it afterward.

The payment increase is not a contradiction. A fixed-rate loan has a fixed principal and interest payment; the total payment is not fixed, because the escrow portion moves with the taxes and insurance it funds. And where the account fell short, he repays the shortage on top of the higher ongoing amount.

What the licensee does: explain the mechanics, and direct him to his servicer with the specific procedure. What the licensee does not do: interpret the letter, contact the servicer without authority, or tell him whether anything is wrong with his account.

Problem 2

A California buyer's escrow estimate used the seller's current tax bill on a home held since 1997. In month fourteen the borrower receives an analysis showing a $4,900 shortage and a payment increase of $520. He also received a supplemental tax bill for $2,300 six months after closing that nobody mentioned.

Diagnose the failure.

Solution. Both are origination failures arriving late, and both were entirely preventable.

A buyer's property taxes rest on a new base year value established on the change in ownership — not on the seller's bill. On a property held since 1997 the seller's figure can be low by a multiple, and an escrow account funded from it is underfunded from the first month. The analysis then finds a shortage, and the borrower's "fixed" payment jumps.

The supplemental bill is the surprise nobody warns about. It captures the difference between the old and new assessed value for the remainder of the tax year, arrives months after closing, and is usually not covered by the escrow account.

What should have been said at application, in writing: the payment includes taxes and insurance and PITI is the number that matters; the California tax figure will be based on a new assessment, so the estimate is an estimate; the payment can change even on a fixed-rate loan; and a supplemental bill will arrive.

A borrower told this at application accepts it. A borrower who discovers it in month fourteen files a complaint — and he is not wrong to be angry.

Problem 3

A seller's payoff demand shows $418,730 where his last statement showed $409,900. The demand is good through the 15th; escrow now expects to disburse on the 20th. The demand states a per diem based on $412,000 at 6.25%. Separately, a borrower who paid off a loan in 2016 finds it still on title.

Explain the difference, compute the extension, and address the 2016 loan.

Solution. A payoff states what satisfies the obligation, not the balance. It contains the unpaid principal, accrued interest to the payoff date, any permitted prepayment charge, late charges and other amounts under the note, permitted preparation and reconveyance fees, and any advances the lender made — force-placed insurance or taxes paid.

Interest is paid in arrears and accrues to the day of payoff, which is the core of it.

Per diem: 412,000 × 0.0625 ÷ 365 = $70.55 per day. Five days beyond the good-through date adds $352.75 — and a demand that expires before disbursement must be refreshed, an ordinary cause of a delayed closing.

On the 2016 loan: payment of the debt does not clear the record. The recorded document does. He needs a reconveyance, and obtaining one from a lender that has merged, been acquired, or ceased to exist can take weeks — which is why an unreleased deed of trust on a preliminary report is a requirement with a deadline, not a formality.

Problem 4

A borrower two payments behind asks his originator whether he can still keep the house, whether he should stop paying so he "qualifies for help," whether a short sale will hurt less than a foreclosure, and whether he will owe the difference. The originator answers all four.

Correct each answer.

Solution. Three of the four questions may not be answered at all, and the second is dangerous.

On keeping the house: explain the mechanism. Reinstatement lets him cure by paying the arrearage and permitted costs — not the accelerated balance — within the statutory window. After it closes, the route is generally redemption before sale, paying the full accelerated amount. Those are materially different sums, and conflating them can cost someone their home.

"Should I stop paying?" — never advise this. It is advice with irreversible consequences, and it is also a foreclosure rescue pattern in its own right.

"Will a short sale hurt less?" — not a licensee's to characterize. Credit consequences are outside the license, a short sale requires every lienholder's approval and a junior lienholder can defeat one, and its deficiency treatment depends on what the lienholders agree to.

"Will I owe the difference?" — a legal question with significant consequences. California restricts deficiency judgments substantially — generally unavailable after a nonjudicial sale, and restricted for purchase money loans in defined circumstances — but whether one is available in his case is for counsel.

What the licensee does: explain that California servicer protections exist — borrower contact before a notice of default, a single point of contact, constraints on foreclosing while a complete application is pending — and refer in writing to counsel, a HUD-approved housing counselor, and a tax professional. A borrower who does not know a protection exists cannot assert it.

Problem 5

A company offers to help the borrower above: $3,500 up front to negotiate a modification, instructions to stop contacting his servicer and to send payments to the company instead, and a proposed sale-leaseback with an option to repurchase in two years. An originator is asked to refer clients to them for a fee.

Assess.

Solution. Every element is a recognized foreclosure rescue pattern, and the referral offer adds two more violations.

The $3,500 up front is an advance fee, and California restricts advance fees for loan modification services specifically. A fee collected before services are rendered is an advance fee whatever it is called.

"Stop contacting your servicer" removes his access to the protections — borrower contact requirements, the single point of contact, and the constraint on foreclosing while a complete application is pending. It is not incidental advice; it disables his defenses.

"Pay us instead" diverts payments and accelerates the foreclosure.

The sale-leaseback with a repurchase option is equity stripping — presented as a rescue, and frequently a transfer the owner cannot undo. California regulates foreclosure consulting and equity purchase specifically for this reason.

The referral fee is separately prohibited. A licensee may not accept anything of value for directing settlement business, and paying for referrals is prohibited whether or not it is disclosed.

What the originator does: decline, escalate to the broker, and do not participate — however the arrangement is framed and however genuinely the borrower needs help.

Problem 6

A borrower asks what happens at a trustee's sale, whether the second he also owes disappears, whether the buyer can change the locks on his tenant the same day, and whether his bankruptcy filing next week "stops everything."

Answer each.

Solution. Four different bodies of law, and two require immediate escalation.

The sale is a public auction conducted by the trustee. The beneficiary may credit bid up to the amount owed; other bidders pay in the form required. Title passes by trustee's deed, and a buyer takes what the sale conveys — generally without an ordinary transaction's protections and subject to whatever senior interests survive.

The second is extinguished as a claim against the property by a senior foreclosure — but the underlying debt may survive as a personal obligation, subject to California's deficiency restrictions. The junior lienholder has lost its security entirely, which is why juniors monitor senior loans and why a broker arranging a second should explain that exposure before the money is placed.

No, the buyer cannot change the locks. Removing an occupant is a legal process with its own requirements, including protections for tenants in defined circumstances — and self-help is prohibited regardless of who now holds title.

The bankruptcy is the item requiring immediate escalation. A filing generally triggers an automatic stay halting collection and foreclosure activity, and continuing activity after a filing can carry serious consequences. The analysis is entirely legal: recognize and escalate immediately.

Problem 7

A borrower emails his originator that his servicer misapplied three payments and will not respond. The originator calls the servicer on his behalf without authorization, tells the borrower the servicer is "completely incompetent," promises to "get it fixed," and takes no notes.

Identify every failure and state the correct handling.

Solution. Four failures, and the first defeated the borrower's actual remedy.

RESPA provides defined procedures — a notice of error and a request for information — each carrying acknowledgment and response obligations with deadlines. Handling the concern as an unrecorded phone call defeats the procedure that would have obligated the servicer to respond. The borrower's remedy was a written submission, and nobody told him it existed.

Contacting the servicer without authority is acting as though authorized when he is not.

"Completely incompetent" is criticism the borrower will repeat, and it commits the firm to a characterization it cannot support.

"I'll get it fixed" is reassurance he cannot support — the sentence that produces the complaint.

No notes means no record, and most servicing disputes are about what the borrower was told, by whom, and when.

Correct handling: answer promptly, because silence escalates; say plainly what he can and cannot do and why; give the specific next step — the procedure, the party, the deadline; put it in writing so the borrower has it after the call; and record what was said and when.

Problem 8

A firm reviews its servicing complaints for a year: "my fixed payment went up," "my payoff was thousands more than my balance," "nobody told me the balance was due at maturity," "my payment tripled after the fifth year," "I was told I could just refinance," and "I didn't know I had to pay my own taxes." The servicing manager says these are servicing problems.

Assess, and state where each originated.

Solution. They are not servicing problems. Every one is an origination failure arriving late.

"My fixed payment went up" — PITI was never explained, and in California the reassessment was never mentioned, so the escrow was underfunded from month one.

"My payoff was thousands more" — accrued interest and the other amounts under the note were never explained. Interest is paid in arrears and accrues to the day of payoff.

"Nobody told me the balance was due at maturity" — the balloon was presented without its number. The obligation was to state the amount due, when, and that the three paths all depend on conditions at maturity.

"My payment tripled after the fifth year" — the fully indexed rate and the worst-case path were never shown. The fully indexed rate is the fact most often omitted, and it tells a borrower whether his start rate is a discount that expires even if markets never move.

"I was told I could just refinance" — a prediction stated as a plan, and the single most damaging sentence in mortgage sales, because the borrower stops evaluating the risk.

"I didn't know I had to pay my own taxes" — the escrow waiver's consequences were never explained, including that failure to pay taxes or maintain insurance is a default even where payments are current and that force-placed coverage is far more expensive and protects only the lender.

Every one is preventable in a conversation that costs nothing at application — which is why this material sits in an origination course.

Chapter summary

Owner, servicer, and originator are three roles that can be three parties, and a servicing transfer requires notice, protects payments briefly, and changes none of the note's terms.

Extra principal must be directed, and a partial payment does not necessarily cure a delinquency.

A fixed-rate loan has a fixed principal and interest payment, not a fixed total — and in California the reassessment problem makes a first-year escrow shortage close to predictable when the estimate used the seller's bill.
